Scored against this map it is almost entirely out of scope, and that is the finding rather than a gap in the research: sixty-four of the eighty-nine rows describe machinery Cosmos does not have, because it has no scene, no objects, no transforms, no materials, no lights and no physics engine, and its own limitation notice says so, stating that the model lacks an explicit physics simulator and that geometry, object permanence and contact dynamics are only approximated. What it does have that this map can see is narrow and worth naming: a camera it can be driven by and can estimate, in nine numbers a frame; a time-sampled action record; scene text as a measured concern; and a guardrail on generation. Four things a standards audience should carry away. The only structured description of a scene in the whole platform is the JSON prompt handed to the generator, and every field in it is prose, so the interchange artefact of a world model is a paragraph in slots. The action trajectory, which is the one numeric record Cosmos both reads and writes, cannot be read by anything else: its columns mean whatever the named embodiment says they mean, its values are normalised by figures taken from the training set, and decoding them needs a projection matrix that lives inside the model. Nothing marks a Cosmos output as generated, though a safety classifier and a face blur do run over the frames. And nothing anywhere expresses a position on the Earth, in a platform trained on ten thousand hours of driving. Two traps for anyone planning on this. The autoencoder in the generation path is not NVIDIA's: it is taken from the Wan2.2 model, published by Wan-AI under Apache 2.0, and kept frozen, so a separately owned component sits inside what an OpenMDW notice appears to cover. And the platform's own publications already contradict each other: the documentation site still gives Apache 2.0 and the NVIDIA Open Model License where the repository, the model card and the technical report all give OpenMDW-1.1, and says the guardrail cannot be disabled where the shipped code documents four ways to disable it.

subjects.name: Tencent Hunyuan World 2.0
subjects.summary: Tencent's HY-World 2.0, which the map lists as Hunyuan World 2.0, is a model that turns a sentence, a photograph, a set of photographs or a video into a three-dimensional place, and its whole argument is that the place should be a file rather than a film: where a video world model draws the next frame forever, this one runs once and hands you Gaussian splats, a fused mesh and a point cloud that an ordinary engine can open. Two halves sit in one repository. Reconstruction takes pictures and returns depth, surface normals, camera poses, intrinsics, points and splats in a single pass, and will take known cameras or depth as a prior. Generation makes a 360-degree panorama, parses it into a mesh and a navigation mesh, has a vision-language model plan collision-free camera routes through it, generates the views those routes would see, and fits a splat scene to the result. It is genuinely open in the sense that weights, code and a detailed report are published, and genuinely not open source: the licence excludes the European Union, the United Kingdom and South Korea, forbids using the outputs to improve any other model, and requires a separate grant above a million monthly users. For a standards audience the important part is what does not come out. Everything it writes is somebody else's format used as-is — splat and mesh PLY, the compressed SPZ form, a COLMAP model, a camera JSON — with no scene graph, no object identity, no units, no licence field, no signature and no statement that the place was manufactured rather than photographed. There is no specification of the output and no conformance test, and the documentation chapter for the generation pipeline reads coming soon. Two claims in the technical report describe a rendering platform called WorldLens, with image-based lighting, collision and character control; it is not in the repository or the open-source plan, so the interactive, lit, walkable world the report shows cannot be reproduced from the release, and the rows here are scored on what was published.

subjects.name: World Labs Marble
subjects.summary: Marble is World Labs' hosted generative world model and the product built on it: give it a sentence, one or several photographs, a 360 panorama, a short video or a coarse block-out you draw in its own modelling tool, and about five minutes later you get back a three-dimensional place you can walk around in a browser. The place is stored as several million three-dimensional Gaussian splats, which the vendor calls its highest-fidelity form, and it can also be handed over as a coarse mesh for physics, as two higher-quality meshes for drawing, as a panorama, or as a recorded video. It can be edited by describing the change, grown past its original edges, varied by changing a seed, and several worlds can be placed beside one another into a larger one. Everything else a shared world needs is absent by design: no session, no participants, no identity, no rules, no sound and no position on the Earth, which is why fifty-eight of the eighty-nine rows here are honestly out of scope. Two traps matter for a standards audience. The first is that Marble writes an open splat format in a coordinate frame that format does not expect, corrects for it in its own viewer, and describes the frame three different ways across three of its own pages - so a conforming reader gets an upside-down world. The second is that the words reconstruct, generate and simulate are used together in the vendor's own framing, while what actually ships simulates nothing: it produces a static asset for someone else's engine to run, and the vendor's own writing places interactivity in the future.

geo.tiles: This is the whole point of the standard, and it says so in its own abstract.
This document describes the specification for 3D Tiles, an open standard for streaming massive heterogeneous 3D geospatial datasets.
render.lod: Each tile carries an error measured in metres, and a rule saying whether children replace the parent or add to it. That pair is what lets a client decide what to draw and what to fetch next.
Permitted refinement types are replacement ( "REPLACE" ) and additive ( "ADD" ).
geo.crs: Right-handed with the vertical axis up for local frames, usually an Earth-centred Earth-fixed frame at the root, and the frame may be named explicitly through a metadata property carrying a geodetic dataset identifier. Note the up axis differs from the common asset format's.
3D Tiles uses a right-handed Cartesian coordinate system; that is, the cross product of x and y yields z . 3D Tiles defines the z axis as up for local Cartesian coordinate systems.
scene.units: Fixed at metres, with no way for a tileset to declare anything else. This matches the common asset format and removes one class of scale error.
The unit for all linear distances is meters. All angles are in radians.
render.volumetric: Point clouds are a named content type in the scope, and the styling language can size individual points and read their position, colour and normal. The dedicated point cloud tile format is deprecated in this version in favour of point primitives in the common asset format. Voxels are not here; they are listed as a feature of the in-development next version.

A Point Cloud is a collection of points that may be styled like other features. In addition to evaluating a point's color and show properties, a Point Cloud style may evaluate pointSize , or the size of each point in pixels.
deliver.version: Every tileset must state the version it targets, and that version fixes both the schema and the permitted tile formats. A second optional field lets a publisher version their own data separately, which is used to defeat caches.
The 3D Tiles version. The version defines the JSON schema for the tileset JSON and the base set of tile formats.
scene.container: It defines the container for the tree, not for the model. Since this version the model payload is simply the common asset format, and the four original tile formats are deprecated and may be removed. The missing half is a real interoperability cost: an implementation must apply an up-axis correction to every tile, which the specification spells out as a step in the transform chain.
The primary tile format in 3D Tiles 1.1 is the glTF Tile Format . It is built on glTF 2.0
These formats were deprecated in 3D Tiles 1.1 and may be removed in a future version of 3D Tiles.
scene.instancing: Repeated objects such as trees and signs are now carried by a ratified extension of the common asset format rather than by this standard's own instanced tile format, which is deprecated.
This extension is specfically designed to enable GPU instancing, rendering many copies of a single mesh at once using a small number of draw calls.
scene.compose: A tile's content may be another tileset, so datasets nest, and one tile may hold several contents that can be grouped and given metadata. What is missing is override: nothing lets one source change a value inside another, and there is no layering with a strength order.
refers to the tile's content in one of the tile formats that are defined in the Tile format specifications ), or another tileset JSON to create a tileset of tilesets
deliver.cdn: Implicit tiling lets a client work out a tile's address by arithmetic from a template rather than reading a manifest, which is what makes planet-scale datasets fetchable at all. What is missing is everything about delivery itself: no caching rules, no compression negotiation, no failure or retry behaviour.
logic.script: There is a real expression language, but only for appearance: it decides whether a feature is shown, what colour it is and how big a point is drawn. It cannot change state, move anything or respond to input, and comments are not supported.
3D Tiles includes concise declarative styling defined with JSON and expressions written in a small subset of JavaScript augmented for styling.
deliver.conformance: There is a conformance clause, and it is unusually candid about its own limits: conformance is measured against one annex of objects and properties, and the machine-readable schema covers only part of that. There are no conformance classes and no test suite in the document.
Conformance is relative to these elements and as partly expressed via the associated 3D Tiles JSON Schema .
geo.pose: A tile carries a four-by-four transform to its parent's frame and the root sits in an Earth-fixed frame, so position and orientation against the Earth are expressible. What is missing is a shared record: this is a matrix in a tileset file, not a portable pose, and the specification never once mentions the pose standard published by the same consortium. Two standards from one body with no link between them is the kind of thing a working group can fix.
An additional tile transform may be applied to transform a tile's local coordinate system to the parent tile's coordinate system.
render.splat: The published version does not mention splats or radiance fields anywhere. The specification's own repository lists gaussian splatting as a feature of a next version that is in development and not published, and that version is built on a newer version of the common asset format that is itself not ratified.
3D Tiles 2.0 uses glTF 2.1, together with a set of geospatial extensions, as the foundation for spatial subdivision.
logic.sandbox: A standard whose whole job is fetching content from remote servers and evaluating expressions in it states outright that no security considerations have been made. Quote that sentence rather than paraphrasing it; it is short, it is in the published text, and it will be checked.
No security considerations have been made for this document.
geo.indoor: Building models are named as content it can carry, but it never describes the inside of a building: no rooms, no doors, no connections between spaces. That belongs to the indoor and building information standards.
3D Tiles does not define explicit rules for visualization of the content; a client may visualize 3D Tiles data however it sees fit.
physics.rigid: A delivery structure for geographic data. It never describes how anything moves.
It defines a hierarchical data structure and a set of tile formats which deliver renderable content.
audio.spatial: Nothing about sound. The scope is renderable geometry and its metadata.
It defines a hierarchical data structure and a set of tile formats which deliver renderable content.
net.replication: A one-way stream from a server to a viewer. There are no sessions, no participants and no shared state; a time-varying form of tiles is listed as future work in the in-development next version.
3D Tiles is designed for streaming and rendering massive 3D geospatial content such as Photogrammetry, 3D Buildings, BIM/CAD, Instanced Features, and Point Clouds.
capture.worldgen: OGC 3D Tiles is a hierarchical structure and a set of tile formats for streaming large geospatial content, and making a whole three-dimensional place from a description or a picture is not an act it performs or specifies.
It defines a hierarchical data structure and a set of tile formats which deliver renderable content.
capture.sim-learned: OGC 3D Tiles is a hierarchical structure and a set of tile formats for streaming large geospatial content, and it never continues a world under a viewer's actions from a learned model; there is no such model here.
It defines a hierarchical data structure and a set of tile formats which deliver renderable content.
capture.photogrammetry: Photogrammetry is named in the scope as a thing this standard delivers, not a thing it performs. It takes the model a photogrammetry pipeline already produced and tiles it; nothing here turns photographs into geometry.
3D Tiles is designed for streaming and rendering massive 3D geospatial content such as Photogrammetry, 3D Buildings, BIM/CAD, Instanced Features, and Point Clouds.
capture.splat-format: The published version does not mention splats or radiance fields anywhere. The specification's own repository lists Gaussian splatting as a feature of a next version that is in development and unpublished, built on a glTF edition that is itself not final.
3D Tiles 2.0 uses glTF 2.1, together with a set of geospatial extensions, as the foundation for spatial subdivision.
capture.stream: This is the row 3D Tiles owns. Photogrammetry and point clouds are named in its own statement of what it is for; a tile carries a geometric error in metres and a refinement rule saying whether children replace the parent or add to it, which is exactly the pair a client needs to decide what to fetch next and what to draw now. A captured scene delivered this way starts before it has all arrived.
3D Tiles is designed for streaming and rendering massive 3D geospatial content such as Photogrammetry, 3D Buildings, BIM/CAD, Instanced Features, and Point Clouds.
This document describes the specification for 3D Tiles, an open standard for streaming massive heterogeneous 3D geospatial datasets.
Permitted refinement types are replacement ( "REPLACE" ) and additive ( "ADD" ).
capture.volumetric-video: OGC 3D Tiles is a hierarchical structure and a set of tile formats for streaming large geospatial content, and it carries no captured, time-varying three-dimensional scene as media, and no camera calibration or mask metadata for one.
It defines a hierarchical data structure and a set of tile formats which deliver renderable content.
capture.point-cloud: Point clouds are a named content type with their own styling, and points can be sized and read for position, colour and normal. The encoding itself is not defined here: the dedicated point tile format is deprecated in this version in favour of point primitives in glTF, so how the points are compressed is that format's answer, not this one's.

A Point Cloud is a collection of points that may be styled like other features. In addition to evaluating a point's color and show properties, a Point Cloud style may evaluate pointSize , or the size of each point in pixels.
capture.multiview-depth: OGC 3D Tiles is a hierarchical structure and a set of tile formats for streaming large geospatial content, and it carries no set of calibrated camera views with per-pixel depth, and no intrinsics or extrinsics to reproject them.
It defines a hierarchical data structure and a set of tile formats which deliver renderable content.
capture.novel-view: OGC 3D Tiles is a hierarchical structure and a set of tile formats for streaming large geospatial content, and it produces no image from a viewing position that no capture camera occupied.
It defines a hierarchical data structure and a set of tile formats which deliver renderable content.
capture.4d: A tileset is one state of a place. Time-varying tiles are listed as future work in the in-development next version, so a capture that moves has to be handed over as separate tilesets with nothing stating the rate.
3D Tiles 2.0 uses glTF 2.1, together with a set of geospatial extensions, as the foundation for spatial subdivision.
capture.relight: OGC 3D Tiles is a hierarchical structure and a set of tile formats for streaming large geospatial content, and it holds no captured scene that could be made to answer the light of the place it lands in.
It defines a hierarchical data structure and a set of tile formats which deliver renderable content.
capture.edit: OGC 3D Tiles is a hierarchical structure and a set of tile formats for streaming large geospatial content, and there is no capture here to crop, delete from or recolour, and no export for such an edit to survive.
It defines a hierarchical data structure and a set of tile formats which deliver renderable content.
capture.gen-edit: OGC 3D Tiles is a hierarchical structure and a set of tile formats for streaming large geospatial content, and there is no generated world here to change by describing the change or pointing at a region.
It defines a hierarchical data structure and a set of tile formats which deliver renderable content.
capture.gen-control: OGC 3D Tiles is a hierarchical structure and a set of tile formats for streaming large geospatial content, and nothing here accepts a specification of a world that should be made.
It defines a hierarchical data structure and a set of tile formats which deliver renderable content.
capture.derived-asset: OGC 3D Tiles is a hierarchical structure and a set of tile formats for streaming large geospatial content, and it derives no collision mesh, drawing mesh, panorama or video from a splat or radiance-field world.
It defines a hierarchical data structure and a set of tile formats which deliver renderable content.
capture.action-io: OGC 3D Tiles is a hierarchical structure and a set of tile formats for streaming large geospatial content, and it carries no agent's actions in or out as time-sampled data with an embodiment, a frame and units.
It defines a hierarchical data structure and a set of tile formats which deliver renderable content.
capture.panorama: OGC 3D Tiles is a hierarchical structure and a set of tile formats for streaming large geospatial content, and it carries no full 360-degree view of a place as an image with its projection stated.
It defines a hierarchical data structure and a set of tile formats which deliver renderable content.
sense.mesh: An open standard for streaming large heterogeneous 3D geospatial datasets. The geometry it delivers was prepared and tiled ahead of time; it is not a device's live reading of the room it is in.
This document describes the specification for 3D Tiles, an open standard for streaming massive heterogeneous 3D geospatial datasets.
sense.semantics: Its metadata describes features in prepared tiles. There is no channel for classes assigned to real surfaces during a session.
This document describes the specification for 3D Tiles, an open standard for streaming massive heterogeneous 3D geospatial datasets.
sense.depth: No depth image of the real world is carried; the format delivers renderable tiles.
This document describes the specification for 3D Tiles, an open standard for streaming massive heterogeneous 3D geospatial datasets.
sense.occlusion: The standard deliberately leaves visualisation to the client, so composing tiles against a real view is outside it.
This document describes the specification for 3D Tiles, an open standard for streaming massive heterogeneous 3D geospatial datasets.
render.passthrough: 3D Tiles is for streaming and rendering geospatial content, and it leaves visualization to the client. Whether a client blends its drawing with a camera view of the room is therefore the client's own presentation and appears nowhere in the standard.
3D Tiles is designed for streaming and rendering massive 3D geospatial content such as Photogrammetry, 3D Buildings, BIM/CAD, Instanced Features, and Point Clouds.
3D Tiles does not define explicit rules for visualization of the content; a client may visualize 3D Tiles data however it sees fit.
input.face: The standard is for streaming and rendering geospatial content, so it has no input model and reads nothing about the person looking at it.
3D Tiles is designed for streaming and rendering massive 3D geospatial content such as Photogrammetry, 3D Buildings, BIM/CAD, Instanced Features, and Point Clouds.
scene.navmesh: Tiles carry renderable content and metadata under bounding volumes, with a subdivision scheme and geometric error to decide what to draw. Nothing in the tileset says which surface is walkable, where the bounds of a body's movement are, or where a visitor arrives — a client that wants to walk a city has to work that out from the geometry.

In 3D Tiles, a subset of a tileset containing a reference to renderable content and the metadata, such as the content's bounding volume, which is used by a client to determine if the content is rendered.
logic.namespace: The standard is for streaming and rendering geospatial content, so a tileset publishes geometry, not units of logic; its declarative styling is expressions evaluated in place, under no published name.
3D Tiles is designed for streaming and rendering massive 3D geospatial content such as Photogrammetry, 3D Buildings, BIM/CAD, Instanced Features, and Point Clouds.
deliver.moderation: The standard is for streaming and rendering geospatial content: it defines how tiles are structured and fetched, with no publishing service where a review could stand and no field saying what review content has had.
3D Tiles is designed for streaming and rendering massive 3D geospatial content such as Photogrammetry, 3D Buildings, BIM/CAD, Instanced Features, and Point Clouds.
geo.map-align: Every tile may carry a 4x4 affine transform that puts its local coordinates into its parent's, and a root tileset is commonly placed in an Earth-centred frame, so a building inside a city inside the Earth all line up. That is alignment inside one tree; the standard declares no map of a place with a version and a lifecycle, and publishes no transform relating its tileset to a second map of the same place.

The transform property is a 4×4 affine transformation matrix, stored in column-major order, that transforms from the tile's local coordinate system to the parent tile's coordinate system—​or the tileset's coordinate system in the case of the root tile.
A tileset's global coordinate system will often be in a WGS 84 Earth-centered, Earth-fixed (ECEF) reference frame ( EPSG 4978 ), but it doesn't have to be
geo.coverage: Coverage is the backbone of the format. Every tile declares a bounding volume that completely encloses its content, and the region form states those bounds in a named geographic frame — latitude, longitude and height in EPSG 4979 — so a client can test whether a tileset is relevant where it is standing before fetching anything.
The region bounding volume specifies bounds using a geographic coordinate system (latitude, longitude, height), specifically, EPSG 4979 .
Each tile has a bounding volume , an object defining a spatial extent completely enclosing its content.

scene.graph: Tiles form a tree with parent-relative transforms, and each glTF payload has its own node hierarchy. The tree is a spatial subdivision for streaming rather than authored relationships between objects, and it has no links beyond parent and child.
In 3D Tiles, a tileset is a set of tiles organized in a spatial data structure, the tree .

The transformation from each tile’s local coordinate system to the tileset’s global coordinate system is computed by a top-down traversal of the tileset and by post-multiplying a child’s transform with its parent’s transform like a traditional scene graph or node hierarchy in computer graphics.
scene.transform: Fixed as right-handed with z up, and tile transforms compose top-down by matrix multiplication. The glTF payload is y up, so a correction is applied at runtime on every tile.
3D Tiles uses a right-handed Cartesian coordinate system; that is, the cross product of x and y yields z .
3D Tiles defines the z axis as up for local Cartesian coordinate systems.
glTF defines its own node hierarchy and uses a y -up coordinate system.
scene.geometry: Mesh encoding is that of the glTF payload; the standard names three glTF extensions for geometry compression: KHR_mesh_quantization, EXT_meshopt_compression and KHR_draco_mesh_compression.
glTF has several extensions for geometry and texture compression.
scene.texture: Image encoding is that of the glTF payload; the standard names one glTF extension for texture compression, KHR_texture_basisu.
glTF has several extensions for geometry and texture compression.
scene.material-x: Materials are carried only as the glTF payload's own material definitions; the standard names no cross-renderer material exchange, and says a client may draw the content however it sees fit, so appearance is not guaranteed to match between renderers.
glTF provides flexibility for a wide range of mesh and material configurations, and is well suited for photogrammetry as well as stylized 3D models.
3D Tiles does not define explicit rules for visualization of the content; a client may visualize 3D Tiles data however it sees fit.

scene.transform: The family disagrees with itself about the coordinate frame. scene.container: This is what the subject mostly is. Five containers are in daily use for captured splat scenes: uncompressed PLY as the source and interchange format, SOG as a quantised bundle of WebP images plus a metadata file, Streamed SOG as a chunked multi-detail directory, Niantic's SPZ as a compressed single file, and binary glTF through the ratified Khronos extension. The reference converter reads eight input formats and writes eleven, which is how the ecosystem actually moves data. A sixth family is on its way from a different direction: MPEG has taken a Gaussian splat profile of its video-based point cloud coding to committee draft stage, so splats will shortly have containers written by a body that had no hand in the five above.

scene.animation: This is the subject's sore point. The research side models time properly: one line of work predicts per-frame deformations of a shared set of Gaussians from a compact spatio-temporal field, another optimises genuinely four-dimensional primitives that rotate in space and time with time-evolving colour, a third adds temporal opacity and parametric motion to each primitive. None of that reaches the wire. No shipping splat format has a time axis: the interchange used in practice is a numbered sequence of complete still frames, the reference 4D implementation exports exactly that, and the runtime format that would compress a sequence is, in the maintainer's own published design note, still to be defined; the same note records that a sequence can be played but not edited. Runtimes leave a programmable hole where a four-dimensional format would go, so every vendor with moving splat content fills it privately.

To start building, you'll use the Android XR SDK, which includes all the tools and libraries that you need to build incredible experiences for a growing set of XR devices, including XR headsets, wired XR glasses, audio glasses, and display glasses.

Searched the Android XR developer guides (developer.android.com/develop/xr and the Jetpack XR SDK, OpenXR, Unity, Godot and Unreal guides linked from it, 227 pages with the Jetpack XR package pages for arcore, scenecore, runtime, compose, projected and glimmer and their class lists) and the ARCore developer guides and API references for Android (Java and C), iOS and Unity (developers.google.com/ar, 482 pages) for physics, collision, collide, rigid body, gravity, joint, simulation, soft body, cloth, ragdoll, friction, restitution and determinism on 2026-10-20; found no soft body, cloth or ragdoll term anywhere in the guides or package listings. The individual class pages of the Jetpack XR reference were not opened, so the absence is not fully checked.

geo.pose: This is the platform's strongest row. The Geospatial interface returns the device's pose against the Earth — latitude, longitude, altitude and an orientation — with an accuracy estimate for each, and any pose in the local session can be converted to and from that Earth-referenced form. Note the frame: the orientation is expressed east, up and south, which is Google's own convention and not the one the Open Geospatial Consortium's pose standard uses, and there is no exchange encoding for it at all.

geo.crs: One reference system, fixed, with a known seam. Horizontal position follows the world geodetic system of 1984 and altitude is metres above that ellipsoid, so ground level is not zero; the documentation itself tells developers to convert an elevation obtained from Google's own maps interface, which uses a gravity-based geoid, before comparing it. There is no way to state or negotiate a different reference system.

geo.anchor-local: Fixing content to a place on one device is the core of both halves. On a phone an anchor holds a pose steady as tracking is refitted, and content can also be pinned to a printed image, with up to twenty tracked at once out of a database of up to a thousand. On a headset an anchor can be created free-standing or attached to a tracked plane, and it can be persisted into the app's own private storage under an identifier and reloaded in a later session.

geo.anchor-shared: Shared across devices on phones, and not on headsets — the same product name covers two different capabilities. A Cloud Anchor uploads a feature map to Google's endpoint, returns an identifier, and lets an Android or an Apple device in the same room resolve the same place later, with an expiry time that can be extended up to a stated maximum. On Android XR there is no cloud anchor: persistence is to the app's private storage, and the sharing extension shares an anchor with other applications running on the same device.

geo.vps: Visual positioning is the reason this subject belongs on the map. Camera pixels are matched against a localization model built from more than fifteen years of Street View imagery, combined into a global point cloud of trillions of points, and the result is a device pose far better than satellite positioning alone. It is a service, not a specification, and the terms of use are part of the capability: you cannot point it at another provider's map, the additional terms forbid building anything that re-creates the features of another Google product, and they bar both the visual positioning interface and cloud anchors from services directed at children.

render.volumetric: Captured scenes reach the screen as splats, and stereoscopic and Apple Immersive Video play through a video component; a point cloud is drawn only inside the object-capture scanning view. There is no general voxel or point-cloud renderer and no volumetric video codec in the frameworks themselves.
Use a Gaussian splat component to display volumetric imagery captured from real environments, coalesced into 3D Gaussian splats (3DGS).
A component that supports general video-playback experience with an AV player.
Apple Developer Documentation: Immersive Media Support
Immersive Media Support enables you to create custom workflows for processing Apple Immersive Video (AIV).
render.text: Text becomes an extruded mesh through a generator on the mesh resource, and USD assets can carry text through Apple's preliminary text schema.
Generates a 3D mesh for rendering static text.
Apple Developer Documentation: OpenUSD schemas for AR
Annotate the environment by displaying text.
render.camera: In an AR session the device camera is the viewpoint; outside one, a perspective camera entity sets it, and RealityRenderer takes an explicit active camera.
During an AR session, RealityKit automatically uses the device’s camera to define the perspective from which to render the scene.
scene.graph: The scene is an entity tree with components attached; Reality Composer Pro authors the same entity-component-system model that the runtime executes.
An element of a RealityKit scene to which you attach components that provide appearance and behavior characteristics for the entity.
Apple Developer Documentation: Reality Composer Pro
Reality Composer Pro is a 3D content creation platform backed by an Entity Component System (ECS).
scene.transform: Every entity carries a transform of scale, rotation as a unit quaternion, and translation. The frame is Y-up and right-handed, which matches OpenUSD and glTF and differs from the left-handed engines.
Apple Developer Documentation: Creating USD files for Apple devices
RealityKit uses Y-up orientation and meters as its unit scale.
A component that defines the scale, rotation, and translation of an entity.

The coordinate system is right-handed—the positive x direction points to the viewer’s right (that is, the face’s own left), the positive y direction points up (relative to the face itself, not to the world), and the positive z direction points outward from the face (toward the viewer).
scene.container: The container is OpenUSD: the loader reads .usd, .usda, .usdc, .usdz and Apple's own .reality file. RealityKit itself only loads; authoring USD is USDKit's job, and Object Capture and RoomPlan are the parts of the platform that write it.

You can load USD files (.usd, .usda, .usdc, .usdz) and Reality files (.reality) this way.
USD is also Apple’s format of choice for 3D Content, including 3D content used for Augmented Reality.
USDKit is the Swift API for authoring, composing, and manipulating Universal Scene Description (USD) content.
scene.geometry: Geometry arrives as USD meshes, in text or binary form; procedural primitives, extruded paths and a low-level mesh with an app-defined vertex layout are all available at runtime.
Apple Developer Documentation: Creating USD files for Apple devices
USDC is a binary format. It is more compact and faster to load than USDA, making it the preferred format for geometry-heavy assets and large scenes.
A high-level representation of a collection of vertices and edges that define a shape.
A container for vertex data that you can use to create and update meshes using your own format.
scene.texture: Textures load into GPU-resident resources with optional ASTC compression, and the USDZ archive is limited to four image encodings.
Apple Developer Documentation: Creating USD files for Apple devices
USD files may use a wide range of texture formats, however USDZ files may only include JPEG, PNG, EXR, and AVIF.
A texture resource holds pixel data accessible by the GPU, organized as an image, a cube of images, an array of images, or a 3D image (volume texture).
Compression allows varying levels of memory usage gains at the cost of image-quality reduction.
scene.material-x: MaterialX comes in, but not without loss. A shader-graph material can be built straight from MaterialX data, and Apple publishes the exact places RealityKit falls short of the specification: one packed texture per material, two UV sets, and only the first texture transform in a material is honoured.
Apple Developer Documentation: Validating feature support for USD files
RealityKit supports only a single packed texture per material.
Apple Developer Documentation: Validating feature support for USD files
A material that comes from a shader graph in a Reality Composer Pro project, or a MaterialX shader.
scene.animation: Animation resources travel inside the asset file and are played, sequenced, grouped and looped at runtime; Reality Composer Pro adds multi-track sequences and an animation graph.
Apple Developer Documentation: Reality Composer Pro

Reality Composer Pro includes editors and workflows for designing materials with Shader Graph, building visual scripts with Script Graph, authoring GPU-driven simulations with Compute Graph, defining character behaviors with Animation Graphs, and editing skeletons.
Animation resources come bundled with an entity when you load the entity from a file.
scene.skeleton: A mesh carries a joint hierarchy and per-vertex joint influences, and the runtime exposes named skeletal poses for reading and writing. One constraint on the way in: Apple asks authors to merge several rigs into a single joint hierarchy before export.

Before exporting models with multiple skeletons to a USD file, merge all the skeletons into a single joint or bone hierarchy.
A skeleton consists of a hierarchy of joints.
A component that exposes the collection of named animation skeletal poses.
scene.morph: Blend shape weights are a component whose named weight sets can be read and written at runtime.
A component that provides access to the current weights associated with all blend shape meshes on an entity.
scene.instancing: A component performs GPU instancing over one entity's model, and instancing of mesh and texture data survives import from USD.

RealityKit supports instancing of mesh and texture data from imported USD files.
A component that performs GPU instancing on the model of the same entity.
scene.compose: This is the strongest interchange story in the subject. Composition is USD's: files reference other files and override what they reference, USDKit exposes layers and stages to Swift, and a USD stage can be rendered straight into an entity hierarchy.
USD files can reference other USD files, and even override the contents of referenced USD files, allowing a completely non-destructive workflow.
Because multiple layers can define or override the same primitive, the stage composes the contributions from each layer to produce the final scene.
A component that renders a USD stage as RealityKit entities.
scene.units: One unit is one metre, and the physics simulation states the same unit independently.

RealityKit uses Y-up orientation and meters as its unit scale.
Each physics simulation component uses meters as its unit of distance

avatar.body: The platform has an avatar — the spatial Persona a person appears as in a shared session — but the app never sees it. The system places and renders Personas; there is no portable body description, no file, and no app-side representation to move anywhere else.

A person who participates in SharePlay activities on Apple Vision Pro has the option to participate using their spatial Persona.

The system arranges spatial Personas around the activity content, giving each person a clear view of the content and each other.
avatar.skeleton: ARKit publishes one named joint hierarchy for tracked human bodies, with a stated neutral height, and a character has to be rigged to it to be driven. It is Apple's own list rather than an agreed interchange skeleton, and it exists for body tracking, not for carrying an avatar between worlds.
ARKit names particular joints that are crucial to body tracking.
The default height of this skeleton is 1.66 meters.
avatar.expression: ARKit's named blend-shape coefficients for the face are the closest thing the industry has to a shared expression vocabulary, and many other systems copy the names. They are a tracking output on iOS front-camera sessions, not a format, and Apple defines no viseme set for speech.
You can use blend shape coefficients to animate 2D or 3D content, such as a character or avatar, in ways that follow the user’s facial expressions.
ARKit provides many blend shape coefficients, resulting in a detailed model of a facial expression
avatar.retarget: A body-tracked entity plays a live person's motion on a virtual character, and a full-body inverse kinematics solver adapts a pose procedurally. Both require the character to be rigged to Apple's skeleton; there is no general mapping between two arbitrary rigs.
An entity used to animate a virtual character in an AR scene by tracking a real person.
A component that allows you to procedurally animate a skeletal model using a full body inverse kinematics solver.
avatar.lod: RealityKit documents a generic LevelOfDetailComponent (introduced in OS 27) that shows or hides child entities by camera distance, screen area or resolution metric. It is not avatar-specific: no reduced avatar representation, crowd rule or avatar profile is defined, and an exchange format for avatar detail levels is not described. The component allows entities to automatically show/hide child entities based on viewing conditions, reducing rendering complexity for distant or small objects.

physics.rigid: A physics body component gives an entity mass and Newtonian response, and a separate motion component carries linear and angular velocity; a simulation component sets gravity and solver iterations for a subtree.
A component that controls localized physics simulations.
A component that defines an entity’s behavior in physics body simulations.
A component that controls the motion of the body in physics simulations.
physics.collision: Collision shapes are a separate component from the visible mesh and also serve queries, ray casts and convex shape casts; box, convex mesh and triangle mesh shapes are named explicitly.
This component holds the entity’s data related to participating in the scene’s physics simulation. It is also used to calculate collision queries, raycasts, and convex shape casts.
physics.joint: Joints link two entities at named pin poses with linear and angular limits, and live on a joints component inside a simulation.
A type that describes physics joints.
physics.material: A physics material resource carries static friction, dynamic friction and restitution.
Material properties, like friction, of a physically simulated object.
physics.determinism: Apple states no determinism guarantee for the simulation. The synchronised multi-device model is authority-and-replication over the network rather than a matching simulation on each device. Animate objects, both manually and with physics simulations.
physics.soft: Cloth is documented: a RealityKit "Cloth simulation" collection (ClothSimulationComponent, ClothBodyComponent, collider, grab and force-volume components) introduced in OS 27 for iOS, iPadOS and visionOS. Missing: no volumetric soft body or other deformable solid is documented, and the collection is a RealityKit runtime API with no exchange format. Add fabric, soft surfaces, and draping materials that bend, fold, and respond to forces and contact in your 3D scenes.
physics.trigger: A trigger volume is an invisible shape that reports entry and exit without taking part in the simulation, and any collision entity can be switched into trigger mode.
A trigger entity doesn’t have any impact on the rigid bodies in the scene, but can trigger code or Reality Composer behaviors when a rigid body entity overlaps it.
An invisible 3D shape that detects when objects enter or exit a given region of space.
audio.source: Sound is played from an entity and follows it; playback is spatial unless the app asks otherwise, and mix groups gather several playing sounds under one gain.
The audio system continuously updates the position and orientation of spatial audio sources automatically, so sounds come from an entity wherever it goes and wherever it points.
A group that manages the playback properties of multiple playing sounds.
audio.spatial: Three rendering modes ship: spatial with distance attenuation and directivity, ambient projected from an angle without reverberation, and channel routed straight to the outputs. Spatial sources are mono only, so a multichannel asset is mixed down before spatialization.
Spatial audio sources emit only a single channel (that is, mono). The engine mixes any stereo or multichannel audio resources down to a single channel before spatialization.
Ambient audio sources emit each channel of an audio resource from an angle projected from the entity, without reverberation.
Channel audio sources route the audio resource’s channels directly to the device’s output without any spatialization or reverberation applied.
audio.room: On visionOS the real room is simulated by default and colours every spatial source; a reverb component overrides it with a named preset for an authored environment.
Spatial audio sources incorporate a person’s environment acoustics so that they blend in naturally with the surrounding area.
In visionOS, an acoustic simulation of a person’s real environment reverberates the spatial audio sources by default.
audio.occlusion: Surfaces have acoustic materials with per-band absorption and scattering, which is the input an occlusion model needs, and a named preset list covers common real surfaces. What is missing is the control: no documented obstruction or occlusion setting, and no way to ask whether geometry blocks a given source.
An audio material defines how a surface absorbs and scatters sound energy across frequency bands.
audio.stream: An audio resource loads from a file or a URL and its loading strategy decides how the data is handled before and during playback, which covers reading a long asset without holding it in memory. There is no network audio delivery of the subject's own.
An audio resource that you load from a file or from a URL.
A container for different strategies on how to handle resources’ data before and during playback.
audio.voice: Neither framework carries live voice. A shared session on this platform runs on a FaceTime call, and the call carries the talking; the app gets synchronised activity data, not an audio channel it can route into the scene.
This framework leverages the FaceTime infrastructure to synchronize your app’s activities and to invite other participants to join those activities.
net.replication: Every entity has a synchronization component with a network identifier, and the multipeer service keeps the scenes of connected devices matching automatically. It is same-app replication: both ends run the same build of the same app.
A component that synchronizes an entity between processes and networked applications.
RealityKit uses this class to automatically sync scenes with other connected devices running the same app.
net.authority: One process owns an entity, the owner can be read, ownership can be handed to a named peer, and a transfer mode governs whether a request is granted.
A Boolean that indicates whether the calling process owns the entity.
Transfers ownership of the given entity to the named network device.
net.interest: Nothing decides what each peer needs; the multipeer session synchronises the scene to all connected devices. A service that provides scene synchronization among all peers in a multipeer connectivity session.
net.prediction: No prediction and no reconciliation of synchronised state is offered. A service that provides scene synchronization among all peers in a multipeer connectivity session.
net.transport: The one transport the subject ships is peer-to-peer: RealityKit's synchronization service is built on Multipeer Connectivity, which runs over infrastructure Wi-Fi, peer-to-peer Wi-Fi and Bluetooth. There is no client-server transport and no internet-scale session.

net.media: Live video reaches the scene, but the transport is not the subject's. A video component takes a player the app supplies and draws its output in three dimensions; nothing in ARKit or RealityKit moves an audio or video stream between participants.

net.session: Joining is done by two other frameworks. Nearby devices invite each other through Multipeer Connectivity, and a shared session across a call is a SharePlay group activity on the FaceTime infrastructure. RealityKit adds only a compatibility check so a host can refuse a peer on an incompatible version.
This framework leverages the FaceTime infrastructure to synchronize your app’s activities and to invite other participants to join those activities.
An opaque token used to check the networking compatibility between two peers in a multipeer connection.
net.handoff: There is no leaving one world and arriving in another with state intact. RealityKit's portal looks into a second world inside the same app's scene, and entities may cross its boundary, but both worlds belong to one process; nothing crosses to another publisher's experience.
A RealityKit portal defines a way to look into a different, immersive world.
net.presence: Within one collaborative session ARKit reports an anchor for each nearby user, giving their pose, and a group activity has a participant list. Both stop at the edge of the session; there is no roster across operators or across apps.
An active participant in a group session.
An anchor for another user in multiuser augmented reality experiences.
net.address: No world is named and no name is resolved. The only address in the subject is a file address: a web page links a USDZ or Reality file and the system opens it in AR Quick Look, which names a model, not a place.

The Multipeer Connectivity framework supports the discovery of services provided by nearby devices and supports communicating with those services through message-based data, streaming data, and resources (such as files).
net.time: No shared clock. Frames carry a local capture timestamp and the physics simulation can be driven by a custom clock, but neither is agreed between devices, and nothing orders events across a session.
A custom clock which drives the physics simulation, defaults to the engine clock.

geo.pose: A location anchor is placed by latitude, longitude and optional altitude, and the session keeps its position and orientation as the user moves, aligned East-North-Up.
A geographic anchor (also known as location anchor) identifies a specific area in the world that the app can refer to in an AR experience.
ARKit aligns location anchors to an East-North-Up orientation, with its x- and z-axes matching the longitude and latitude directions.
geo.crs: One frame, fixed. Coordinates are latitude and longitude in WGS 84 with altitude in metres against sea level, and the local frame is East-North-Up. There is no way to name a different reference system, and no transformation machinery.
Vertical distance, in meters, between this anchor and sea level.
The latitude and longitude associated with a location, specified using the WGS 84 reference frame.
geo.anchor-local: Anchors are the core primitive on both device families: an ARKit anchor fixes a transform in the session's world space on iOS, and a world anchor does the same on visionOS, with a RealityKit anchor entity tethering content to a plane, image or fixed point.
An object that specifies the position and orientation of an item in the physical environment.
A fixed location in a person’s surroundings.
An anchor that tethers entities to a scene.
geo.anchor-shared: Three routes, all first-party. A world map serialises the mapped space and its anchors so a second device can relocalise into it; a collaborative session streams the same knowledge continuously; and on visionOS a world anchor can be created shared with nearby participants, with a provider that establishes a shared coordinate space. Persistence across runs is stated for world anchors.
Initialize a world anchor with a transform and indicate if it should be shared with nearby participants.
ARKit persists world anchor UUIDs and transforms across multiple runs of your app.
With two devices tracking the same world map, you can build a networked experience in which both users can see and interact with the same virtual content.
Provides ability to establish a shared coordinate space among multiple participants.
geo.vps: ARKit recovers precise pose from camera imagery by matching the live frame against Apple's own street-level localization imagery, downloaded for the area around the user's satellite position. Two limits the map should record: outdoors only, and only where Apple has captured imagery.
By comparing the device’s current camera image with this imagery, the session matches the user’s precise geographic location with the scene’s local coordinates.
Localization imagery is available for specific areas in over 20 countries, including many metropolitan areas in Australia, Europe, Japan, and North America.
geo.tiles: No tiled terrain or city streaming; location anchors carry no geometry. geo.indoor: ARKit itself classifies detected planes as floor, wall, ceiling, door, window, table or seat, which is a start but not a room description. The structured interior comes from a separate framework, RoomPlan, which scans a room into parametric data and exports it as USD.

The object that manages the major tasks associated with every AR experience, such as motion tracking, camera passthrough, and image analysis.
An object that incorporates spatial tracking capabilities into your RealityKit apps.

Apps running in visionOS receive input events only when the person is looking at the app’s window.

A Boolean value that indicates whether the current runtime environment supports a particular provider type.

render.raster: CesiumJS owns its whole rasterisation path: a Scene object drives a fixed, ordered list of render passes with multi-frustum depth splitting for precision at planetary range, weighted blended order-independent translucency and multisampling, in three scene modes. The pass list is internal and hardcoded, so there is no configurable render graph an outside party could target.
The container for all 3D graphical objects and state in a Cesium virtual scene.
The render pass for a command.
render.gpu-api: CesiumJS targets WebGL only. A WebGL 2 context is requested by default with automatic fallback to WebGL 1, though several newer subsystems now require WebGL 2. There is no WebGPU support: no such code exists in the source tree and the change log has never mentioned it; the only artifact is a tracking issue open since 2017 with no work attached.
It uses WebGL for hardware-accelerated graphics
[requestWebgl1=false] If true and the browser supports it, use a WebGL 1 rendering context
render.material: Two separate material systems: Fabric, a Cesium-specific JSON language compiled to shader code for globe and primitive surfaces, and a physically based metallic-roughness path for loaded glTF models with several Khronos material extensions.
JSON schema called Fabric which gets parsed and assembled into glsl shader code
render.lighting: Direct sun and directional lights, cascaded shadow maps, image-based lighting with dynamic environment maps and specular cube maps, plus a physical sky and atmosphere; there is no baked global illumination, no lightmaps and no light probe volume system.
Properties for managing image-based lighting on tilesets and models.
The number of cascades to use for the shadow map. Supported values are one and four.
render.post: A post-process stage library ships eighteen ready-made stages including bloom, ambient occlusion, depth of field, edge detection, silhouette, blur, lens flare and five tone mapping operators, chainable as composites and extensible with custom shader stages. High dynamic range rendering is available but off by default.
Contains functions for creating common post-process stages.
render.lod: Detail selection is driven by screen space error over a tile tree, the mechanism the 3D Tiles standard defines, with replace and add refinement, per-tileset error budgets and prioritised tile requests. Terrain and imagery run a separate quadtree with its own, much tighter, error target, so the globe and the tilesets on it are refined by two independent rules.
[maximumScreenSpaceError=16] The maximum screen space error used to drive level of detail refinement.

render.splat: Three-dimensional Gaussian splats render natively through the Khronos glTF splatting extension and its compressed variant, delivered as 3D Tiles content, with spherical harmonics and a worker-based depth sorter.
Added spherical harmonics support for Gaussian splats, supported with the SPZ compression format.
render.volumetric: Point clouds are fully supported, including 3D Tiles point tiles, attenuation and eye-dome lighting; voxel rendering exists but is marked experimental and exempt from the deprecation policy, and there is no volumetric video.
@experimental This feature is not final and is subject to change without Cesium's standard deprecation policy.

render.text: Text is drawn as viewport-aligned labels positioned in the scene, specified with ordinary browser font strings and rendered through signed distance field glyphs so they stay crisp at any scale, with fill, outline and background styling. What is missing is glyph geometry laid out in three dimensions: labels always face the viewer, and CesiumJS carries no font file format of its own.
Labels are viewport-aligned text positioned in the 3D scene.
Settings for the generation of signed distance field glyphs
Fonts are specified using the same syntax as the CSS 'font' property.
render.camera: A camera defined by position, direction, up and right in world coordinates, set from a geographic destination plus heading, pitch and roll, with perspective and orthographic frusta, flight paths between viewpoints and entity tracking.
The camera is defined by a position, orientation, and view frustum.

scene.geometry: Decodes Draco-compressed meshes and point clouds, meshopt-compressed buffers and quantised vertex attributes, plus the quantised-mesh terrain encoding; it also builds procedural geometry for polygons, corridors, walls and solids.

scene.animation: Two unrelated mechanisms: glTF animation channels played per model, and time-varying entity properties sampled against the scene clock with linear, Lagrange or Hermite interpolation, which is how the Cesium scene language animates position over time.

geo.pose: Position and orientation against the Earth are core, and the default orientation for an object is exactly the local east-north-up frame at its position, authored as heading, pitch and roll or as a quaternion. The trap is that CesiumJS neither reads nor writes the Open Geospatial Consortium GeoPose encoding: the word GeoPose appears nowhere in the source tree or the whole release history, and the GeoPose standard in turn never mentions Cesium. The two models line up conceptually, so a converter would be short, but nothing today exchanges poses as GeoPose documents.

geo.crs: The frame is stated unambiguously: World Geodetic System 1984 as the default ellipsoid, Earth-centred fixed Cartesian metres for all internal maths, longitude, latitude and height for authoring, plus geographic and Web Mercator map projections and a transform to the inertial celestial frame. The default ellipsoid can be changed to the Moon or Mars. Limits worth naming: only those two map projections and two matching tiling schemes exist, there is no general reprojection engine so data must arrive in a supported frame, and heights are above the ellipsoid. There is no geoid model in the library; the one exception is Indexed 3D Scene Layer data, which can be shifted to ellipsoidal height by supplying an external gravity model elevation service.

geo.tiles: This is the capability CesiumJS defines rather than merely implements. Cesium created 3D Tiles, which the Open Geospatial Consortium approved as a community standard in 2018, and CesiumJS is its reference implementation, covering versions 1.0 and 1.1 including implicit tiling, subtrees, structural metadata and the styling language. Terrain streams as quantised mesh or as 3D Tiles, imagery streams from web map service, web map tile service, tile map service and template sources, and Esri Indexed 3D Scene Layer data is transcoded to glTF on load. One caveat for a standards audience: although 3D Tiles 1.1 is used in production throughout the library, the implicit tiling classes are still marked experimental in the source and are outside the project's deprecation promise.

So there is no session start, run and end handshake with a headset runtime, and content built on the standard web immersive path will not drive CesiumJS.

render.raster: Nothing is rasterised, because there is no geometry to rasterise. Pixels are produced by denoising latent tokens and decoding them through a video autoencoder, and that autoencoder is not NVIDIA's own: the generation encoder is taken from the Wan2.2 model, published by Wan-AI under Apache 2.0, and is frozen during training. There is no render pass, no draw call and no render graph anywhere in the platform.
In Generator Mode, noisy image, video, audio, and action tokens are denoised through full attention, allowing the model to jointly generate coherent multimodal outputs.
Cosmos 3: Omnimodal World Models for Physical AI, technical report
For visual generation, we use the video VAE encoder from Wan2.2-TI2V- 5B (Wan et al., 2025a).

The ViT encoder for understanding is jointly trained with the backbone, while the VAE encoder for generation is kept frozen during training.

render.camera: The camera is the one part of a scene Cosmos can be told about numerically. Camera motion is an action stream of nine numbers per frame, a three-dimensional translation and a six-dimensional rotation expressed as a relative transform in metric scale, and the model both follows it and predicts it. What is absent is a camera object: no intrinsics in the request, no projection, no field of view, no named viewpoint. Several synchronised views are handled by concatenating them into one image and putting the layout in metadata.

capture.volumetric-video: NVIDIA Cosmos is a world model: text, images, video or actions go in and frames, sound and action values come out, and it carries no captured, time-varying three-dimensional scene as media, and no camera calibration or mask metadata for one.
| Output formats | JPG image, MP4 video, AAC sound stream muxed into MP4, JSON action values, text string |
capture.point-cloud: No point cloud is read or written. Depth exists only as an annotation stream inside the released synthetic datasets and as one of the control modalities a control video may carry, which is a picture of depth rather than a set of points.
| Output types | Image, video, sound, action state, text |
Cosmos 3: Omnimodal World Models for Physical AI, technical report
a control-conditioned video-to-video benchmark covering four spatial control modalities: blur, edge, segmentation, and depth.
capture.multiview-depth: NVIDIA Cosmos is a world model: text, images, video or actions go in and frames, sound and action values come out, and it carries no set of calibrated camera views with per-pixel depth, and no intrinsics or extrinsics to reproject them.
| Output formats | JPG image, MP4 video, AAC sound stream muxed into MP4, JSON action values, text string |
capture.novel-view: Camera-motion forward dynamics produces the picture from a viewpoint no camera occupied, which is this row, done by prediction rather than by reprojection. It is also the sharpest contrast the row can draw: the same answer as a splat renderer, reached with no geometry at all.
| **Forward dynamics** | Text, vision, action | Vision | Future-state rollout from action and visual context |
capture.4d: What is produced is a video, so it moves and a receiver plays it at the rate the container states. It is not a captured three-dimensional scene that changes over time: there is no scene, and detail is chosen once per request as a resolution tier that also caps the clip length.
| Output formats | JPG image, MP4 video, AAC sound stream muxed into MP4, JSON action values, text string |
Condition and output resolution **tier**, not a pixel dimension.
capture.relight: NVIDIA Cosmos is a world model: text, images, video or actions go in and frames, sound and action values come out, and it holds no captured scene that could be made to answer the light of the place it lands in.
| Output formats | JPG image, MP4 video, AAC sound stream muxed into MP4, JSON action values, text string |
capture.edit: NVIDIA Cosmos is a world model: text, images, video or actions go in and frames, sound and action values come out, and there is no capture here to crop, delete from or recolour, and no export for such an edit to survive.
| Output formats | JPG image, MP4 video, AAC sound stream muxed into MP4, JSON action values, text string |
capture.gen-edit: There is no world object to go back to. Each request produces a recording, and changing it means asking again with a different prompt; nothing edits a region of a world already made, extends one past its edges or keeps earlier versions.
| Output types | Image, video, sound, action state, text |
capture.gen-control: The specification of what to generate is unusually structured for this family: the generator is trained on structured JSON captions covering subjects, background, lighting, aesthetics and cinematography, and the input formats are a text string, ordinary image files, an MP4 and a JSON action array. What is missing is any interchange format for the scene itself, so an authoring pipeline cannot hand over the geometry it already has.
| Input formats | Text string, JPG/PNG/JPEG/WEBP image, MP4 video, JSON action array |
Cosmos 3: Omnimodal World Models for Physical AI, technical report
The Cosmos 3 Generator is trained on structured JSON captions that provide fine-grained control over scene composition, covering subjects, background, lighting, aesthetics, cinematography
capture.derived-asset: Nothing conventional comes out. The output types are image, video, sound, action state and text, so a receiving engine gets a recording and never a mesh, a collider or a panorama it could place in a scene.
| Output types | Image, video, sound, action state, text |
capture.action-io: The one subject on the map with a real action interface, and the row was proposed for it. Actions arrive as a two-dimensional array of frames by embodiment-specific dimensions, per-dimension normalisers scale the channels to roughly minus one to one, and separate projection layers per embodiment domain mean the numbers only mean anything alongside the embodiment that produced them.
Cosmos 3: Omnimodal World Models for Physical AI, technical report
we compute per-dimension normalizers from the training data and scale action channels to a comparable range of roughly [−1, 1]
The full input is a 2D array shaped (T, D), where T is the number of frames and D is the embodiment-specific dimensionality listed below.
capture.panorama: NVIDIA Cosmos is a world model: text, images, video or actions go in and frames, sound and action values come out, and it carries no full 360-degree view of a place as an image with its projection stated.
| Output formats | JPG image, MP4 video, AAC sound stream muxed into MP4, JSON action values, text string |
sense.mesh: A world foundation model that generates images, video, sound, action state and text from prompts and conditioning. It invents a world rather than reading the one a device is standing in; there is no live session with sensors.
| Output types | Image, video, sound, action state, text |
sense.semantics: It can be conditioned on segmentation as a control modality, but that is an input steering generation, not a labelled reading of the real room delivered to an application.
| Output types | Image, video, sound, action state, text |
sense.depth: Depth appears for the same reason — as one of the spatial control modalities it accepts — not as a metric measurement it produces of the space around a device.
| Output types | Image, video, sound, action state, text |
sense.occlusion: Its outputs are images, video and action values. Nothing in it decides whether a real surface hides virtual content.
| Output types | Image, video, sound, action state, text |
render.passthrough: Cosmos generates video and world states. It never presents to a headset, so mixing with a camera view of the room is not something it does.

deliver.resolve: Resolving nested scene-resource identifiers belongs to an authored scene-container system; the pinned generator/reasoner does not emit that scene contract. Required function: Resolving scene resource identifiers against a context or resolver so the referenced resources can subsequently be accessed.
scene.bounds: Preload traversal of bounded 3D scene geometry is outside the declared image/video/audio output and reasoning contract. Required function: Bounding volumes associated with scene content, organized for spatial rejection, traversal, or selection before detailed geometry is loaded.
scene.collection: Named scene-object operation sets require an authored scene object model; world-image prediction does not define one. Required function: Named or rule-defined sets of scene objects that consumers can use as targets for scene operations.
scene.variant: Selecting named configurations of one authored 3D asset is outside the generator's declared image/video/audio output types; generated media alternatives are not an asset variant set. Required function: Named alternatives of an asset's authored configuration, with a defined selection mechanism.
scene.voxel: Exchanged spatial cell volumes/properties and updates require a 3D scene representation, outside the pinned multimodal generation/reasoning output contract. Required function: Interchanging spatial cell volumes and their properties, including updates, as a scene representation.
geo.pose-graph: The framework linked by Cosmos 3 reads JSON camera-to-world 4x4 trajectories anchored to the first frame, and supplies explicit absolute/relative transform conversions with matching reconstruction conventions. Camera frames therefore have a declared relation to the shared initial/world frame. This is the camera-conditioning utility in the named framework snapshot, not a general-purpose scene hierarchy exchange.

render.compute: The Cosmos 3 framework contains Triton RMS-normalization kernels for its DC-AE video tokenizer. The source launches a fused kernel with an explicit grid and binds input, weight and output tensors. This establishes programmable non-raster GPU compute in that named framework route; it does not claim an external compute API for generated worlds.

render.raster: UEFN draws with Unreal Engine 5's renderer, and the only account of the pipeline given to creators is a performance story: the CPU assembles a manifest, the GPU rasterises and shades it. There is no render graph, no pass order and no shader code; the one authoring surface is the material graph, which does include a post-process material domain. Nanite is on or off per session rather than per creator decision.

render.gpu-api: No low-level graphics interface is named anywhere in the Fortnite creator documentation, and a creator cannot choose or query one. render.material: Creators author their own materials in a node graph, make instances of them, and can put a material into the post-process domain to filter the whole frame. Material function wrappers let one material carry different behaviour per platform tier. What a material means is Unreal Engine's model, not a published exchange model.
Navigate to Fortnite > Materials > Functions, where you will find MF_QualitySwitch_MaterialAttributes, MF_QualitySwitch_Scalar, and MF_QualitySwitch_Vector.

render.post: Post-processing is a placed volume with priority and an unbounded option, carrying colour grading, exposure, chromatic aberration and vignette, and it accepts a creator-authored material in the post-process domain. Epic warns creators that not every device supports every effect.

Post processing is a non-destructive way of defining the overall look of the whole or part of an island by using placed volumes in Unreal Editor for Fortnite (UEFN).

World Partition divides an island into grid cells and streams the ones near a player; hierarchical LOD collapses distant groups into one mesh built from the lowest LOD of its parts; per-asset LODs have screen-size thresholds and per-quality-level minimums, and a validator flags a large mesh that has only one LOD.

The Screen Size value determines how much space on the screen your asset can occupy before the asset drops to a lower level of detail.

Epic Developer Community: Left-Up-Forward Coordinate System

physics.joint: What is published is not a joint between two bodies but a lock on one. Because Verse logic runs on the server, the FieldOfViewDegrees field is specified as a horizontal field of view assuming a 16:9 aspect ratio.

physics.soft: Cloth simulates and nothing else does, and the authoring happens outside the platform: the meshes are made in a package such as Marvelous Designer, converted into a Chaos cloth asset in Unreal Engine 5 with two plugins enabled, then imported and driven by a Chaos Cloth component in UEFN.

physics.trigger: Regions that fire events are the oldest idea in Fortnite Creative and the best specified: a trigger device relays a signal, and separate switches decide whether players, damage, items, vehicles, creatures, sequencers, water or carried objects set it off, filtered by team and class.

audio.source: Sounds are placed and heard by distance. The Audio Player device plays a sound wave or sound cue with attenuation minimum and falloff distances, a linear or logarithmic falloff curve, and a choice of who hears it and from where; sound cues add distance crossfades and a Doppler node; Scene Graph entities take a sound component.

Use the Audio Player device to play audio in your project with your own custom sound waves and sound cues.

audio.spatial: There is spatialisation and there is no spatialisation model. The only control published is a boolean whose whole description is panning by position relative to the listener; the glossary defines spatialisation and 3D audio in general terms, and no page in the documentation set names head-related transfer functions, binaural rendering or ambisonics.

Sounds that are spatialized, or located audibly in three-dimensional or virtual space.
audio.room: No space colours a sound. There is no reverb zone, no room model and no submix a creator can reach; the mixer works on volume control buses only, and the one reverb-shaped tool is a Patchwork echo device that sits in a music signal chain before an output device.
Epic Developer Community: The Audio Mixer Device
Use the Audio Mixer device to adjust the volume for groups of sounds with dynamic and automatic control of a game’s volume mix, much like a professional mixing console would.

The Echo Effect (FX-ECHO) device repeats the incoming audio signal at a specified delay and feedback level. It is an optional part of the signal chain before the audio is sent to an Output device for players to actually hear it.
audio.occlusion: Nothing blocks or muffles sound with geometry. The complete list of sound cue nodes available to UEFN creators — concatenator, distance crossfade, delay, Doppler, enveloper, looping, mixer, modulator, oscillator, random and wave player — contains no occlusion or obstruction node, and no device or component option mentions one.
Epic Developer Community: Audio Player Device
This device plays a sound wave or sound cue asset when activated.
Epic Developer Community: Adding Audio to Your Project
Sound cues provide freedom to dynamically change parts of a sound effect design by arranging and modifying sound nodes.
audio.stream: Audio is an imported asset that is cooked with the island, not a stream. Four formats come in by drag and drop and become sound waves; the documentation's own definition of streaming is a player broadcasting their gameplay to Twitch or YouTube, which is the opposite direction.

Import audio files into your projects in Unreal Editor for Fortnite (UEFN) by dragging your audio files directly from your computer into the Content Browser.
Broadcasting your gameplay in real time, most commonly via Twitch or YouTube.
audio.voice: Live voice is a first-class, addressable thing. Verse defines voice channels as groups of agents who can talk to each other, an agent can be in more than one, and a channel carries up to eighty members. Island settings add proximity chat with a volume range and a falloff distance, a compulsory speaker indicator, and the existing reporting, muting and blocking controls.

A voice_channel defines a group of agents who can communicate via voice chat.

With Proximity Chat, you can use the Proximity Chat option in Island Settings under Voice Chat to control volume range and the additional distance over which the volume gradually drops to zero.

A feature that lets players talk to each other during a game. It can be toggled ON and OFF in the island settings.
net.replication: There is obviously replication and there is no replication model for a creator. The published facts are structural: UEFN runs on a dedicated server, the multiplayer game runs centrally and clients connect to it, and Verse logic runs on the server. Which state is shared, how often, and in what form is nowhere in the documentation set, and a creator has no way to declare it.
Because Verse logic runs on the server, the FieldOfViewDegrees field is specified as a horizontal field of view assuming a 16:9 aspect ratio.
UEFN is accessed through a dedicated server that connects Fortnite clients for editing and playtesting.
A client program, or client, is a software program on a desktop or other device that can access programs and information on a central server.
net.authority: Authority is unambiguous and stated: the server decides. Verse runs there, the client renders the answer, and the consequence is visible in odd places — a field of view is authored server-side against a 16:9 assumption and rescaled per client. Failure is server-side too: a Verse runtime error halts all further execution for that device.
Because Verse logic runs on the server, the FieldOfViewDegrees field is specified as a horizontal field of view assuming a 16:9 aspect ratio.
UEFN is accessed through a dedicated server that connects Fortnite clients for editing and playtesting.
