net.interest: Nothing published lets a creator send one client less than another, and nothing describes the platform doing it. The only radius-shaped control is World Partition streaming, and the documentation is careful that it governs what counts against a player's memory, not what the server transmits.
Epic Developer Community: Streaming and HLODs
Checking Enable Streaming makes only the cells surrounding the player's current position count toward the Current Memory Usage, with a few exceptions.
net.prediction: No prediction, reconciliation or rollback appears anywhere in the creator documentation. Latency is present only as a symptom in the glossary, and the structural reason is the same one that decides the other network rows: creators cannot run logic on the client at all.
Because Verse logic runs on the server, the FieldOfViewDegrees field is specified as a horizontal field of view assuming a 16:9 aspect ratio.
The effect of a latency in online gaming where a moving object appears to leap from on place to another instantly.
net.transport: The wire protocol carrying session traffic is not published and not reachable. The single network surface a creator touches is outbound and unrelated: a Verse WebAPI client, available to licensed users only, makes an HTTP GET to a backend the licensee has configured, with the derived client identifier acting as the private key to that backend.

Licensed users create a derived version of client_id in their module.

net.media: Video exists as a fixed menu rather than a pipe. The Video Player device plays one of a handful of Epic-supplied Fortnite music videos, chosen from a dropdown, with a stream priority setting, and only one video stream can play at a time on an island. No creator-supplied video and no live media transport is documented.
Epic Developer Community: Video Player Devices
You can add media to your gameplay with the Video Player device that incorporates Fortnite-themed music videos.
Epic Developer Community: Video Player Devices
Though multiple instances of the same video can be shown, only one video stream can play at a time.
net.session: Joining is a configured queue, not a connection. Island settings set maximum players up to a hundred, team count and size, matchmaking privacy as public, private or the party's choice, a minimum player count, an overtime target and the durations of the main and overtime queue phases — with the queue cancelled if the minimum is never reached.
Epic Developer Community: Island Settings in UEFN
Island Settings provides a way to control factors as varied as how many players can play at the same time to the time of day on your island.

Public games can be joined by anyone. Private games are restricted to groups of players in the same party. Party Choice gives the player the option of choosing either public or private.
net.handoff: Leaving one world for another is a shipped device and carrying state across is not. A matchmaking portal warps players to another island by island code, and creators may let players type a different code, with a cooldown and a choice of whether the new code sticks. What arrives on the other side is a fresh session; nothing in the documentation carries state through the portal.
Epic Developer Community: Matchmaking Portal Devices
You can use the Matchmaking Portal to create a portal that warps players from one island to another.
Epic Developer Community: Matchmaking Portal Devices
This is the island code the portal will point to. The text field is limited to 50 characters.
net.presence: The one presence signal is the Epic party, and it is deliberately narrow. GetLocalParty returns the group a player formed across Fortnite, the launcher and Epic's mobile apps — not a team and not a matchmaking group — but it holds only the members present in the current session, and the rest of a player's party is invisible. There is no presence across operators.
Epic Developer Community: Party-Based Gameplay Using the Social Synergy API
A party is the group a player formed in the Epic ecosystem (Fortnite, Epic Games Launcher, and Epic Games mobile apps). It is not a team, and it is not a group produced by matchmaking.

net.address: The island code is the name and it resolves everywhere inside Fortnite, including for islands the recommendation system has stopped promoting: an unlisted release still has a code, and an underperforming island stays reachable by code, library, favourites and profile pages. The namespace is Epic's and resolution happens only in the Fortnite client.

net.discovery: Discovery is a documented, measured system rather than a directory. New islands get a testing window of up to two weeks, engagement is the primary ranking signal, metadata too similar to an existing island is demoted, automated scoring is backed by human review, and a public metrics interface returns plays, minutes, peak concurrency and retention for any public island without authentication.

When you publish a new island, Discover tests your content for up to 2 weeks.

net.time: Verse gives two clocks and defines both. A wall clock returns Unix time and is guaranteed stable within a transaction, which is what makes it usable in a language that can roll work back; a simulation clock returns seconds since the world began simulating. Both are server-side, so every participant reads the same value.
Epic Developer Community: Verse API Reference: GetSecondsSinceEpoch function
Returns the number of seconds since January 1, 1970 UTC, ignoring leap seconds. I.e, this function implements Unix time. This function always returns the same value within the same transaction.

identity.root: The root identifier is the Epic account and the platform's own machinery hangs off it — team invitations go to an Epic account name, age state and parental consent are account properties. What a creator gets is thinner: a player value that lasts a session, and per-player persistent storage scoped to their island and module. No stable account identifier is published for an island to read.

identity.credential: No verifiable claim format of any kind appears in the Fortnite documentation. The nearest thing is a fact Epic holds about an account and acts on itself — the cabined state of an under-age account — which is a policy flag inside one company's system, not a claim a second party could verify.
Epic Developer Community: cabined account (Fortnite Glossary)
If a player indicates they are under 13 or their country’s age of digital consent, whichever is higher, their account will be a Cabined Account.
identity.exchange: There is no protocol for requesting or presenting a claim. The only documented way an island reaches an outside party at all is a Verse WebAPI client making an HTTP GET to the licensee's own backend, keyed by a private client identifier — a private integration, not a credential exchange.

Licensed users create a derived version of client_id in their module.
identity.capability: Three permission systems, all readable only inside Epic. Creator Portal team roles decide who may publish, edit metadata and see monetisation; a per-island permission decides who may edit it in Create mode; and entitlements in Verse grant a player what they bought, with immutable name, description and icon. None is legible to a party that did not issue it.

identity.privacy: Selective disclosure does not arise, because the player discloses nothing to the island. Attributes stay with Epic and are enforced by Epic — parental controls decide whether a player may talk to an AI character, and a cabined account waits for consent before certain features unlock. The creator sees the outcome, never the attribute.

If a player indicates they are under 13 or their country’s age of digital consent, whichever is higher, their account will be a Cabined Account.

identity.social: One relationship is portable into gameplay and only one: two players in the same Epic party receive the same group object, so comparing them answers whether they came together. That is genuinely useful and genuinely bounded — it stops at the session, it says nothing about friendship or standing, and no other social graph is exposed.
Epic Developer Community: Party-Based Gameplay Using the Social Synergy API
Two players in the same party receive the same group object, so comparing two results tells you whether the players are in the same party.

The group holds only the party members who are present in the current session. A player's party can extend beyond your island, and those members are outside the group.
identity.rights: Rights are enforced, by Epic, before the content runs rather than at the point of use. Every release passes moderation; metadata too close to an existing island is shown less often, with first publication deciding who owns a title or thumbnail; and what a player buys cannot be resold or traded. Terms attached to a work by its author are not enforced anywhere.

Islands, including their metadata, that are highly similar to an existing experience, whether published by you or by another developer, are shown less frequently in Discover.

Players redeem V-Bucks for digital content. Reselling and trading content purchased with V-Bucks is not supported.
geo.pose: Fortnite islands have no relationship to the Earth. There is one Cartesian frame per island, expressed in centimetres from the island's own origin, and a full-text search of the documentation set returns no page about latitude, longitude or altitude. The platform is also not an augmented-reality client: the whole published sensing surface is gamepad, keyboard, mouse and touch.

geo.anchor-local: Fixing content to a real place is not something Fortnite does. The published input hardware a player can have is a gamepad, a keyboard, a mouse or a touch screen; no camera, depth sensor or tracking pose reaches a creator, and no page in the documentation set mentions anchors, planes or passthrough.

geo.anchor-shared: The same reason as local anchors, one step further out: with no world sensing and no real-world frame there is nothing to share or persist. Places in Fortnite are islands, addressed by island code, not by position on the Earth.

Unlisted: This means your project has successfully passed moderation, and it has an island code, but is not available in Discover.

The available_input_devices struct describes the hardware input capabilities available to a player. Each field is a logic value indicating whether that capability is present.
geo.vps: No visual positioning. Camera imagery never reaches a creator: the input capability struct a Verse program can read lists a gamepad, a keyboard, a mouse and touch, and nothing else.
Epic Developer Community: Player Input Device Info
The available_input_devices struct describes the hardware input capabilities available to a player. Each field is a logic value indicating whether that capability is present.
geo.tiles: Streaming exists and it is not geospatial. World Partition divides an island into a grid and loads cells around a streaming source; the grid is the island's own, indexed from its origin, with no terrain or city data referenced to ground position.

geo.indoor: There is no structured description of an interior. A building on an island is meshes with simple or complex collision and navigation laid over the walkable parts for NPCs; no room, floor or opening is named as data.

Collision is what prevents objects in your world from intersecting. Without collision, the player would be able to walk through the mesh.
input.session: There is no immersive session to start or end. Fortnite runs on PCs, consoles, mobile devices and cloud services as a flat-screen game, and the lifecycle a creator manages is a match — a queue, a round and a game phase — not a device session.
Epic Developer Community: Island Settings in UEFN
Island Settings provides a way to control factors as varied as how many players can play at the same time to the time of day on your island.

Many devices support multiple input types at the same time. For example, a Nintendo Switch supports both gamepad and touch simultaneously.
input.controller: Input is a proper API rather than a fixed set of events. A player_input class carries input actions, which produce logic values for buttons and float values for analog triggers, grouped into input mappings that must be added to a player before their actions fire — so a creator turns whole control contexts on and off as gameplay changes. A cross-platform virtual pointer adds pointing, swipes and pinches on touch, mouse and stick.
The /Verse.org/Input module provides a player_input class that serves as the main interface between your Verse code and a player's physical inputs.
Input mappings must be added to a player before their input actions will produce events. Without the mapping active, subscriptions to its actions will not fire.
The Virtual Pointer lets players interact with on-screen elements in a way that works on all supported input devices.
input.hand: No articulated hand pose exists. The struct that reports what a player's hardware can do has exactly four fields — gamepad, keyboard, mouse and touch — and touch is finger contact driving a pointer, not a tracked hand.
Epic Developer Community: Player Input Device Info
The available_input_devices struct describes the hardware input capabilities available to a player. Each field is a logic value indicating whether that capability is present.
On touch, this is driven by finger contact.
input.eye: No gaze input, and no privacy question to answer because no eye data exists. The published hardware capability list is gamepad, keyboard, mouse and touch.
Epic Developer Community: Player Input Device Info
The available_input_devices struct describes the hardware input capabilities available to a player. Each field is a logic value indicating whether that capability is present.
input.haptic: Haptics is defined in the glossary as a thing games do, and nothing in the documentation lets a creator do it: no device option, no island setting and no Verse call sends touch feedback to a player. Touch-side output is visual instead — creators reposition, restyle or hide the on-screen touch controls through a HUD controller device.
Haptics is a technology used to enhance a game experience by adding a tactile sensation — usually vibrations — in sync with an event in the game.

The default touchscreen control set — actions such as Jump, Shoot, Reload, Aim, Crouch, and Sprint — can be repositioned anywhere on the HUD.

Epic's own example is a Switch, which reports gamepad and touch at once.

logic.script: Verse is the rules language and it is unusually well specified for a platform language: statically checked, with effects such as transacts and suspends written into every signature, a language reference kept as a public GitHub repository that accepts pull requests, an editor-integrated toolchain, and a runtime error dashboard in the Creator Portal for what static checking cannot catch.
The Verse compiler currently cannot detect conditions in Verse code that would produce errors at runtime, such as integer overflows or infinite recursion.
Verse is a statically-checked programming language with an emphasis on gameplay programming.
Epic Developer Community: Verse Language Reference: Book of Verse
The reference is hosted as a public GitHub repository available for all to read and request changes or updates from in the form of pull requests.
logic.behaviour: Interactivity travels with content twice over. A Verse component saved into a prefab is part of that prefab, so every instance placed anywhere in the project — or in another project — carries the behaviour. Verse tags are the loose-coupling half: a class-derived tag marks devices and entities, and code finds all of them at run time without wiring references by hand. None of this leaves Fortnite.
You can even turn the objects you create into reusable prefabs, and use them across different projects.
Epic Developer Community: Prefabs and Prefab Instances
From the Prefab Editor, add a new component or create a Verse component to add functionality like movement or intractability to the prefab.
With Verse tags, you can find objects (both Creative devices and entities) marked with a specific tag while the game is running.
logic.sandbox: Two boundaries, and only the runtime one is a sandbox. At run time creator code is confined to the server and a runtime error stops that device's execution rather than the island's. At author time there is no sandbox at all, and Epic says so bluntly: a downloaded UEFN project can run scripts that reach your computer's data, and the advice is to open only projects from people you trust.
When a runtime error occurs, all further Verse execution for the current device is halted.
Epic Developer Community: Project and Asset Security
UEFN projects can contain scripts that execute code and access data on your computer in ways that you may not be aware of and may not be comfortable with.
logic.agent: This is the strongest agent story on the map and it is shipping. Rule-based NPCs have published state machines, perception and hire-and-patrol behaviours, and creators can write their own behaviour in Verse. Above them sit personas: a Scene Graph persona component puts a large language model into a character that players talk to by voice, with Epic naming the models it uses and stating that player audio is not stored or used for training. As of 2026-09-19 the maturity of that persona route is undetermined: Epic's own page for LLM Conversations still stands and tags itself experimental, while the Scene Graph experimental-features index no longer lists it, and no public source says whether it was promoted or withdrawn.
We use Google’s Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite models to process audio inputs and generate text responses. ElevenLabs’ Eleven v3 is used to convert these into voiced outputs.
The Scene Graph persona_component and the Persona Modifier in UEFN together provides an LLM that players can interface with in your island through a voice chat.

A common way to visualize states is through a Finite-State Machine (FSM).

logic.budget: The budget is a gate, not advice. Memory is computed from cooked data against a bar of 100,000 units per streaming cell, and an island that exceeds it anywhere cannot be published; a creator may keep working over the limit but cannot ship. A separate validator bounds asset types, texture sizes and property edits, and runs again on Epic's servers after upload.

When you have objects with properties that don't meet UEFN’s conditions, your project won't process properly.

persist.world: Nothing about the world survives; what survives is the player. Verse persistence is a module-scoped weak map keyed by player, saved per player and per module, loaded when they join, with a size limit and a hard rule that a failed load keeps the player out rather than risk overwriting their data. A second weak map keyed by session holds shared state that is deliberately thrown away between rounds.
Epic Developer Community: Using Persistable Data in Verse
Use persistable data in your Verse scripts to store information that is saved on a per-player, per-module basis.
Epic Developer Community: Using Persistable Data in Verse
If the player has persistable data for an island and the data load fails, the player will not be able to join the island.
Epic Developer Community: Using Persistable Data in Verse
Data is only stored during the current session and does not persist across subsequent rounds.
persist.inventory: Inventories are a proper system, and closed. An inventory component knows every item inside it, governs what may enter or leave, decides merging, and owns the item entities it holds; inventories nest, so an item added to a player's root can find its way down to the right sub-inventory. Items are bought with V-Bucks as entitlements, and Epic states that purchased content cannot be resold or traded.
Epic Developer Community: Custom Items and Inventory Overview
Inventories are containers for items and control what happens to those items.
Epic Developer Community: Custom Items and Inventory Overview
Since an item may only exist inside one inventory at a time, inventories also determine the ownership of item entities.
Epic Developer Community: In-Island Transactions Overview
Players redeem V-Bucks for digital content. Reselling and trading content purchased with V-Bucks is not supported.
persist.prefs: No island can read a player's settings or accessibility choices; a search of the documentation set finds no interface for them. The one thing that genuinely follows a player between islands is their Locker, and even that is opened by the player through a device rather than read by the island.
Epic Developer Community: Changing Booth Devices
The Changing Booth device lets players access their Locker while a game is in progress.
persist.content-addr: Content is named, not hashed. Exposing an asset to Verse turns its file name into a compiler symbol and its folder into a module, so a mesh is Meshes.MySphere and a Fab purchase is reached through a Verse path in a global namespace. Nothing in the documentation refers to content by a digest of its bytes.
Epic Developer Community: Exposing Assets with Asset Reflection to Verse
When you expose an asset to Verse, the name of the asset becomes the identifier, a compiler symbol, that you can then use in your Verse code, and you can access your asset from its Verse Path.

When you place your assets in subfolders in the project Content folder, the subfolder name becomes the name of the Verse module.
deliver.bundle: There is a package and the creator never holds it. Launching a session cooks every asset in the project; a memory calculation produces a private version code that identifies that upload; the project is then processed, validated and run on Epic's servers. Two Epic container types do move — .island and .upack import into a project — but a runnable experience is not a file anyone can take away.
Epic Developer Community: Validation and Fix-Up Tool
UEFN projects are processed, validated, and run on Epic’s servers.

deliver.cdn: Delivery is entirely Epic's and the creator's only lever is size. The project size tool reports what was last uploaded, what the current session would upload, and a projected download size padded for the way different consoles render the island — so download cost is visible and controllable, while the mechanism that gets the island to a player is not described at all.

deliver.version: Versioning is first-class and visible. geo.pose: The whole point of the standard: one agreed way to hand the position and orientation of a real or virtual object from one system to another, in a frame tied to the Earth or to another astronomical body.
defines requirements (rules) for the interoperable exchange of the location and orientation of real or virtual geometric objects (poses)
geo.crs: The two simple forms fix the frame: an implicit world geodetic system of 1984 datum with a local tangent plane. The flexible form instead carries three strings naming an outside authority, an identifier and parameters, and the standard says reading them is not its job. So the frame is named but never defined, and two conforming systems can exchange a pose whose frame they interpret differently.
The interpretation of the contents of these fields is outside the scope of GeoPose.
scene.transform: Axis order and rotation order are pinned down: East, North and Up map to X, Y and Z; yaw, pitch and roll are three rotations about the local z, y and x axes applied in that order; quaternion parts are written w, x, y, z. What is missing is scale and any general transform composition, because version 1.0 allows only movement and turning, and the word handed appears nowhere in the document.
This abstraction is constrained in GeoPose v1.0 to only allow transformations involving translation and rotation.
scene.units: Units are fixed for the pose itself: height in metres above the reference ellipsoid, latitude and longitude in decimal degrees. Nothing is said about the size of whatever content is placed at that pose, so it does not settle whether an imported model arrives at the right scale.
SHALL be expressed as a height in meters above the WGS-84 ellipsoid
net.time: Time series and stream forms carry a time stamp per pose, but the time model is deliberately thin: whole and fractional seconds of one common clock count, with no clock agreement, no ordering rules and no drift handling. It timestamps poses; it does not give two machines a shared clock.
GeoPose v1.0 has a very restricted idea of time position, limited to seconds of UNIX Time.
deliver.conformance: It carries a normative abstract test suite as Annex A, eight independent conformance classes with no dependency between them, and published schemas that encoded objects must validate against. This is one of the few subjects on this map that ships a test suite with the specification.
Conformance with this standard shall be checked using all the relevant tests specified in Annex A of this document.
OGC GeoPose 1.0 Data Exchange Standard, Annex A Abstract Test Suite
A.4.4 Advanced SDU Conformance Class; A.4.2 through A.4.9 define eight SDU conformance classes; A.3 defines three common classes; A.2 defines a global class; A.5 defines eight JSON encoding classes
geo.anchor-shared: It supplies the shared vocabulary two devices need to state where a thing is, and nothing else. There is no anchor identifier, no way to store or fetch an anchor, no persistence rule and no service, and the standard says outright that it does not constrain services or interfaces. Treat it as the payload for a shared anchor, not as shared anchoring.
the Standard does not assume or constrain services or interfaces providing conversion between GeoPoses of difference types or relying on different external reference frame definitions.
net.address: A pose is not an address. A full text read of the standard finds no occurrence of the word resolve, and no resolution mechanism of any kind. Anyone hoping this fills the place-naming hole should look elsewhere.
the Standard does not assume or constrain services or interfaces providing conversion between GeoPoses of difference types or relying on different external reference frame definitions.
geo.vps: Recovering a pose from camera pictures appears only in the use case table, as work that produces a GeoPose. The standard specifies no method, no imagery handling and no matching. It is the output container for a visual positioning system, not the system.
Instantaneous and time series location and orientation of an optical imaging device using Simultaneous Location And Mapping (SLAM)
geo.tiles: It carries a pose, not the content placed at it. There is no tiling, no geometry payload and no streaming of terrain or city data. That boundary is worth stating explicitly, because the other geospatial subject on this map does exactly that job.
The Frame Transform is the core abstraction in the GeoPose Standard.
render.camera: It can carry where a camera is and which way it points, which is a listed use case, and that is the whole contribution. It defines no field of view, no projection, no viewpoint binding and no rule for moving between viewpoints.

scene.container: This is the whole purpose of the format: a single file, plain text or binary, that carries a model between a creation tool and a runtime.
glTF is an API-neutral runtime asset delivery format.
scene.geometry: Section 3.7 defines meshes, primitives and accessors; two ratified extensions add compression, KHR_draco_mesh_compression and EXT_meshopt_compression.
Meshes are defined as arrays of primitives . Primitives correspond to the data required for GPU draw calls.
The following extensions have been ratified by the Khronos Group:
scene.texture: The core carries only two image formats. A device-friendly compressed format arrives through the ratified KHR_texture_basisu extension.
This extension adds the ability to specify textures using KTX v2 images with Basis Universal supercompression.
render.material: One fixed surface model in the core, with a normative appendix giving the shading equations, plus twelve ratified extensions that add effects such as clearcoat, sheen and transmission.
glTF uses the metallic-roughness material model.
scene.material-x: Surfaces are described by named numbers rather than by shader code, which is what lets the same file look the same in two different renderers.
Using this declarative representation of materials enables a glTF file to be rendered consistently across platforms.
scene.animation: Section 3.11 defines keyframe channels and samplers. One limit matters: the core animates only node transforms and morph weights, and nothing else. A ratified extension, KHR_animation_pointer, lifts that limit by letting a channel point at any property.

glTF 2.0 only supports animating node transforms and morph target weights. Extensions or a future version of the specification may support animating arbitrary properties, such as material colors and texture transformation matrices
This extension provides a standardized way of animating arbitrary glTF properties
scene.skeleton: Skins bind a mesh to a joint hierarchy with inverse bind matrices. The bones exist and move correctly; what they are called is not specified, which is a separate problem recorded under avatar.skeleton.
linear blend skinning A skinning method that computes a per-vertex transformation matrix as a linear weighted sum of transformation matrices of the designated nodes.
scene.morph: Morph targets are defined per mesh primitive and driven by a weights array, which is what facial expression work is built on.
A morph target is a morphable Mesh where the primitives’ attributes are obtained by adding the original attributes to a weighted sum of the target’s attributes.
scene.transform: A single fixed convention with no author choice, which is why imports rarely arrive rotated. Note that a widely used geospatial standard puts the up axis elsewhere and has to apply a correction.
glTF uses a right-handed coordinate system. glTF defines +Y as up, +Z as forward, and -X as right; the front of a glTF asset faces +Z.
scene.units: Fixed at metres, with no unit statement and no way for a file to declare anything else.
The units for all linear distances are meters.
scene.graph: Nodes form a strict tree, one parent each, gathered into scenes. There is no shared graph and no way for one node to appear in two places.
All nodes listed in scene.nodes array MUST be root nodes, i.e., they MUST NOT be listed in a node.children array of any node.
render.camera: Cameras carry projection settings only. They are placed by attaching them to a node, and nothing in the file says which one to start with.
Each camera defines a type property that designates the type of projection (perspective or orthographic)
deliver.version: Three separate mechanisms: a file version, a minimum version a reader must support, and lists of extensions used against extensions required, so a reader knows in advance whether it can load the file at all.
The minVersion property allows asset creators to specify a minimum version that a client implementation MUST support in order to load the asset.
deliver.conformance: The specification names an adopter programme as the route to claiming conformance, and the body publishes an official validator in its own repository. The validator checks files, not renderers, so two conforming readers can still draw the same file differently.
must become Adopters under the process defined by Khronos for this specification
scene.instancing: EXT_mesh_gpu_instancing, which is on the ratified list despite the vendor prefix. The core has no instancing at all: repeating an object means repeating a node.
This extension is specfically designed to enable GPU instancing, rendering many copies of a single mesh at once using a small number of draw calls.
render.lighting: KHR_lights_punctual is ratified and covers directional, point and spot lights. Environment lighting comes from EXT_lights_image_based, which is a multi-vendor extension and not ratified. Nothing here defines shadows, probes or baked indirect light.
This extension defines three "punctual" light types: `directional`, `point` and `spot`.
This extension provides the ability to define image-based lights in a glTF scene.
render.lod: MSFT_lod only. It is a single-vendor extension outside the body's patent framework, and there is no Khronos level-of-detail extension in the registry at any stage.
Vendor extensions are not covered by the Khronos IP framework.
This extension adds the ability to specify various Levels of Detail (LOD) to a glTF asset.
scene.licence: KHR_xmp_json_ld is ratified and exists precisely to attach attribution and licensing terms to an asset or to individual objects. The core carries only a free-text copyright string. The extension states terms and enforces nothing, and tools routinely drop it on export.
A copyright message suitable for display to credit the content creator.
Metadata is used to transmit information (such as attribution, licensing, creation date) about the glTF asset.
audio.spatial: The only spatial audio in the registry is MPEG_audio_spatial, a vendor extension contributed from the moving picture standards body. The graphics body itself has ratified nothing for audio. A file using this is portable only to readers that implement someone else's standard.
The `MPEG_audio_spatial` extension adds support for spatial audio and it may be included at top level or attached to any node in the scene.
scene.provenance: The ratified metadata extension carries who made the asset and when, but nothing signs it. There is no hash, no certificate and no way to detect that the record was altered, so the missing half of this capability is the whole trust half.
Metadata has no normative effect on the glTF asset appearance and rendering.

render.splat: KHR_gaussian_splatting was announced 2026-02-03 and is ratified: read on 2026-09-06 its status line says Complete, Ratified by the Khronos Group, and the extension registry lists it under the ratified Khronos extensions rather than in the in-progress table. The same text defines how splats are drawn, with reconstruction, projection, sorting and alpha blending normative for the ellipse kernel. Neither ground this row once gave for partial - not ratified, and no rendering defined - holds against the text as it stands. Splats reach glTF through the extension and not through the core, and compression is still outside it.
This extension defines basic support for storing 3D Gaussian splats in glTF assets

The following extensions have been ratified by the Khronos Group:
KHR_gaussian_splatting, the ellipse kernel rendering section

To render a field of 3D Gaussian splats, the renderer reconstructs each Gaussian splat using the same forward pass algorithm used during training, projects it onto a 2D plane, computes its color, and composes it with other splats.
render.volumetric: A mesh primitive can use point topology, so a plain point cloud fits. Nothing in the core covers voxels, volumetric video, or the per-point attributes a real capture pipeline needs.

physics.rigid: Nothing ratified. KHR_physics_rigid_bodies sits at review draft, two stages below ratified, in an open pull request with no merged specification folder. The word physics occurs once in the entire ratified text, as an invented vendor name in an example of how to list extensions.

Do not state a ratification target for one.

render.text: There is no text primitive, no font reference and no layout of any kind. Every occurrence of the word font in the published document is in its own page styling, not the specification body. Text has to be baked into geometry or textures before export, which is why three-dimensional labels do not survive a round trip.
Any node MAY contain one mesh, defined in its mesh property. The mesh MAY be skinned using information provided in a referenced skin object. The mesh MAY have morph targets.
scene.compose: A file is self-contained. There is no layering, no referencing of one file from another, and no way to override part of a scene from a second source. The registry lists a separate project for external references, at proposal stage, the earliest rung.
render.raster: A delivery format, not a renderer. It says what to draw, never how the frame is assembled.
glTF is an API-neutral runtime asset delivery format.
render.gpu-api: Deliberately tied to no graphics interface. The specification says so in its opening sentence.
glTF is an API-neutral runtime asset delivery format.
render.post: Nothing about the frame after the objects are drawn. This belongs to whatever runtime consumes the file.
glTF is an API-neutral runtime asset delivery format.
logic.script: A data format with no execution model. A retired extension once carried shader programs and is now archived as not recommended for new files.
Archived extensions may be useful for reading older glTF files, but they are no longer recommended for creating new files.
capture.worldgen: glTF 2.0 is a runtime asset delivery format for models, and making a whole three-dimensional place from a description or a picture is not an act it performs or specifies.
glTF is an API-neutral runtime asset delivery format.
capture.sim-learned: glTF 2.0 is a runtime asset delivery format for models, and it never continues a world under a viewer's actions from a learned model; there is no such model here.
glTF is an API-neutral runtime asset delivery format.
capture.photogrammetry: glTF 2.0 is a runtime asset delivery format for models, and turning a set of ordinary photographs into a textured three-dimensional model is not among its jobs.
glTF is an API-neutral runtime asset delivery format.
capture.splat-format: KHR_gaussian_splatting is ratified, and it is the one named way splat data travels in glTF: position, rotation, scale, opacity and spherical harmonics stored as attributes on a point primitive, with a required kernel and colour space. Compression is not in it. The extension says compression extensions should extend this base, and none of the three open compression proposals is ratified.
Complete, Ratified by the Khronos Group
This extension defines basic support for storing 3D Gaussian splats in glTF assets, bringing structure and conformity to the 3D Gaussian splatting space.
Compression extensions that operate on 3D Gaussian splatting data SHOULD extend this base extension to ensure compatibility.
capture.stream: Nothing in glTF says what should arrive first. The only detail-level mechanism in the registry is a single-vendor extension outside the Khronos patent framework, and it swaps a whole representation rather than delivering one capture by region and detail.
Vendor extensions are not covered by the Khronos IP framework.
This extension adds the ability to specify various Levels of Detail (LOD) to a glTF asset.
capture.volumetric-video: No captured, time-varying media, and no camera calibration or mask metadata anywhere in the ratified set. Volumetric media reaches a glTF scene only through the MPEG vendor extensions, whose normative text is ISO/IEC 23090-14 and which is a separate subject on this map.
The following extensions have been ratified by the Khronos Group:
This document specifies extensions to existing scene description formats in order to support MPEG media, in particular immersive media.
capture.point-cloud: A mesh primitive may use point topology, so a plain set of points travels in the core, and the splat extension leans on exactly that fallback. What the core does not define is any point-cloud compression or the per-point attribute set a capture pipeline produces, so a lidar or photogrammetry point cloud arrives as ordinary vertex attributes and nothing states what they mean.
Since the extension treats the 3D Gaussian splats as point primitives, a graceful fallback to treating the data as a sparse point cloud is possible.
Allowed values : 0 POINTS 1 LINES 2 LINE_LOOP 3 LINE_STRIP 4 TRIANGLES
capture.multiview-depth: glTF 2.0 is a runtime asset delivery format for models, and it carries no set of calibrated camera views with per-pixel depth, and no intrinsics or extrinsics to reproject them.

capture.novel-view: glTF 2.0 is a runtime asset delivery format for models, and it produces no image from a viewing position that no capture camera occupied.
glTF is an API-neutral runtime asset delivery format.
capture.4d: The core animates authored nodes, skins and morph targets against a timeline. It carries no captured scene that changes over time, and the splat extension is static: a Gaussian set has no time axis, so a moving capture has to be handed over as unrelated files.
This extension defines basic support for storing 3D Gaussian splats in glTF assets, bringing structure and conformity to the 3D Gaussian splatting space.

capture.relight: The format states the problem and declines to solve it. Splat colour is display-referred, so scene lighting, exposure and tone mapping generally do not affect it, and any material on the primitive must be ignored; the extension then permits an implementation to relight the splats anyway and defines no data and no method for doing it. A receiver may therefore relight, and two receivers will not agree.
Unless specified otherwise by additional Gaussian splats extensions, the glTF material referenced from the mesh primitive (if any) MUST be ignored for splat rendering.
Still, implementations can relight the splats, e.g., to simulate shadows or additional light sources, or to adjust the rendered splats for an environment different than the one they were trained in.
capture.edit: glTF 2.0 is a runtime asset delivery format for models, and there is no capture here to crop, delete from or recolour, and no export for such an edit to survive.
glTF is an API-neutral runtime asset delivery format.
capture.gen-edit: glTF 2.0 is a runtime asset delivery format for models, and there is no generated world here to change by describing the change or pointing at a region.
glTF is an API-neutral runtime asset delivery format.
capture.gen-control: glTF 2.0 is a runtime asset delivery format for models, and nothing here accepts a specification of a world that should be made.
glTF is an API-neutral runtime asset delivery format.

render.raster: Three rendering methods ship in the engine: Forward+ using clustered lighting for desktop, Mobile using traditional single-pass forward lighting, and Compatibility using non-clustered forward. All three are forward renderers; the documentation has a section explaining why deferred rendering is not used. There is no public render graph interface, though one exists internally.
Overview of renderers - Godot Engine (stable) documentation
Internal rendering architecture - Godot Engine (stable) documentation
This is a forward renderer that uses a clustered approach to lighting.
render.gpu-api: Forward+ and Mobile go through RenderingDevice onto Vulkan, Direct3D 12 or Metal; Compatibility uses OpenGL, meaning OpenGL ES 3.0, desktop OpenGL 3.3, or WebGL 2.0 in the browser. Two details matter for a standards audience: the Direct3D 12 driver is still documented as experimental in 4.7, while the Metal driver is native and now uses Metal 4; and there is no WebGPU backend, which is the reason the advanced renderers cannot run on the web at all.
Internal rendering architecture - Godot Engine (stable) documentation
Godot's renderers are built entirely on OpenGL and RenderingDevice, which is our abstraction over Vulkan/Direct3D 12/Metal.
RenderingDevice is not available when running in headless mode or when using the Compatibility rendering method.
Exporting for the Web - Godot Engine (stable) documentation
Godot currently does not support WebGPU, which is a prerequisite for allowing Forward+/Mobile to run on the web platform.
render.material: StandardMaterial3D is a physically based, energy-conserving material on a metallic-roughness workflow; ORMMaterial3D is the same thing reading occlusion, roughness and metallic from one packed texture. Custom looks are written in the engine's own shading language, which is close to OpenGL ES 3.0 shading language, or built as node graphs.
A PBR (Physically Based Rendering) material to be used on 3D objects.
Standard Material 3D and ORM Material 3D - Godot Engine (stable) documentation
Godot uses a metallic model over competing models due to its simplicity.
Godot uses a shading language similar to GLSL ES 3.0.
render.lighting: Directional, omni and spot lights with shadow maps, cascaded shadows for the sun and optional contact-hardening soft shadows. Indirect light has four routes: baked lightmaps and reflection probes work in every renderer, while voxel global illumination, signed distance field global illumination and screen-space indirect lighting need the Forward+ renderer.
Introduction to global illumination - Godot Engine (stable) documentation
Not available when using the Mobile or Compatibility renderers
3D lights and shadows - Godot Engine (stable) documentation
There are three types of light nodes: DirectionalLight3D, OmniLight3D and SpotLight3D.
Signed distance field global illumination (SDFGI) - Godot Engine (stable) documentation
It provides semi-real-time global illumination that scales to any world size
render.post: One WorldEnvironment per scene carries glow, tone mapping, screen-space reflections, ambient occlusion and indirect lighting, fog and colour adjustment, with exposure and depth of field moved onto a separate camera attributes resource. Anti-aliasing and upscaling are viewport settings. For custom work the compositor lets a project insert its own passes at named stages, though that class is marked experimental and works only on Forward+ and Mobile.
Environment and post-processing - Godot Engine (stable) documentation
The WorldEnvironment node can be added to any scene, but only one can exist per active scene tree.
The compositor is a new feature in Godot 4 that allows control over the rendering pipeline when rendering the contents of a Viewport
This resource defines a custom rendering effect that can be applied to Viewport
render.lod: Detail selection is covered: meshes get automatically simplified versions at import using the meshoptimizer library, chosen by a screen-space metric, with hand-authored visibility ranges and software occlusion culling alongside. The interoperability half is absent. Godot loads whole resources, and mesh streaming, texture streaming and level streaming are all still open proposals in the engine's own tracker, so there is no streaming order to interoperate with.
Mesh level of detail (LOD) - Godot Engine (stable) documentation
The meshoptimizer library is used for LOD mesh generation behind the scenes.
occlusion culling works by rasterizing the scene's occluder geometry to a low-resolution buffer on the CPU
Mesh streaming aims to solve this.
render.splat: Nothing in core, and nothing in the official asset library. Searched the Godot 4.7 stable documentation search index (1,591 pages, including the class reference) for splat, splatting, nerf and radiance on 2026-10-19; splat, splatting and nerf have no match, radiance appears only in lighting, sky, reflection and texture-import pages, and gaussian only in blur and post-processing pages. The asset library search API returned no results for splat. A search of the godot-proposals tracker for gaussian on the same date returned 11 results, and the 8 read were all about blur or filtering. Community projects exist on code hosting outside official channels, typically hooking in through the compositor.
Internal rendering architecture - Godot Engine (stable) documentation
Godot's renderers are built entirely on OpenGL and RenderingDevice, which is our abstraction over Vulkan/Direct3D 12/Metal.
Godot Asset Library API search for splat (no results)
render.volumetric: Volumetric fog with local fog volumes is built in, but only on the Forward+ renderer. Point clouds are not first class: there is a points primitive type on meshes and a single-point mesh resource for billboarded sprites, but no point cloud node, importer or volumetric video path.
Volumetric fog and fog volumes - Godot Engine (stable) documentation
Volumetric fog is only supported in the Forward+ renderer, not the Mobile or Compatibility renderers.
Render array as points (one vertex equals one point).
Mesh with a single point primitive.
render.text: Two routes: Label3D draws text on textured quads and can face the camera, and TextMesh extrudes real geometry from vector glyph outlines. Both share the engine's font resources, including multi-channel signed distance field rendering for crisp text at any size, over a text server that uses HarfBuzz, ICU and Graphite for bidirectional and complex scripts.
Godot provides 2 methods to do this: the Label3D node and the TextMesh resource for a MeshInstance3D node.
An implementation of TextServer that uses HarfBuzz, ICU and SIL Graphite to support BiDi, complex text layouts and contextual OpenType features.
Multi-channel signed distance field (MSDF) font rendering allows rendering fonts at any size
render.camera: Cameras register themselves with the nearest viewport and exactly one is current at a time, with perspective, orthogonal and offset-frustum projections. In an immersive session the pose comes from the headset instead: XRCamera3D positions itself from tracking data under a tracking-space origin node, and most of its properties are then overridden by the active immersive interface.
Cameras register themselves in the nearest Viewport node (when ascending the tree). Only one camera can be active per viewport.
A camera node which automatically positions itself based on XR tracking data.
scene.graph: The whole engine is built on it: nodes form a tree, a tree with a single root is a scene, and a saved scene can be instantiated inside another scene and then behaves like one node. This is Godot's central idea and the reason it has no separate prefab concept.
Nodes and Scenes - Godot Engine (stable) documentation
Together, nodes form a tree, which is a powerful feature to organize projects.
Once you have saved a scene, it works as a blueprint: you can reproduce it in other scenes as many times as you'd like.
scene.transform: Right-handed, Y up, minus Z forward, following the OpenGL convention; transforms are a Transform3D made of a Basis of three vectors plus an origin.
Following the OpenGL convention, X is the Right axis, Y is the Up axis and Z is the Forward axis.
scene.container: Two answers that must not be confused. For transfer, Godot reads glTF 2.0 in both text and binary form and can export a scene back out as glTF from the editor. For authoring it uses its own formats, tscn and scn for scenes and tres and res for resources, and no other runtime reads those.
Godot has support for both text (.gltf) and binary (.glb) formats.
To export a scene in the editor go to Scene > Export As... > glTF 2.0 Scene...
GLTFDocument supports reading data from a glTF file, buffer, or Godot scene.
scene.geometry: Meshes are read and written through glTF and the engine's own ArrayMesh, but Godot does not implement the Draco mesh compression extension, so compressed models from common web pipelines fail to import. An open proposal in the engine's own tracker asks for hooks so an outside extension could add it.
Add additional hooks to GLTFDocument to support draco decompression via GDExtension
Godot doesn't support the KHR_draco_mesh_compression extension
scene.texture: Import-time compression covers S3TC and BPTC on desktop and ETC2 or ASTC on mobile and web, with a Basis Universal mode that transcodes to whatever the device wants at load time.
This alternative VRAM compression mode encodes the texture to a format that can be transcoded to most GPU-compressed formats at load-time.
scene.material-x: Standard metallic-roughness materials survive a glTF round trip, but there is no MaterialX or OpenPBR support in the engine, and anything written as a custom shader is dropped on export, so hand-authored looks do not travel. A third-party module and open proposals exist; nothing ships.
scene.animation: Animations are keyframe tracks in an Animation resource held by an AnimationPlayer, grouped into animation libraries; almost any property of any node can be a track, including script variables and function calls.
Introduction to the animation features - Godot Engine (stable) documentation
A keyframe defines the value of a property at a point in time.
scene.skeleton: Skeleton3D holds the bone hierarchy, a Skin binds a mesh to it, and BoneAttachment3D hangs other nodes off a named bone; skeletons come in through glTF import.
A node that dynamically copies or overrides the 3D transform of a bone in its parent Skeleton3D.
scene.morph: Meshes carry blend shapes, imported from glTF morph targets, and each shape's weight can be read and set at runtime on the mesh instance.
Sets the value of the blend shape at blend_shape_idx to value.
scene.instancing: MultiMesh with MultiMeshInstance3D draws many copies of one mesh cheaply with per-instance data; the level of detail system works with it, though every copy uses the same detail level at a given moment.
useful to optimize the rendering of a high number of instances of a given mesh
scene.compose: Layering by reference works: an instanced scene keeps a live link to its source file, per-instance property changes override the source, and Editable Children opens the instance's inner nodes for local edits. What is missing against the definition is composition from several sources at once with declared strength ordering, the way a layered scene description format does it; a Godot node has exactly one source scene.
Changing a property on an instance always overrides values from the corresponding packed scene.
scene.units: One unit is one metre and the engine states plainly that physics and everything else are tuned for that scale.
Godot uses the metric system for everything in 3D, with 1 unit being equal to 1 meter.
scene.licence: The glTF exporter carries exactly one asset-header field bearing on rights: a free-text copyright string, written on export when it is non-empty and read back on import. That states who claims an asset; it does not state what a recipient may do with it, and nothing reads it at the point of use. Import metadata otherwise records import settings only. Correction: an earlier version of this row said nothing survives a glTF export. That was wrong - the copyright string does.
The copyright string in the asset header of the glTF file. This is set during import if present and export if non-empty.
scene.provenance: The only authorship-adjacent field anywhere in the transfer path is the free-text copyright string in the glTF asset header. It is unsigned, so it records a claim rather than proving one. There is no signing, no key material and no content credential in the asset pipeline.
The copyright string in the asset header of the glTF file. This is set during import if present and export if non-empty.
avatar.body: Nothing in the engine core. The VRM add-on maintained outside the Godot Foundation, and listed in Godot's own asset library, imports VRM 0.0 and 1.0 and exports VRM 1.0, and brings the MToon shader with it. Treat this as a community route, not an engine feature.
V-Sekai/godot-vrm - Importer/Exporter for VRM avatars and MToon shader
This Godot addon fully implements an importer and exporter for models with the VRM specification
VRM Importer for 3D Avatars and MToon Shader - Godot Asset Library
This asset provides an importer and exporter for VRM characters, as well as a full implementation the high quality VRM Toon Shader "MToon" for Godot Engine 4.1 and higher.
avatar.skeleton: SkeletonProfileHumanoid defines a fixed 56-bone humanoid layout in four groups and exists, in the engine's own words, for standardization. But it is Godot's naming, not an agreed cross-vendor one, so it standardises inside Godot and needs a bone map at the boundary. The hand tracking system also standardises on this humanoid skeleton.
A SkeletonProfile as a preset that is optimized for the human form. This exists for standardization
OpenXR hand tracking - Godot Engine (stable) documentation
the hand tracking implementation in Godot has been standardized around the Godot Humanoid Skeleton
avatar.expression: XRFaceTracker carries named expression weights taken from the Unified Expressions set, including eye and eyelid shapes, so tracked expression has an agreed vocabulary on the input side. There is no expression or viseme format for an avatar asset itself in core, and the class is marked experimental.
The blend shapes come from the Unified Expressions standard
avatar.retarget: The import pipeline has a retarget section: a bone map onto a skeleton profile, a bone renamer, and a rest fixer that can overwrite bone rest axes and force a reference silhouette, so animation authored for one body plays on another. The docs are candid that it cannot fix silhouettes that are too different.
cannot fix silhouettes which are too different
avatar.wearable: BoneAttachment3D gives a real attachment point on a named bone, so a held or worn item follows the body. There is no portable description of that attachment: the binding lives in the Godot scene and does not travel with an exported asset.
This node selects a bone in a Skeleton3D and attaches to it.
avatar.lod: Generic mesh level of detail and visibility ranges apply to avatar meshes like any other, but there is no avatar-aware reduction, no crowd imposter and no agreed reduced avatar representation.
Mesh level of detail (LOD) - Godot Engine (stable) documentation
Mesh LOD works with any node that draws 3D meshes.
physics.rigid: RigidBody3D, StaticBody3D, AnimatableBody3D and CharacterBody3D cover the usual cases. Two engines ship: the built-in Godot Physics and Jolt Physics, added in 4.4, which new projects use by default and which is chosen with one project setting. A third engine can be substituted entirely from outside, because PhysicsServer3D is a public interface with an extension point.
Using Jolt Physics - Godot Engine (stable) documentation
By default, new projects will use it as the physics engine.
Intended for use with GDExtension to create custom implementations of PhysicsServer3D.
physics.collision: Collision shapes are separate child nodes from the visible mesh, covering box, sphere, capsule, cylinder, convex hull and concave triangle mesh, with documented advice on the cost of each.
Concave shapes are the slowest option but are also the most accurate in Godot.
physics.joint: Pin, hinge, slider, cone twist and generic six-degree-of-freedom joints all exist. The gap is between the two engines: under Jolt a number of joint properties, mainly the soft limit settings, are not supported, so the same scene can behave differently depending on which engine is selected.
Using Jolt Physics - Godot Engine (stable) documentation
there are a number of joint properties that are not supported, mainly ones related to configuring the joint's soft limits
physics.material: PhysicsMaterial carries friction and bounce with rough and absorbent flags controlling how two surfaces combine.
Holds physics-related properties of a surface, namely its roughness and bounciness.
physics.determinism: There is a fixed physics tick rate, but no claim anywhere in the documentation that the same inputs give the same result on two machines, and the engine states that ordinary floating point maths is not guaranteed to be exact. Anyone planning lockstep or rollback networking on Godot has to prove determinism themselves.
Math done using the float type is not guaranteed to be exact and will often result in small errors.
physics.soft: SoftBody3D simulates cloth and other deformable meshes; the class documentation recommends running it on Jolt rather than the built-in engine because that implementation is faster and more reliable.
A deformable 3D physics mesh. Used to create elastic or deformable objects such as cloth, rubber
physics.trigger: Area3D is a region that reports bodies and other areas entering and leaving, and can also override gravity, damping and the audio bus inside itself.
Emitted when the received body enters this area.
audio.source: AudioStreamPlayer3D places a sound in the world with a choice of inverse, inverse square, logarithmic or no distance attenuation, plus unit size and maximum distance.
Plays audio with positional sound effects, based on the relative position of the audio listener.
audio.spatial: Direction is rendered by panning between output channels, with a per-node panning strength over a project-wide setting. There is no head-related transfer function and no ambisonic path in the engine, so binaural rendering has to come from an add-on or the platform.
Scales the panning strength for this node
audio.room: Reverb is real and routable: buses carry effects in order, and an Area3D can send the sounds inside it to a named reverb bus with an amount and a uniformity. What is missing is any acoustic model of the room itself; the reverb is authored, not derived from geometry.
The name of the reverb bus to use for this area's associated audio.
Audio buses can contain all sorts of effects. These effects modify the sound in one way or another and are applied in order.
audio.occlusion: There is a low-pass attenuation filter on each 3D sound, but it is driven by distance and by area masks, not by geometry between source and listener. Real occlusion has to be scripted with ray casts that drive that filter.
The cutoff frequency of the attenuation low-pass filter, in Hz.
audio.stream: Audio streams are local resources loaded from the project or from disk. Nothing in the engine delivers audio over a network at scale; on web builds the playback type setting only chooses between browser samples and streaming inside the page.
It exists so Web exports use Web Audio-API based samples instead of streaming all sounds to the browser.
audio.voice: No voice transport ships. AudioEffectCapture hands a project raw samples off a bus and the documentation names network transmission as a use for it, but the codec, the jitter buffer and the transport are all the developer's problem.
Exposes audio samples from an audio bus in real-time, such that it can be accessed as data.
net.replication: This is the part that is unusual for an open engine. MultiplayerSynchronizer replicates a declared list of properties from the authority to remote peers on a configurable interval or on change, and MultiplayerSpawner replicates the creation and removal of nodes. Remote procedure calls with reliability and ordering modes sit alongside it.
Synchronizes properties from the multiplayer authority to the remote peers.
automatically replicates spawnable nodes from the authority to other multiplayer peers
net.authority: Every node has a multiplayer authority, the server by default, settable per node; remote calls can be restricted to the authority or opened to any peer.
Only the multiplayer authority can call remotely. The authority is the server by default
net.interest: Per-synchronizer visibility can be set for a peer directly or computed by visibility filter callbacks, which is the mechanism for sending each client only what it needs. The policy is entirely the developer's: there is no spatial partition, no area of interest and no automatic culling by distance.
Adds a peer visibility filter for this synchronizer
net.prediction: No client-side prediction, reconciliation or rollback in the engine. Replication is authority to peer, and the multiplayer guide names client-side prediction as something a project has to add. Searched the Godot 4.7 stable documentation search index (1,591 pages, including the class reference) for predict, rollback, reconcili and netcod on 2026-10-19; rollback, reconcili and netcod have no match, and the only networking page that mentions prediction is the high-level multiplayer guide quoted here.

This comes with some tradeoffs (such as server-side performance and complexity due to the need for client-side prediction), but will make it much harder for attackers to cheat by sending falsified data.
net.transport: Three peers ship behind one interface: ENet over UDP for native builds, WebSocket, and WebRTC data channels. A project can add its own peer implementation.
ENetMultiplayerPeer, one based on WebRTC (WebRTCMultiplayerPeer), and one based on WebSocket (WebSocketMultiplayerPeer)
ENet only uses UDP, not TCP.
net.media: The WebRTC integration exposes data channels only; there is no audio or video track handling, and no media transport of any kind in the engine.
A WebRTC connection between the local computer and a remote peer.
net.session: Joining is covered inside one application: a peer connects, an optional authentication callback can hold it in an authenticating state until the project completes or times out the handshake, and spawners bring the joiner up to date. There is no standard for what that handshake contains and no cross-operator session concept.
The callback to execute when receiving authentication data sent via send_auth().
net.handoff: Nothing for leaving one world and arriving in another with state intact. Changing scene inside one application is not the same thing and does not cross an operator boundary: the outgoing scene is removed from the tree and then freed, so nothing carries across unless the project saves and reloads it by hand.
The current scene node is immediately removed from the tree.
net.presence: Inside one session the server can notify clients of other peers connecting and disconnecting, which gives a roster. Across operators there is nothing.
notifies clients of other peers' connection/disconnection, and relays messages between them
net.address: A client connects to a host address and port. There is no name for a place, and no resolution step between a name and a reachable destination.
net.discovery: No lobby, matchmaking or service discovery in the engine; projects hand-roll it or buy it. A client must already hold the server's address and port before it can connect, which is the opposite of finding a world without knowing it in advance.
Create client that connects to a server at address using specified port.
net.time: There is a fixed physics tick and a Time singleton, but the singleton reads the local machine's own clock and converts between formats. There is no shared clock, no offset estimation and no agreed event ordering across peers, so two peers can disagree and nothing in the engine reconciles them.
The Time singleton allows converting time between various formats and also getting time information from the system.
identity.root: A game engine, not an identity provider. The only identifier the engine issues is a peer number handed out at connection time: the server is always 1 and every client gets a random positive integer. It is scoped to one session and means nothing outside it.
Every peer is assigned a unique ID. The server's ID is always 1, and clients are assigned a random positive integer.
identity.exchange: The multiplayer authentication callback is a bring-your-own hook where a project could carry a credential exchange, but the engine defines no protocol, no message shape and no verification.
If the Callable is empty (default), peers will be automatically accepted as soon as they connect.
geo.pose: No Earth-referenced position or orientation. Large world coordinates can be enabled to give double precision for big scenes, which helps a geospatial project, but the engine defines no Earth frame.
geo.anchor-local: The core OpenXR module exposes spatial entities: spatial anchors that the runtime keeps registered to a real place, plane tracking for walls, floors, ceilings and tables, and marker tracking for QR codes, micro QR codes, Aruco codes and April tags.
OpenXR spatial entities - Godot Engine (stable) documentation
Spatial anchors allow us to map real world locations in our virtual world
geo.anchor-shared: Half of the definition is met and the engine says so plainly. Anchors can be made persistent so they come back in the right place next time the application starts, if the runtime supports it. Sharing anchors between devices is stated as not supported, which the docs attribute to the spatial entities specification rather than to Godot.
OpenXR spatial entities - Godot Engine (stable) documentation

geo.vps: No visual positioning in the engine. Where a runtime does it, the result reaches Godot already resolved, as an anchor the AR platform identified and placed, not as a pose service the engine exposes or a query a project can make.

render.material: A surface is not described by data in the file. Normal maps are not supported at all and nothing is double-sided. No renderer outside Horizon reads material intent out of a name, so a material cannot survive the trip in either direction.

Static and dynamic light gizmos exist, but a model that already carries its own lighting cannot be used in a custom model world. Every other system in this map keeps lighting and geometry apart; Horizon fuses them, so a mesh authored for Horizon arrives elsewhere with Horizon's light stuck to it.

scene.container: This is the row that decides everything else. Horizon reads exactly one model format, FBX, with PNG textures beside it, and it reads no glTF and no USD even though Meta's own Spatial toolkit for other products reads glTF. Going the other way the desktop editor really can write an FBX of a whole world or a selection, into a folder next to the app, and Meta has since improved that export to carry several materials per object, material textures, several texture coordinate channels and mesh names. But the published world is not a container at all: it lives in Meta's store, is edited live, and only geometry, materials and textures come back out. Gizmos, scripts, colliders, lighting and saved state stay behind.
To complete this procedure, you need a custom 3D model (an FBX file and one or more PNG texture files) to import.

Meshes go back out through the world export, which now writes several coordinate channels and keeps mesh names, so this one is genuinely two-way, but what comes back has already lost its pivots and its tree.

scene.instancing: Repeating an object is done by spawning it from an asset, either one at a time through a spawn controller or from a pool gizmo that holds copies ready. scene.compose: A large world can be split into sublevels, each of which is a separate published Horizon world holding its own meshes, gizmos and scripts, which a parent world references by a link and a script loads, unloads or holds in memory. Teams can work on different sublevels and stitch them together. Two things are missing: there is no override mechanism, so a parent cannot change anything inside a sublevel, and composition is the same for everyone, because loading a sublevel loads it for every player at once.

scene.units: Horizon works in metres and tells creators to build at real-world scale and to set the units correctly when exporting the FBX. physics.rigid: Bodies move by rule. An entity switched to simulated falls when gravity is on and reacts to what it hits, and simulation always works in world space, so a simulated child ignores its parent's motion. Recorded animation and physics cannot both drive one object: turning on animation cancels simulation and scripted motion.

physics.collision: Collision shapes are separate from visible geometry and are declared in the FBX by the name of the mesh: a prefix picks a box, a sphere, a capsule, a convex hull or a full mesh. Meta points out that this is the same name-based approach Unreal, Houdini and Unity use, which makes it one of the few genuinely shared conventions in this record. It runs one way only: shapes come in from the model file, and nothing in the world export says colliders are written back out.

physics.determinism: Horizon does not aim at the same result on two machines; it names one machine the owner and copies its answer to the rest. Meta says that when ownership moves, state is lost and the script restarts, so the creator has to pack the state up and send it across. That is the opposite of a shared deterministic simulation, and no determinism guarantee is published anywhere.

audio.source: Sound is placed in the world inside an audio gizmo with a full set of properties: play on start, loop, volume and volume randomness, pitch in semitones and pitch randomness, a global switch that removes distance falloff, minimum and maximum distance in metres, a low-pass cutoff frequency, and an event when playback finishes. A script can play, pause and stop with a fade and can aim the sound at named players. Files go in as MP3, WAV, FLAC or Ogg Opus at five listed sample rates; no export path for audio is published.

audio.spatial: Horizon takes mono files for anything placed in space and names one real standard for the wider bed: first-order ambisonic files must be in Ambix channel order so they point the right way. That is a checkable convention, and it is the only one in Horizon's audio. What is missing is the renderer: Meta never says how direction is turned into two ears, gives creators no control over it, and tells them not to bake spatialisation into the file. audio.occlusion: Geometry does not block sound. The only shaping Horizon offers is a minimum and a maximum distance and a fixed low-pass cutoff frequency that dulls a sound the same way whatever stands between the listener and it.

audio.stream: Streaming here means off the local disk, not off the network: anything above two and a half megabytes is streamed rather than held in memory, and only one such file should play at once. Uploads are capped at fifty megabytes. There is no way to pull live audio from an outside host into a world.
Audio assets that are larger than 2.5 MB are streamed from disk.
audio.voice: Live voice works and a creator can shape it: the environment gizmo carries the voice settings and a script can change them, and voice counts as one of the sixty-four sounds a world may play at once. Meta also runs captions over it, in English only, with translation into four languages. All of that lives inside the runtime and nothing about the transport is published, so a creator can turn voice up and down but nobody outside Horizon can carry it.
is available to configure how players hear each other in the world.

net.replication: Everything that moves is replicated, and it goes to everybody. Meta's own performance advice says so and tells creators the remedy is to have fewer moving things. A creator cannot choose what replicates, cannot set a rate, and is given no schema or wire form; the only lever is the ownership model, which decides which machine is the source of truth.
All moving (dynamic) objects in the world have their positions synchronized between clients, where updates are sent to every player in the world.
net.authority: This is the best documented part of Horizon. Ownership decides which machine holds the truth for an entity and therefore where its script runs. The server owns everything by default, which keeps the view common and stops a client cheating. Ownership moves to a player automatically when they grab a thing or collide with it, or by hand from a script, and a keep-ownership-on-collision setting turns the automatic case off. Meta explains when not to hand ownership over, with worked examples of bowling pins and racing cars.
Ownership is a mechanism used to determine which client (either the server or a user’s device) is the authority for a particular entity’s state.
Entity ownership automatically transfers from one client to another whenever a player in the game grabs something (for example, a gun), or when a player collides with something.
net.interest: Nobody is sent less than anybody else. Movement updates go to every player in the world, and even the coarse tool that could have helped, sublevel streaming, is explicitly the same for everyone: loading a sublevel loads it for all players at once, and per-player streaming is not supported. A creator has no way to give two people in one world different content.
Per-player world streaming is not supported
updates are sent to every player in the world
net.prediction: Horizon's answer to latency is not to guess and correct but to move the work. Meta tells creators that a script running on the owning player's own device has no latency problem, and that the way to get a good feel is to hand that player ownership. No prediction and no reconciliation is documented anywhere.

net.time: No shared clock is published. Meta scans recorded sound for copyrighted music, blocks or mutes it, repeats the scan later so something already published can be silenced afterwards, and flashes the gizmo red while emailing the creator. The appeal route is an email address. That is central after-the-fact takedown, which is the opposite of a licence a receiving runtime could read and honour on its own.

logic.script: World rules are written in real TypeScript, which is a genuine strength next to platforms that invented their own language. The restrictions are heavy though: exactly one compiler version is supported and no other, there is no eval, no typed arrays and no proxies, bundled or minified libraries are not supported, and a script is capped at sixty-four thousand bytes unless the world uses file-backed scripts. logic.behaviour: Horizon has a visual block language, authored in the headset, which reads at a glance like the portable declarative interactivity other systems are converging on. It is not. The blocks are Meta's own, they live on entities inside Meta's world record rather than inside an asset, and the world export writes geometry, materials and textures and nothing else. Behaviour therefore never travels with a thing: take an object out of Horizon and it arrives inert.

logic.sandbox: There is a real boundary and Meta explains why it is where it is: scripts run on the server by default so a hostile client cannot change them, which Meta names as its anti-cheat argument. Scripts moved to a player's own device are then denied things: they cannot spawn assets, cannot touch texture assets, and cannot reach the persistent store, all for stated security and integrity reasons. The missing part is any permission model within a world: the split is between server and client, and there is nothing that isolates one creator's script from another's.

logic.agent: Autonomous characters are one of Horizon's strongest published areas. Characters can hold a conversation driven by a model, speak with a generated voice, exist without a body at all, and there is a documented route for reporting abuse by one. None of it is expressed in any form another platform could take.

logic.budget: Horizon bounds guest content harder than almost anything else in this map, and the bounds are gates, not advice. A world cannot be published unless it is under one hundred per cent in four separate areas, and Meta enforces a six gigabyte memory ceiling by refusing to let a creator publish or even add assets above it. On top of that sit runtime vertex and draw-call budgets, download-time budgets tied to slower connections, a cap of one thousand and twenty-four sound sources with sixty-four audible, ten kilobytes per saved object, five variable groups of one hundred and fifty variables each, and sixty-four thousand bytes of script.
