persist.world: A world can keep state of its own. Meta added world-level data persistence for things like a shared counter or a complex world state, with a documented way to update a world variable safely when several people change it at once, and a world can be restored from a backup. What is not published is the thing a standards reader would ask: what an instance keeps when the last person leaves, and whether the next instance sees it. The documented limits conflict and are preserved here: the variable groups page says creators are no longer restricted to six groups per world yet also says a world must have fewer than six groups to add one and caps a group at 100 variables, while the persistent variables page says a world can contain up to 5 groups of up to 150 variables each.

persist.prefs: This is the surprise in the record. Saved player data really does follow a person between worlds: Meta says persistent variables persist across the worlds a player explores, a variable group can be added to many worlds, and a creator can share a group with other creators so their worlds read the same values, though the sharer keeps sole control of its shape. The store is a numbers-and-objects key store, capped at ten kilobytes an object and flushed every five seconds, and it is unreachable from a script running on the player's own device. It is not accessibility or preference portability, and it never leaves Horizon, but it is cross-world player state, which several comparable platforms forbid outright.

persist.content-addr: Content is referred to by identifier and version, not by what it contains. deliver.bundle: There is no runnable package. A world is a live record in Meta's store, edited in place, and Meta's own version control advice makes the consequence plain: every save is the equivalent of forcing a push straight onto the main branch that everyone shares. Publishing hands it to Meta, which caches it for a minute or two before players get a fast load and emails the creator if that fails. The only artefact a creator ever holds is an FBX of the geometry, written into a folder beside the app. Nothing about the world can be handed to another runtime, archived, or signed.
When you publish your custom model world, it takes anywhere from one to two minutes for it to be cached.
Clicking export will create a file in a folder called FBXExport located wherever the Horizon app is installed.
In Git terms, this would mean every time one of your teammates updates a script file locally, it’s immediately force-pushed to the main branch of your repository.
deliver.cdn: Delivery is entirely Meta's and the creator's only role is to keep inside the budget. Meta publishes download-time budgets aimed at people on slower connections, caches a published world server-side and emails the creator when caching fails so loads will be slow, and serves assets from its own hosts. There is no creator control over where anything is served from and no way to serve it elsewhere.

deliver.version: Assets are versioned properly: a pool spawns a pinned version rather than whatever is newest, templates carry draft version notes, and worlds can be restored from a backup. Scripts are written straight into the shared world with no branch and no merge, so Meta's advice is to keep a separate copy under real version control and copy changes across by hand.

render.raster: It rasterizes, but only Gaussians. The trainer and both viewers draw the scene through a modified copy of the gsplat CUDA rasterizer, with render modes for colour, depth, alpha and normals; there is no render graph, no pass structure and no path for ordinary triangle meshes, which are exported for other engines to draw.
Uses `gsplat_maskgaussian` (our custom gsplat fork with integrated MaskGaussian) for differentiable rasterization and adaptive probabilistic Gaussian pruning
render.gpu-api: The renderer targets CUDA, not a graphics interface. Drawing runs through hand-written CUDA kernels in the bundled gsplat fork, and the install instructions require CUDA 12.8 and a FlashAttention backend, so nothing in this subject runs on a machine without an NVIDIA GPU. Content leaves as splat and mesh files that other runtimes draw with their own interface; the subject itself will not interoperate with Vulkan, Metal or WebGPU renderers.
render.material: Appearance is per-Gaussian colour and opacity, not a material. Spherical harmonic degree defaults to zero and the report says view-dependent effects were dropped deliberately in favour of a flat colour per Gaussian, so a surface has no roughness, no metalness and no view-dependent response. The exported mesh carries only the colour fused into it from rendered views.
render.lighting: Light is baked into the Gaussians at training time and there is no lighting model in the released code: no probe, no shadow, no global illumination pass. The technical report claims automatic image-based lighting in a rendering platform called WorldLens, which is described in the report and is not in the open-source plan or the repository, so nothing in the release can be checked against that claim.

Also, we introduce WorldLens, a high-performance 3DGS rendering platform featuring a flexible engine-agnostic architecture, automatic IBL lighting, efficient collision detection, and training-rendering co-design, enabling interactive exploration of 3D worlds with character support.
render.post: No presentation-time effect stack. The one image-space correction in the code is a bilateral grid applied during optimisation to absorb per-photograph exposure differences, which is a fitting device rather than a post-processing pass a viewer would run.
Depth, normal, and LPIPS loss regularization for high-quality geometry
render.lod: Detail is decided once, at training time, and never again. Adaptive pruning cuts the Gaussian count by about three quarters to make real-time drawing possible, and the mesh is decimated by quadric edge collapse, but the result is a single fixed level: the exported files carry no level-of-detail hierarchy and no streaming order, so a client must take the whole world or none of it.
The full configuration retains comparable visual quality while reducing 77% Gaussian count compared to the baseline.
render.splat: This is the subject's core. Both halves of the system end in 3D Gaussian splats: reconstruction predicts splat means, scales, rotations, opacities and spherical harmonics in one forward pass, and generation optimises a splat scene and exports it. The bundled viewer reads a standard splat PLY, with the usual x, y, z, rot_*, scale_*, opacity and f_dc_* fields, and draws it.
a unified feed-forward model that simultaneously predicts depth, surface normals, camera parameters, 3D point clouds, and 3DGS attributes in a single forward pass
render.volumetric: Point clouds are first-class: the pipeline predicts them, writes them as coloured PLY, and the web demo displays them beside the splats. Voxels and volumetric video are absent; the only voxel in the code is a grid used to merge points and to fuse depth into a mesh, not a thing that is drawn.
Upload images or videos and visualize 3DGS, point clouds, depth maps, normal maps, and camera parameters in your browser.
**Voxel merging**: Points within each voxel (size controlled by `compress_pts_voxel_size`) are merged via weighted averaging.
render.text: No text of any kind is placed in the scene. The output is a captured or generated appearance; letters exist only where they were in the photographs or the generated imagery, as colour.
render.camera: The camera is the one thing this subject models rigorously. Reconstruction predicts camera-to-world matrices and intrinsics per view in the OpenCV convention and writes them to a documented JSON file; the same file can be fed back in as a prior. Generation plans the viewpoints itself, writing a camera file per trajectory, and the checkpoint stores an up direction, a facing direction and a centre point for a viewer to start from.
The camera parameter file follows the same format as the `camera_params.json` output by the pipeline:
scene.graph: There is no scene graph and no object identity. A generated world is one undivided set of Gaussians plus one fused mesh; the only per-object record anywhere is a list of things a vision-language model spotted in the panorama in order to plan a camera route, and it never reaches the exported world.
Uses VLM (Qwen3-VL) to identify interesting targets
is utilized to yield 2D semantic masks for these objects.
scene.transform: Conventions are stated where cameras are concerned — camera-to-world matrices in the OpenCV convention, and a coordinate system conversion on export to the compressed splat format, from right-down-front to right-up-back — but the scene itself has no declared frame. Poses are normalised against the first input view, so origin, orientation and scale are whatever that view happened to be, and the exported PLY carries no statement of any of it.
pack_options.from_coord = spz.CoordinateSystem.RDF  # from RDF to RUB
**Extrinsics alignment:** The pipeline automatically normalizes all extrinsics relative to the first view, consistent with training behavior.
scene.container: It writes into other people's containers and defines none of its own. A finished world leaves as splat PLY, optionally the compressed SPZ or SPX form, a mesh PLY, a coloured point PLY, a camera JSON and, on request, a COLMAP sparse model. There is no packaged scene: no glTF, no OpenUSD, no manifest tying the parts together. The only container it reads back is a splat PLY in its own viewer.
Exports to `.ply`, `.spz` (compressed), and mesh (TSDF fusion) formats
scene.geometry: Mesh geometry is produced but not encoded in any considered way. Rendered colour and depth from every training view are fused into a truncated signed distance volume, marching cubes extracts a surface, small components are dropped and the result is decimated; it is written as a plain PLY with no compression, no index scheme and no material binding.
we further extract a mesh from the optimized 3DGS representation
scene.texture: Nothing is textured. The exported mesh has no parameterisation and no image maps; its colour comes from fusing rendered views into the volume it was extracted from, so appearance lives per vertex on the mesh and per Gaussian in the splats. Device texture compression is not addressed anywhere.
scene.material-x: There is no material to exchange. Appearance is a colour per primitive, so the question a material exchange format answers does not arise for this subject.
scene.animation: The worlds it makes do not move. Video appears only as an intermediate — point-cloud renders along a planned route, and the keyframes the expansion model generates — and is consumed by the next stage rather than kept as an animation.
| **Output** | Pixel videos (non-editable) | Real 3D assets — meshes / 3DGS (fully editable) |
scene.skeleton: It reconstructs and generates places, not articulated bodies. No bone hierarchy exists anywhere in the model outputs.
scene.morph: No deformation of any kind. Every representation the subject writes is static.
scene.instancing: Nothing is repeated cheaply because nothing is an object. The viewer has a debugging switch that draws copies of the whole scene in a grid, which is not instancing of scene content.
parser.add_argument("--scene_grid", type=int, default=1, help="repeat the scene into a grid of NxN")
scene.compose: The pipeline composes internally — a panorama, planned routes, generated keyframes and a reconstruction are fused into one world — but the result cannot be composed with anything else. There is no layer, no reference to another scene and no override; a second world can only be placed beside the first by whatever engine imported them both.
scene.units: Scale is recoverable only when the caller supplies it. The report states plainly that calibrated intrinsics are what resolve metric scale ambiguity, and intrinsics are one of the three priors reconstruction accepts; without them, and in the generation path where there is no real camera at all, the world has no real-world size. No exported file declares a unit either way.
calibrated intrinsics resolve metric scale ambiguity
WorldMirror 2.0 accepts three types of geometric priors as conditioning inputs.
**Intrinsics resolution:** Values should correspond to the **original image resolution**.
scene.licence: Nothing about rights travels with the asset. The licence on the model is heavy — it excludes three jurisdictions outright, demands a notice file on every redistribution and requires a licence from Tencent above a million monthly users — yet the splat and mesh files it produces carry no licence field, no notice and no pointer to the agreement. The obligation is on the person, and the file that leaves the machine says nothing.

physics.rigid: It simulates nothing. The system produces the geometry another engine would simulate against, and the report is explicit that this is the intent; see the collision row.
To support downstream applications such as collision detection and physics simulation, we further extract a mesh from the optimized 3DGS representation.
physics.collision: It manufactures collision geometry and runs no contact test at run time. Two kinds are produced: a navigation mesh built with recastnavigation, used during planning so the virtual camera does not walk through walls, and the fused mesh, extracted expressly so that a downstream engine can do collision and physics against it and deliberately simplified to keep loading cheap. net.handoff: This is the subject and the only capability it fully specifies. Two calls in a fixed order, query then teleport, correlated by a teleport identifier, bounded by an expiry the destination checks, ending with the destination client launched, the source client closed, and a callback to the source saying it worked or it did not. Four communication paths are defined for the second call: device to device, through the clouds, hybrid, and through a user agent.
IWPS Base Specification, section 5.3.3 Teleport API
ultimately logging in the User to the Destination Client and closing the Source Client
net.address: The resolving half is real and specified: a portal link conforms to RFC 3986, uses http or https, must be called with POST, and the query call made on it returns a destination address, so a name genuinely resolves to a reachable endpoint. The naming half is not. The place-designating segment is an optional free-text field described as coordinates in a form the destination world determines, with the destination free to pick the spot if none is given. So the only published design that resolves a portal does not standardize the name inside it, and no two worlds can write each other's landing addresses.
IWPS Base Specification, section 5.3.3 Teleport API
is a spatial position in the target world
IWPS Base Specification, section 5.3.3 Teleport API
Coordinates in a form determined by the Destination World.
net.discovery: There is no registry, no index and no search. The specification says a portal link reaches a person through the developer's website, a direct message, a friend's referral, or a code on a billboard or a television advert. The one lookup that exists, an OpenAPI file that resolves a versioned decentralized identifier to the portal's metadata, needs the identifier in hand first, so you still cannot find a world you do not already have a link to.
IWPS Base Specification, section 5.3.3 Teleport API

net.session: The crossing ends in a session and the specification takes it right up to the door: the teleport call logs the person into the destination client, security profiles and identity arrangements are named, and the destination shows a confirmation number before login. What is missing is the joining itself. How the destination cloud launches its own client is stated to be implementation-dependent and outside scope, and no join, authenticate or ready message is defined for the destination world.

net.transport: The wire is ordinary and that is a strength: calls are http or https, always POST, content sent as a string, responses in JSON, and a server need not support every queried field, in which case it simply omits it from the response. input.devcaps: The most concrete part of the specification and the one nearest to useful. The source sends a mandatory bundle describing the device: instruction set, word size, operating system, operating system version and client type, and the destination uses them to decide whether the teleport is possible and which address and download link to hand back. Missing is an agreed value space. The operating system list is written as a closed set but ends with etc., and the version is typed as a floating point number, so a version like 10.15.7 cannot be expressed. Two implementations will disagree on the values while agreeing on the fields.

There is no walkable surface, no bounds and no list of spawn points travelling with a place, and nothing tells the source client whether the landing location it names is somewhere a body may actually stand.
IWPS Base Specification, section 5.3.3 Teleport API
Portal URI | URI that the User uses to create a Portal, optionally including parameters such as the landing location in the Destination World.
logic.namespace: IWPS is a pair of calls that set up and execute a teleport. It names worlds and clients so a teleport can be addressed, publishes no units of logic and operates no namespace for them.
IWPS Base Specification (OMA3 draft, repository commit f09c0da), section 4.2 API Overview

The document defines two API calls—Query API and Teleport API,—which together facilitate the process of setting up and executing a teleportation between clients and their corresponding cloud services.
deliver.moderation: A destination takes an arriving user and, in the wider OMA3 work, arriving assets, and this is exactly where a receiving world would want to know what review something has had. The base specification defines two calls, Query and Teleport, and neither carries a review record, a content rating or any statement of what the source has already checked.
IWPS Base Specification, section 5.3.3 Teleport API

scene.containment: IWPS defines portal traversal — moving a person from one world to another with two API calls over web protocols. It sends the visitor elsewhere rather than hosting another's experience. The specification explicitly addresses world-to-world crossing, the opposite of containment.

net.world-coupling: IWPS defines portal traversal where a person carries the change by crossing between worlds. Its two-call protocol assumes a participant is present and crossing. Unattended coupling — state changing in another world with nobody present — is not addressed by the specification.

KIRI Engine, 3D Gaussian Splatting feature page, Blender add-on
This 100% free, open-sourced add-on allows you to access and render 3DGS files within Blender the same way they appear on the online preview panels.
3DGS Render for Blender README, what it does
Import and view 3DGS `.ply` files in Blender.
render.gpu-api: No graphics interface is named or exposed anywhere in the product or the add-ons.
KIRI Engine, 3D Gaussian Splatting feature page, Blender add-on
This 100% free, open-sourced add-on allows you to access and render 3DGS files within Blender the same way they appear on the online preview panels.
render.material: Physically based material maps with normals are generated for meshes, which is a real material contribution, and they travel in whatever the export format carries. Splats have no material at all.
PBR Materials Production-ready PBR maps with accurate normal
KIRI Engine on the App Store, export formats
Formats: Export in OBJ, STL, FBX, GLTF, GLB, USDZ, PLY, XYZ, compatible with Blender 3D, Unreal Engine, Autodesk Maya, etc.
render.lighting: Lighting is baked into a capture, and the open Blender add-on adds two experimental ways to make it behave: sampled shadow proxies so splats cast shadows onto meshes, and baking light into splats. Neither is a lighting model that travels with a file.
3DGS Render for Blender README, what it does
Create sampled Eevee shadow proxies so splats can cast approximate shadows onto Blender meshes. *(Experimental.)*
render.post: No post-processing chain is offered by the product; the After Effects plug-in is compositing in another tool.
KIRI Engine, 3D Gaussian Splatting feature page, Blender add-on
This 100% free, open-sourced add-on allows you to access and render 3DGS files within Blender the same way they appear on the online preview panels.
render.lod: Decimation reduces a mesh's polygon count on demand, which is level-of-detail authoring by hand. No level structure or streaming order is carried in what is written.

render.splat: Gaussian splat capture, editing and real-time rendering are a headline feature, on phones and in a browser, with a free open add-on that renders the same files in Blender.

identity.capability: Grants exist and are scoped: a token may carry the positioning service, the site-management service or both, and a production backend can mint different scopes for different users. scene.transform: Marble writes files in an open splat format but not in that format's frame. The format stores right-up-back by default, following the graphics and three.js convention; Marble's generated files declare a raw computer-vision frame, and Marble's own viewer corrects for it with a half-turn about the X axis before drawing. A conforming reader that follows the format therefore renders a Marble world upside down, which is exactly the question the vendor's own export page answers. Worse for a reader trying to comply, three vendor pages disagree: a release note says exports moved to the graphics frame in December 2025, the export specification page still states the computer-vision frame, and the developer page names a raw computer-vision convention for generated files.
Default world labs worlds are in OpenCV coordinate system (+x left, +y down, +z forward).

avatar.body: This is its declared job: one portable description of an avatar that different systems can write and read. Do not call it the first, though. The same committee published a standard in 2016 whose stated job is moving a virtual object or its characteristics from one virtual world to another, and that earlier work is the prior art any working group will be asked about.

scene.container: It defines more than one container for carrying an avatar, and the entry point is a readable document listing the parts and where the binary data sits. This is an avatar container, not a general scene container.

scene.skeleton: A skeleton is a root plus a list of joints, each joint a node with a parent, children, a local transform and a bind matrix; a skin ties one mesh to one skeleton with a weight per vertex per joint. The structure is fully specified. Whether the joints mean the same thing in two files is a separate question, covered in the avatar skeleton row.

Each skin definition provides three main pieces of information: the mesh and skeleton to connect, and the skinning weights.
scene.morph: Face and detail shapes are carried as blendshape sets. One trap for anyone writing a converter: a shape here is a whole replacement mesh with the same topology, not the per-vertex offsets the common asset format uses, so a straight copy across will be wrong.

Note that this is another mesh and not vertex displacements (e.g., this is not like morph targets in glTF).
scene.animation: Animation is split off from the avatar itself into a stream of timed units, each one either stream setup, face weights, joint transforms, landmark positions or texture weights, every unit carrying its own time stamp. It can come from a file or straight off a tracking device.

avatar.lod: An avatar asset can carry several detail levels, each a full alternative description of the same asset at a different rendering quality, each with an identifier a receiver can name in the animation stream.
Implementation guidelines for MPEG-I Avatar representation formats, ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 29/WG 3 N1881, 2026-07-21
Each asset object can have one or more Level of Details (LoD). Each LoD in an asset is another definition of the same asset, but with a different quality of rendering.
avatar.skeleton: This is the load-bearing gap. It gives the structure but not the agreement: joint identifiers must match an outside animation framework, named by a reference string in the file header, and the group's own worked example names one headset maker's full body tracking. So the naming that would make an avatar move correctly somewhere else is borrowed from elsewhere, and two files can both conform while agreeing on nothing.
Implementation guidelines for MPEG-I Avatar representation formats, ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 29/WG 3 N1881, 2026-07-21
The ids of nodes of a skeleton shall be consistent with an animation framework.
avatar.expression: Same pattern as the skeleton. Named face shapes exist, but their meaning comes from an outside face animation framework named in the file header, and the worked examples name one headset maker's face tracking and one phone maker's landmark set. The standard carries the shapes; it does not settle what a smile is called.
Implementation guidelines for MPEG-I Avatar representation formats, ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 29/WG 3 N1881, 2026-07-21
each animatable component is related to an animation framework
avatar.retarget: An avatar can be animated by a framework it was not built for, if the file carries a mapping: weighted sums for the simple case and a controller-style mapping for the harder one. What is missing is the body problem. This maps parameter to parameter between tracking frameworks, not motion between bodies of different proportions, and the mapping has to be authored into the file in advance rather than worked out on arrival.
Implementation guidelines for MPEG-I Avatar representation formats, ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 29/WG 3 N1881, 2026-07-21
An animatable component is always defined for a specific animation framework. However, another one can be used if a mapping is provided.
avatar.wearable: Clothing and similar items ride as separate assets that an application may switch on or off, sharing the avatar's skeleton. What is missing is attachment: there are no named attachment points, and nothing describes how an item authored for one avatar should sit on another.
Implementation guidelines for MPEG-I Avatar representation formats, ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 29/WG 3 N1881, 2026-07-21

avatar.identity: The group states that the draft carries means to check an avatar is genuine and to stop someone passing themselves off as another. Read that narrowly: the public announcement names the mechanism without describing it, and says nothing about tying an avatar to an identifier or a credential issued by anyone else. The text that would settle this is behind a paywall we did not cross.

scene.geometry: It defines how geometry is referenced and grouped but not how it is encoded: in the group's own worked examples every mesh is a binary file in the common asset format, readable by ordinary tooling for that format. So this draft sits on top of that format rather than replacing it, which is worth knowing before anyone treats the two as rivals.
Implementation guidelines for MPEG-I Avatar representation formats, ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 29/WG 3 N1881, 2026-07-21
This GLB contains single mesh and associated materials (no animations, skins, morph targets, etc.) and can be loaded with any conformant glTF software.
scene.transform: Node transforms are four by four matrices written the other way round from the common asset format, so the row that holds the position in one is the column that holds it in the other. A converter that copies the sixteen numbers straight across loads without error and puts the avatar in the wrong place. The same document flags a second clash: what this draft calls a skeleton is what the common format calls a skin. Both traps come from the group's own guidance, not from outside criticism.
Implementation guidelines for MPEG-I Avatar representation formats, ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 29/WG 3 N1881, 2026-07-21
Compared to glTF, these matrices are transposed.
net.replication: The one piece of live shared state a formal standard now defines for avatars: a wire form for the moving parts, sent as timed units a receiver applies at the stated time. Everything around it is absent. There is no session, no rule for who owns an avatar, no way to send each viewer only what it needs, and no correction after a late packet.

audio.source: Sound is placed in the scene as objects with position and orientation, and sources may also carry a size and shape, from a piano up to a forest. Channel beds and ambisonic fields are carried too.
MPEG-I: Immersive Audio, official MPEG standard page
The scenes consist of audio objects and acoustic properties of the room including the simulation of acoustics like reverberation, early reflections, occlusion, diffraction and Doppler-shift.
ISO/IEC 23090-4:2025 catalogue record, Information technology - Coded representation of immersive media - Part 4: MPEG-I immersive audio
supports the real-time interactive rendering of an immersive virtual or augmented reality audio presentation while permitting the user to have 6DoF movement in the audio scene
audio.spatial: The listener can walk as well as turn, which is the step past the earlier three-axis standard. Output is either to headphones as a two-ear mix or to a loudspeaker rig from six up to twenty-four channels.
MPEG-I: Immersive Audio, official MPEG standard page
In addition to the 3DoF head movements (yaw, pitch and roll), which had already been supported by MPEG-H 3D Audio, the listener can now move within the acoustic scene (x,y,z).
audio.room: Rooms are first-class: each acoustic environment has its own late reverberation, early reflections are computed from the transmitted geometry, and openings between rooms pass sound from one to the next. A separate listening space description carries the shape and surfaces of the real room the listener is standing in.
MPEG-I: Immersive Audio, official MPEG standard page
The scenes consist of audio objects and acoustic properties of the room including the simulation of acoustics like reverberation, early reflections, occlusion, diffraction and Doppler-shift.
audio.occlusion: Blocking and part-blocking of sound by geometry are separate named stages of the renderer, and bending around an edge is handled alongside them so a hidden source is still heard from the right direction.
White Paper on MPEG-I Immersive Audio, ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 29/AG 03 N150
The Occlusion stage provides occlusion information with respect to a direct path from source to user.
audio.stream: The standard defines the coded form itself, sized for narrow links, and works either as a file or as a live stream.
ISO/IEC 23090-4:2025 catalogue record, Information technology - Coded representation of immersive media - Part 4: MPEG-I immersive audio
It defines metadata to support this rendering and a bitstream syntax that enables efficient storage and streaming of immersive audio content.
net.media: It defines the stream and how the six-axis metadata is packed alongside the coded audio, using three new packet types in the older audio stream format. It does not define the network protocol that carries those packets, and it carries no video.
White Paper on MPEG-I Immersive Audio, ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 29/AG 03 N150
The MPEG-I immersive audio bitstream transport relies on MHAS (MPEG-H Audio Stream), by introducing three new packet types to carry the 6DoF metadata alongside the MPEG-H 3D audio signal assets.
audio.voice: It can render a talker's voice into the scene once that voice has arrived, which is listed as a social use case. It defines nothing about getting live voice from one participant to another: no capture, no codec choice for speech, no session and no mixing rules. This is the gap next to an otherwise complete audio standard.
White Paper on MPEG-I Immersive Audio, ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 29/AG 03 N150
enabling acoustic interaction with the scene supporting e.g. virtual meetings
scene.geometry: It carries its own copy of the scene shape, as boxes, meshes or solid blocks, because the renderer needs surfaces to reflect and bend sound off. What is missing is any tie to the visual asset: this is an acoustic description authored separately, so the same room gets described twice, once for pictures and once for sound.
White Paper on MPEG-I Immersive Audio, ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 29/AG 03 N150

a dedicated scene description file format has been developed called Encoder Input Format (EIF) that holds definitions for e.g. sources and their positions, scene geometry (primitives, meshes or voxels), transforms, material acoustic coefficients, etc.
physics.material: Worth stating so nobody double-counts it. The standard does define surface materials, but they are sound properties: how much energy a surface passes, reflects, couples and soaks up, by frequency. There is no friction, no bounce and nothing a contact solver could use.
White Paper on MPEG-I Immersive Audio, ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 29/AG 03 N150
These materials are characterized by parameters describing transmitted, reflected, coupled and absorbed audio energy parts.
physics.trigger: A scene can name a region and fire a change when the listener enters it. What is missing is everything outside sound: the change may only alter the acoustic scene, so this is not a general rule engine and will not drive world logic.
White Paper on MPEG-I Immersive Audio, ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 29/AG 03 N150
Conditional scene updates define a specific condition that triggers the scene update.
geo.anchor-local: For augmented use it places virtual sound content into the real room the listener occupies, using the measured room description. What is missing is anything shared or lasting: no anchor identifier, no storage, nothing that another device or a later session could reuse.
White Paper on MPEG-I Immersive Audio, ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 29/AG 03 N150
an anchor mechanism is used for placing scene content in appropriate positions in the listening space
persist.prefs: Hearing needs are handled inside the renderer rather than bolted on afterwards: a listener can ask for less late reverberation or for sources away from where they are looking to be quietened. What is missing is portability. The published description has those choices arriving through a local interface, and says nothing about a format that would carry them from one service to the next.
White Paper on MPEG-I Immersive Audio, ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 29/AG 03 N150
the audio rendering process can be adjusted according to the user-specific sensory conditions

Frames form a directed acyclic graph: a device has a body frame, sensors have frames relative to the body, and the body frame is related to a map frame by a transform.

EntityBinding is intentionally flat — it does not express parent-child relationships, ownership, or transform inheritance. Consumers requiring hierarchical scene graph semantics SHOULD build their own entity hierarchy from the bindings received.

render.raster: The engine does not own a pipeline. It builds draw lists on a compositor thread and hands them to an ANARI device, which decides how to draw them; the shipping device is Halogen, an ANARI implementation over Google Filament. Geometry reaches the device as spheres, curves, boxes, panels and triangle meshes, and the frame is either read back to a buffer or drawn straight into a Vulkan swapchain on a native window.

render.gpu-api: Sneeze targets no low-level graphics interface itself; it targets ANARI and lets the loaded device choose. Vulkan, Metal and DX12 appear only inside Halogen's Filament backend and inside the separate Vox compute path. A standards reader should note the consequence: swapping the renderer is a library-name change, but nothing in the browser states which interface a given build actually used.

A node names an external resource by a 128-byte reference string, the browser fetches it and decides what it is by sniffing the bytes, and a glTF or binary glTF file is parsed with fastgltf into a renderer-agnostic model. Only the default scene is read. The MetaversalCorp copy adds Draco and meshoptimizer decode units; the Forum copy has neither.

scene.animation: The glTF loader builds meshes, materials, textures and a node hierarchy and stops there; there is no animation array in the model it produces and no clip playback anywhere in the engine. scene.units: Geometry is accumulated in metres and a panel's world size is authored in metres, which is a real unit agreement. The part that is missing is any declaration: the manifest has no units field, and after traversal the whole scene is multiplied by one factor chosen so its extent fits a fixed render volume of five units. Body radii are then magnified by a power law and moons are pushed outward by a hard-coded factor, so what is drawn is deliberately not to scale. The module contract does not help either: the position, scale and bound setters an author calls take bare 64-bit floats, and the documentation that names their frame names no unit at all. geo.anchor-shared: Half met, and the missing half is in the specification rather than in implementations. Persistence across sessions is ratified: XR_EXT_spatial_persistence and XR_EXT_spatial_persistence_operations give an anchor a stable identifier that survives a reboot. Sharing is absent. The persistence store has exactly two scopes, one read-only and system managed, the other bounded to the same device, the same user and the same application, and the anchor extension defers sharing to other extensions that do not exist in ratified form. Every extension in the registry with sharing in its name is single-vendor and unratified: XR_FB_spatial_entity_sharing, XR_META_spatial_entity_sharing, XR_META_spatial_entity_group_sharing, XR_BD_spatial_anchor_sharing and XR_ANDROID_anchor_sharing_export. Godot's documentation says sharing is not supported in the spatial entities specification, and that claim holds.

The ratified spatial plane tracking extension, built on the spatial entity framework, is the cross-vendor way to get planes with their bounds, polygon and a 2D mesh. render.raster: The runtime has its own frame graph of render passes driving a forward renderer with clustered lighting and an ordered layer composition; there is no deferred path.
A frame graph represents a single rendering frame as a sequence of frame passes.
Layer Composition is a collection of Layer that is fed to Scene#layers to define rendering order.
render.gpu-api: Targets WebGL 2 and WebGPU behind a graphics-device abstraction, plus a null device for headless use; WebGL 1 was removed at version 2.0.0, and the documentation still calls WebGPU beta while the repository does not.
The engine will seamlessly fall back from WebGPU to WebGL based on browser support.
PlayCanvas is an open-source game engine built on WebGL2 and WebGPU.
render.material: A general-purpose standard material using the metalness workflow, plus lower-level shader materials and a shader-chunk system with parallel GLSL and WGSL trees.
A standard material is the main, general purpose material that is most often used for rendering.
Physically Based Rendering | PlayCanvas Developer Site
a metalness property which makes this stuff simple by defining a material as either a metal, or a non-metal
render.lighting: Directional, omni and spot lights with area shapes, cascaded and variance shadow maps, clustered lighting on by default, image-based lighting from a skybox, and a lightmap baker inside the runtime; there is no reflection-probe or light-probe system, so indirect specular comes from one scene skybox or a per-material cubemap.
The PlayCanvas Engine has built in lightmap generation.
Clustered lighting is enabled by default from PlayCanvas Engine v1.56 onwards.
render.post: A high-dynamic-range camera frame pass covers bloom, ambient occlusion, depth of field, temporal anti-aliasing, grading, lookup tables, vignette and tone mapping; it lives under the repository's extras folder but that folder is re-exported from the main entry point, so it ships in the published package.
Implementation of a simple to use camera rendering pass, which supports SSAO, Bloom and other rendering effects.
Extras is a collection of supplementary APIs designed to extend the capabilities of the PlayCanvas Engine.
render.lod: Level of detail and streaming order exist only for Gaussian splats, where a spatial tree of chunks is fetched by camera distance; for meshes there is no level-of-detail system at all, only per-asset preload flags and on-demand loading, so mesh detail selection is left to the application.
Streamed SOG level-of-detail streaming, PlayCanvas user manual
dynamically loading appropriate levels of detail (LOD) based on the camera's distance
Preloading and Streaming | PlayCanvas Developer Site
Every asset in your project has a property called preload, which is set to true by default.
render.splat: Gaussian splats are a first-class component with their own asset pipeline, global depth sort across components, shadow support and level-of-detail streaming; it reads point-cloud PLY, the compressed SOG format, streamed SOG, Niantic SPZ through a bundled parser script, and glTF carrying the Khronos gaussian-splatting extension, which makes PlayCanvas one of the earliest runtimes to reach this depth.
The GSplatComponent enables an Entity to render 3D Gaussian Splats.
Splat File Formats, PlayCanvas user manual
Binary glTF with the Khronos KHR_gaussian_splatting extension.
render.volumetric: Ray-marched volumetric fog lit by a directional light was added to the camera frame pass at version 2.21.0, but there is no point-cloud loader, no voxel renderer and no volumetric-video path; the raw points draw mode exists only as a drawing primitive.
A raymarched height fog lit by a directional light.
render.text: Text is drawn from multi-channel signed-distance-field font atlases through the element component, one quad per character, in screen space or world space; turning a font file into an atlas is a hosted-editor job, and the runtime only consumes the finished asset.
Text elements are rendered to the screen using a single quad for each character in the string.
Fonts are stored as multi-channel signed distance field (MSDF) atlases rather than fixed-size bitmaps
render.camera: A camera component defines perspective or orthographic viewpoints with clip planes, layer masks, render targets, priority ordering and helpers to move between screen and world space, and it is the object handed to the immersive session.
The CameraComponent enables an Entity to render the scene.
scene.graph: A hierarchy of graph nodes, where an entity is a graph node carrying components; the documentation calls this an entity component system, but the storage is a hash of component instances per entity rather than the data-oriented layout that name usually implies.
The GraphNode class represents a node within a hierarchical scene graph.
Entity Component System (ECS) | PlayCanvas Developer Site
PlayCanvas uses an Entity Component System (ECS) to organize and manage the objects in your application.
scene.transform: Right-handed space with Y up and negative Z forward, column-major matrices and intrinsic X-then-Y-then-Z Euler order, with a full local and world transform split; note that none of these conventions is stated normatively in the documentation, only in source comments.
The 3D space is right-handed, so the rotation around each axis will be counterclockwise

physics.rigid: Static, dynamic and kinematic bodies are provided by a rigid-body component that ships in the runtime but does nothing until the application or project separately loads ammo.js, a browser port of Bullet that is deliberately not bundled because of its size.

But PlayCanvas defines no containment boundary protocol — no event propagation or consumption rule for how a contained experience's messages interact with the host.
PlayCanvas uses a component-based entity system for building interactive 3D applications.
net.world-coupling: PlayCanvas is a client-side web engine. It has no built-in inter-world networking, no world-state mechanism, and no concept of coupling between worlds.

commerce.payment: The PlayCanvas engine builds interactive three-dimensional content in the browser. The hosted editor and publishing service is a separate product; the engine defines no payment exchange for a resource or service.

geo.crs: Earthatile, a separate MIT-licensed project in the PlayCanvas organisation, fixes one Earth frame, the WGS84 ellipsoid, and converts between longitude, latitude, altitude and Earth-centred Cartesian coordinates for its 3D Tiles scenes. Missing: any way to name or choose a different reference system; the runtime itself has no Earth frame.
geo.pose: Earthatile's PlayCanvas integration places the camera at a longitude, latitude and altitude and reads them back from a Cartesian position. Missing: orientation expressed against the Earth, such as heading or a local east-north-up frame; the runtime has no Earth-referenced pose.
scene.parametric: A PlayCanvas geometry class generates a shape's mesh from a few parameters such as a radius and band counts, so a shape can be tessellated at the resolution asked for. Missing: any stored or exchanged curve or surface in mathematical form; every asset format the runtime reads carries meshes.
A geometry class generates the vertex data of a shape on the CPU.
scene.voxel: PlayCanvas publishes a specified voxel format, version 1.1, that stores a sparse voxel octree of a Gaussian splat scene as a JSON header plus a binary tree; the splat-transform tool writes it and the SuperSplat Viewer reads it for collision. Missing: per-voxel properties beyond solid or empty, updates, and any reader in the engine runtime itself.
The format stores a solid/empty voxelization of a Gaussian splat scene as a sparse voxel octree (SVO) in the Laine–Karras node layout
scene.bounds: The streamed splat format carries a binary tree of axis-aligned bounding boxes in its metadata, so a viewer picks which chunks to fetch before loading their splats; for meshes the camera culls mesh instances by their bounding boxes, though only after the mesh is loaded.
The Streamed SOG Format specification, PlayCanvas user manual
Every node carries an axis-aligned bounding box
If enabled, the camera will only render mesh instances whose axis-aligned bounding boxes intersect with the camera's view frustum.
scene.thumbnail: A hosted PlayCanvas project carries an artwork image used for dashboard thumbnails and sharing, and the splat viewer accepts a poster image shown while a scene loads. Missing: a preview image packaged inside an asset file such as glTF or the splat formats.

render.raster: FrooxEngine does not rasterize itself. It runs as a separate .NET process and drives a Unity renderer over inter-process communication and shared memory. The renderer is deliberately replaceable and its source is published under MIT, so a third party can in principle write a substitute renderer against the published IPC contract — but the contract only serves Resonite's own engine, it is not a general rendering standard.

Resonite uses a unique multi-process architecture, where the majority of Resonite is a fully custom engine running with a modern .NET 10 runtime. The engine communicates with the Unity Renderer process via IPC (inter process communication) and shared memory
This architecture allows for much higher performance and properly isolates the renderer from the rest of the engine, allowing it to be replaced in the future.
render.gpu-api: Direct3D 11 through Unity, stated plainly in the optimisation documentation. That means Windows-first, and no Vulkan or Metal path is documented. Nothing about the graphics interface is exposed to creators — it is an implementation detail of the replaceable renderer process.
Resonite currently uses Direct3D 11 for rendering in Unity.

render.material: Materials are first-class data-model components backed by a fixed set of built-in shaders. Custom shaders are explicitly not supported, which caps what an imported material can be reproduced as. This is a closed material set, not an exchangeable material description.

render.lod: The engine does frustum culling for rendering only; it does not cull CPU work, and there is no general level-of-detail or streaming-order system. Creators are told to build their own world culling. There is an LOD component but the documentation frames real LOD systems as future work.

scene.graph: Resonite's scene graph is a tree of Slots holding Components, and everything in it — down to individual fields — is a data-model element with a reference ID that can be saved, loaded and synchronized. This is a genuinely uniform reflective model, but it is entirely Resonite's own; there is no published mapping onto any external scene-graph standard.
The data model allows for change detection, value synchronization, unified structure, and serialization of any and all types that FrooxEngine encounters.

Workers are, in essence, containers for sync elements and other workers to provide a specific, individual task for the engine. Examples of workers include slots, components, sub-classes of components, and streams.

scene.transform: Resonite uses a LEFT-handed, Y-up, +Z-forward frame, matching Unity. glTF — the format Resonite imports most cleanly — is right-handed with -Z forward, so every transform, rotation sign and winding order has to be flipped on the way in and on the way out. Rotations are quaternions internally. Positions, rotations and scales live on every slot whether or not it renders anything.
Resonite uses a left-handed coordinate system. Rotation about any axis is, therefore, positive in the clockwise direction, and negative in the counterclockwise direction.
This makes Resonite's coordinate system follow the same convention as Unity.
scene.container: Resonite's own container is `.resonitepackage`, a ZIP holding record files plus an Assets folder of SHA256-named blobs. It is documented, and it is explicitly a distribution format — but the docs state outright that compatibility with Unity packages and with other VR platforms is a NON-goal, and that it is not meant to be produced by third-party tools. So it carries Resonite content out of Resonite for backup and re-import into Resonite, and nothing else. The raw data-model file is `.brson`: Brotli-compressed BSON, no assets embedded.
FrooxEngine data tree files are compressed with Brotli and are serialized in the BRSON format. These files do not contain any referenced assets such as meshes and textures.

On the way out, the export wizard offers Collada and OBJ only; FBX is listed as currently disabled and glTF is not offered at all. Exported skinned meshes lose bone weights and shape keys, which Resonite's own docs concede. Draco is explicitly unsupported on import, which is also why VRM 1.x cannot be loaded, and meshopt appears nowhere in the documentation.

scene.material-x: There is no material exchange format. Because model formats disagree about PBR, Resonite works around it with a filename convention: put textures next to the model named `_albedo`, `_normal`, `_metallic` and so on, and the importer wires them into a material. That is a local heuristic, not an interchange mechanism, and it only works for single-material models each in their own folder. Nothing carries material definitions back out.

Because there's no well supported standard for PBR materials in model files, Resonite's model importer allows using a naming convention to automatically map texture files to the material based on the file naming.

physics.determinism: Resonite makes no determinism claim. The whole networking design removes the need for it: one machine is the host and its data model is replicated to everyone else, so clients do not independently simulate and do not need to agree bit-for-bit.
When a user starts a new session for a world, they become the host, with other users connecting to them as clients.
net.replication: This is Resonite's single most distinctive property. Replication is not something a developer opts into per object — the data-model primitives are built so that everything in them replicates and persists automatically, over a binary protocol. Fields marked as "driven" are the documented exception and stay local. It is a genuine full-data-model sync, and it is entirely proprietary: nothing outside Resonite speaks it.
the value of a driven field will not be synchronized across the network. This allows for per-user values or local calculations of things that would otherwise be expensive to network.
Resonite is built on a novel engine architecture, which makes real-time networking, persistence and interoperability a solid guarantee without any extra work involved.

At the core are various programming primitives, which are equivalents of variables, references, arrays, dictionaries, trees and other common building blocks, but designed so they can be automatically replicated over network or persisted.
Real-time replication uses a highly efficient binary protocol, designed to save processing and memory resources as well as network bandwidth.
net.time: There is a synchronized world time available to in-world scripting, exposed through a component that outputs current world time and through ProtoFlux nodes. It is a session-local clock for ordering in-world events, not a cross-operator time standard.
Component:AuthorityTimeBase: A component used to control the world time.
net.address: Resonite has a real, documented, human-readable addressing scheme for saved content: `resrec:///[OWNER]/[RECORD_ID]` or `resrec:///[OWNER]/[PATH/TO/RECORD]`. It is registered as an operating-system protocol handler so a link in a browser opens the item in game, and public records resolve over the HTTP API without authentication. It resolves only against Resonite's cloud, so it names places and things inside one operator's namespace.
resrec:///[OWNER]/[RECORD_ID] identifies a record by its owner and ID.
These links are also associated with Resonite on the operating system level, so clicking a recrec:/// URL in a browser will spawn out the item in-game.
Records may be accessed externally via the API. Records that are public can be accessed without authorization, while records that are private require appropriate authorization to access.
logic.script: In-world programming is ProtoFlux only. There is also a documented C# plugin path loaded with a `-LoadAssembly` command-line argument, but the docs are blunt that a plugin touching the data model makes your session unjoinable for anyone without the identical plugin, and there is no distribution system. So plugins are a local extension mechanism, not a portable scripting runtime.
A plugin is a compiled Assembly / DLL written in C# that can be loaded into Resonite at runtime with a launch argument.
If you use plugins that modify the Data model, other players will not be able to join sessions you host with them active, unless they have the same version of each applicable plugin.
There is no built-in distribution system. You are in charge of distribution
logic.sandbox: There is no engine-level sandbox with limits. What exists is a per-world role permission system expressed as components in the world graph — Admin, Builder, Moderator, Guest, Spectator, each inheriting the one below, governing saving, spawning, transferring objects out, avatar swapping and streaming. Above that sits one coarse gate, "Unsafe Mode", which a world must opt into before experimental nodes such as writing files to disk will run, and which can be restricted by a startup-config allowlist. Below it there is nothing: no memory cap, no CPU quota, no execution timeout for guest ProtoFlux, and an impulse chain that does not yield will stall the whole engine. The documented advice for protecting content is social — do not give strangers Builder rights. Note also that Resonite's own security policy does not treat your IP address as private, because sessions are peer to peer.
The data model can only function without issue when everyone in a session agrees on what the data model should be.
Avoid setting users as Builder in a world you want protected" and "Avoid spawning items in sessions with users you do not know or trust

A non-async impulse chain will run entirely in one engine update, halting the engine for as long as it takes to complete.
logic.budget: There is no enforced resource budget for guest content. All the substantial documentation is advisory optimisation guidance — what makes worlds slow and how to profile it — with no engine-side cap on memory, node count, polygon count or CPU time. The only hard numeric limits documented anywhere are administrative rather than runtime: cloud storage starting at one gigabyte, 256 cloud-variable definitions per user and 8192 per group, a default of 64 audio voices, and a 128-triangle cap on custom 3D badges. Nothing bounds an imported avatar or a spawned item.
In general, slot count does not inherently matter for the performance of an object.

persist.content-addr: This is a real, shipped content-addressing implementation, not a design intention. Every asset is named by the SHA-256 hash of its own bytes, referenced as `resdb:///<hash>.<ext>`, de-duplicated on upload and against the user's storage quota, and fetchable over plain HTTPS at `assets.resonite.com/<hash>`. Two caveats matter: the links are unauthenticated, so possession of a hash is possession of the content; and Resonite's own release notes advise creators to prefer `resrec:///` because `resdb:///` links are not guaranteed.

avatar.body: There is no portable avatar description. An avatar is an ordinary Resonite slot hierarchy with Resonite components on it, saved as a record or a `.resonitepackage`. Resonite READS FBX, glTF and Blender rigs and turns them into its own structure; it cannot WRITE any avatar format back out, and VRM — the one widely adopted portable avatar standard — is explicitly not supported on import. Community tooling converts VRM to `.resonitepackage` outside the platform.

avatar.skeleton: Resonite does not require an agreed bone standard — it guesses. On import it runs case-insensitive, substring-tolerant name heuristics ("cheese_hips" resolves to the hip bone) and fills in its own `BodyNode` enum, which is close to but not the same as Unity's HumanBodyBones: it adds Root, View, LeftController, RightController, palms and per-finger tips. The heuristic is what makes rigs built for other platforms work, so in practice it interoperates well, but nothing is guaranteed and there is no declared bone standard to conform to. Digitigrade legs are not supported.

When you import a model, Resonite uses pattern matching and heuristics to figure out the layout of your Model's Bones. This means that bone names are largely case insensitive and can have additional data around the name.
If you have a rigged model that's compatible with other VR Platforms such as VRChat etc, then it should work out of the box.
BodyNode is an Enum, which refers to a part of the body within the Standard Resonite Avatar System. It has a lot of values which loosely map to a human skeleton.
This is created and assigned to by the Assimp import system that FrooxEngine uses internally, and cannot be edited in game without mods.
avatar.expression: Two halves, and they point opposite ways. Visemes ARE an external set: Resonite's Viseme enum is index-for-index the Oculus/OVR LipSync fifteen, proven by Yellow Dog Man's own OVRCompat source. Facial EXPRESSIONS are not: Resonite ships roughly ninety proprietary AvatarExpression names and deliberately does not adopt ARKit or VRCFT Unified Expressions. Adding Unified Expressions to the matching heuristics is an open, unimplemented issue in Resonite's own tracker, and users currently bridge the gap with a third-party mod. Blendshape auto-assignment does opportunistically match VRChat's `vrc.` prefix and some Japanese kana.
In Resonite we use a fairly standard list of Visemes loosely based on similar platforms and products in the space

Due to the prevalence of the prefix vrc. on a large amount of commonly found avatars, when a blend shape that contains the prefix vrc. is found, it takes preference over all over blend shapes for that one Viseme.

avatar.retarget: Resonite has no humanoid animation retargeting. Its animation format binds tracks to a node name and a field name, not to a body-part abstraction, so an animation authored for one body does not transfer to another. The documentation goes further and says you cannot drive a VRIK rig with an animation at all — the engine fights it — and recommends posing users with anchors instead.
To drive a VRIK like a person however, you cannot currently drive one directly or switch out the drivers with a VRIK at runtime. The game will actively fight what you are doing.
the animation being imported onto a full VRIK rig will prevent the VRIK from being generated.
Node indicates which object in the hierarchy given track controls, while Property specifies which of its fields will be controlled when the animation is bound to a scene objects.
avatar.wearable: The engine gives you attachment machinery — AvatarObjectSlot and AvatarPoseNode let separate avatar pieces bind to named body nodes, and Snapper handles accessories such as hats and glasses — so items genuinely do travel with a user between worlds inside their inventory. The wiki's "Avatar standard" page is explicitly a user proposal, with at least one widely used competing fork, and it admits blendshape names are avatar-specific.

avatar.lod: There is no avatar level of detail, no avatar performance ranking, and no built-in avatar culling. Resonite's own comparison table for incoming VRChat users lists avatar performance blocking as not applicable.

There is no perfect user culling system. All of them have some disadvantage or oddity due to a current lack of flexibility in Resonite to make something that works consistently, for every avatar, and in a reliable and simple way.

avatar.identity: An avatar can be bound to one cloud user for permission purposes — SimpleAvatarProtection names a single user who may wear, save or export it — but that is asset ownership, not identity. Resonite's docs explicitly warn that what an avatar displays about who you are is not trustworthy: nameplates and badges are avatar-author-controlled and can be faked, and users are told to check the server-side Session screen instead. There is no credential or attestation concept.
it is possible for a user to pretend to be a Mentor, Moderator, or Resonite Team member.
the SimpleAvatarProtection component prevents all users, other than the single user listed on the component, from saving the avatar, grabbing materials off of it, or equipping it.

scene.animation: Resonite has its own animation formats: AnimX, a raw binary format with an "AnimX" magic word and optional LZ4 or LZMA encoding, and AnimJ, a JSON authoring format that must be imported and converted to AnimX before it can be used. AnimJ is a genuine third-party authoring route — you can write animation as JSON outside Resonite and bring it in. But neither has a vendor-published specification: the AnimX binary layout on the wiki is community reverse-engineering, `Elements.Assets` is not a public repository, and there is no AnimX repo in the Yellow Dog Man organisation. Bezier tracks are documented as not yet supported.
AnimJ is a custom import format for Animation asset files in Resonite. It allows you to build arbitrary animation tracks as external JSON files and import them as native Animation assets.
They must first be converted to AnimX by importing them into Resonite.
An Animx is encoded in raw binary, and as such is a little difficult to decode.

scene.skeleton: Skeletons come in through Assimp from FBX, glTF or Blender and are mapped by name heuristics into Resonite's BodyNode enum, stored on a BipedRig component as a dictionary from body node to slot. There is no way to write a skeleton back out to an interchange format — the model export wizard offers Collada and OBJ, and OBJ carries no rig at all.

scene.morph: Blend shapes are supported and are the mechanism behind visemes and facial expressions, with heuristic auto-assignment by name. SlowRealtimeAccurate uses the actual transformed geometry for bounds calculation ... it will respect things like blendshapes in addition to bones.
We split all blend shape names by any non-letter character into segments for searching.
scene.instancing: GPU mesh instancing happens automatically where a static mesh and material combination repeats, and the docs are specific about what defeats it: skinned mesh renderers are never instanced, and differing material property blocks break instancing across copies. Procedural assets are not instanced across copies; baking them to static meshes enables instancing and lets one copy live in memory.
If you have multiple instances of the same static mesh/material combination, they will be instanced on most shaders.

SkinnedMeshRenderers are not eligible for GPU instancing. Additionally, different material property blocks will prevent instancing across different copies of the same mesh, even if the underlying material is the same.
input.eye: Eye tracking is a strong, first-class feature rather than a bolt-on. The EyeManager component is set up automatically for avatars with detectable eyes and exposes a detailed per-eye model — openness, widen, squeeze, frown, brow verticals, and pupil size in millimetres — plus simulated saccades when no hardware is present. Several trackers are natively integrated. The data model is Resonite's own; the only external piece is OSC used as a transport for Steam Link data.

render.volumetric: Point clouds import from LiDAR LAS/LAZ and ASCII PTS, and from ordinary 3D formats in a vertex-extraction mode. Internally they are MeshX with point topology rather than triangles. There is no documented point-cloud EXPORT at any format, so LiDAR data goes in and cannot come back out. Volumetric video is not documented.

render.camera: Cameras exist as in-world objects and worlds define spawn points, but the documentation treats viewpoints as ordinary slots with components rather than as a defined, bindable camera model. Nothing describes moving a viewpoint between systems.

net.transport: Three documented session transports — LiteNetLib over UDP, QUIC (experimental, still missing NAT punch-through), and Steam Sockets — plus a NAT punch-through service and regional relay fallback. All ports are dynamic; port forwarding and UPnP are explicitly unsupported. The transports are ordinary technology but what rides on them is a closed binary protocol, so a third party cannot speak it. Live session traffic is documented as unencrypted by default.
Depending on your settings and the settings of the session host you'll connect with either one of the following protocols:" listing "LNL (LiteNetLib)", "QUIC", "Steam Sockets
Resonite does not currently offer support for port forwarding or uPNP/NAT-PMP.
The relay acts as a third point between both clients, and all traffic is routed through it.
All live session traffic, such as Data model updates, voice streams, audio streams and locally shared files, are not encrypted.
net.authority: Authority is coarse and centralised: exactly one host per session, and if the host leaves the session ends. There is no documented host migration. Below that, exclusive write control over an individual element is expressed as "linkage" — a driver takes exclusive control of a field — rather than as transferable per-object ownership. Roles (Admin, Builder, Moderator, Guest, Spectator) govern what a user may do, not who owns what.
Linkage is a way to give exclusive control of a sync element to one source, often referred to a driver.
Builder: Full editing permissions of the world.
A session has exactly one host; if the host quits the game, the session will close.
net.interest: There is no interest management. The design replicates the whole world to everyone, and the documented consequences follow: initial world synchronization time scales with total element count, and voice is sent to every user in the session regardless of whisper range — whisper only changes how far it can be HEARD, not who receives the stream. Video is relayed through the host to all clients.
Changing your microphone to whisper mode will only change the max range it can be heard, the data stream will still be sent to all users in a session.
Initial synchronization of a world. The more slots, components, whatever elements there are in a world, the longer it will take to synchronize the world state.
Because steams are sent to the host and from there to each client, be aware that this can use a lot of bandwidth
net.session: Session establishment is fully documented and works: six access levels from Private through Anyone, bearer-token authentication with optional TOTP two-factor, and a public unauthenticated listing endpoint. The catch is the compatibility hash — a client can only join if its data-model hash matches the host's exactly, which locks joining to one build of one implementation.
The compatibility-hash sessions needs to have. A Resonite client can only join a session if this hash matches between client and server.
SessionAccessLevel controls the access level of a session. Possible values are: Private / LAN / Contacts / ContactsPlus / RegisteredUsers / Anyone
net.discovery: Public session discovery is real and open: `GET /sessions` returns running public sessions and needs no authentication, worlds are searchable through a paged search endpoint, and there is an MIT-licensed official web browser listing every public world and session. Discovery covers Resonite's own cloud only, and Universes deliberately partition it — a Universe's sessions are invisible from the main list and vice versa.
GET /sessions — Returns a list of public sessions filtered by the given parameters. Does not require authentication
It features a list of all worlds and all currently running public sessions in Resonite, allowing you to quickly open them inside Resonite.
Users in your universe will not be able to see Sessions from other universes or the regular Resonite session list.
net.presence: Presence works well inside Resonite: a SignalR connection over WebSocket carries status updates, session updates and contact changes, and contacts are bilateral. It is single-operator. Nothing federates presence across operators, and Universes explicitly hide their users from the main network.
The Resonite API uses the SignalR protocol for server-driven notifications such as informing the client of new chat messages or status changes.
Resonite considers two users to be contacts when both users have each other as a contact with the status 'Accepted'
Users not in your universe will not be able to see your Sessions
net.handoff: You can carry state between worlds, in two ways. Your cloud inventory follows you everywhere. And "transfer grabbing" lets you literally hold an object while changing worlds and arrive with it — but the docs warn that anything referenced in the world's Assets slot is lost because the references break. So objects move; the things they point at do not reliably move with them.
Transfer Grabbing (sometimes called "grab smuggling") is a Resonite feature that allows a user to transfer items (Slot's ObjectRoot or Grabbable) from one world to another.
You can transfer anything, but the down side is that anything referenced in the Assets Slot will be lost as references will be broken
net.media: Live video sharing exists and is host-relayed over the session's own transport, needing no external server. Ingest is a fixed localhost RTMP endpoint with h264 video and AAC audio and no negotiation — not WebRTC, not SRT. Inbound remote streams accept RTMP and RTSP but not their encrypted variants. Streaming can be disabled per role.
Neither the Unity Native or the libvlc backend support the encrypted variants, rtmps and rtsps.

this feature allows sharing of either your desktop or of a custom video stream(For example, from OBS or FFmpeg) to other uses in the session through Resonite's internal networking, requiring no external servers or setup.
audio.voice: Voice is Opus, from a Yellow Dog Man fork of the reference library, with RNNoise for noise suppression. Five modes: Mute, Whisper, Normal, Shout and Broadcast, where Broadcast turns spatialization off entirely. The codec is a real standard; the transport is Resonite's own unencrypted session stream, and voice goes to everyone in the session regardless of mode.
Update opus library (used for encoding voice & audio streams) from 1.3.1 to latest 1.5.2
Normal is the typical spatialized voice mode, Shout has increased volume, and range- good for large maps, and Broadcast disables spatialization
net.prediction: Latency hiding with later correction is documented for the data model: a local change applies at once, and when the host keeps a different value it re-syncs the authoritative one to the client, rolling the local change back. Missing: no motion prediction, extrapolation, interpolation of remote movement or lag compensation is documented, so the correction covers conflicting writes only, not smoothing of what other users do. Searched the Resonite Wiki (wiki.resonite.com, MediaWiki search over all pages including release notes and podcast transcripts) on 2026-10-20 for prediction, reconciliation, reconcile, rollback, rolling back, optimistic, lag compensation, client-side prediction, extrapolation, dead reckoning and latency; the hits that bear on networking are Data model synchronization (optimistic concurrency, rolling back a discarded update) and Networking information (clients connect to the session host over LNL, QUIC or Steam sockets); the other hits were physics-rate interpolation in a podcast, quaternion and value extrapolation in release notes, a ProtoFlux optimisation page that uses 'dead-reckoning' to mean guessing instead of testing, a world named for a story, animation and texture interpolation, audio buffer latency and mesh-upload latency.
When you connect to a Resonite session, you're starting a connection to the session's host.
When an update is discarded, the host will re-sync the authoritative value for that piece of data with the client (effectively rolling back the 'optimistic' local change the client made).
persist.world: Persistence is explicit, not automatic. Nothing survives a session unless someone saves it, and a session ends the moment its host leaves. Autosave exists but is off by default on headless servers. Individual slots carry a `Persistent` boolean, and turning it off excludes that slot and everything under it from the save. The persistence serialization is a deliberately different mode from the network protocol and is built for forwards and backwards compatibility.
For persistence, a different binary serialization mode is used than the real-time synchronization, which is designed for both forwards and backwards compatibility across Resonite versions.
Persistent | Bool | Whether this slot will be saved, for example to the Inventory. If this is disabled, the slot and all its descendants will not be saved.
Saving must be configured or invoked, saving is not automatic.
persist.inventory: This is one of the few real cross-world inventory implementations in the study. Every user gets a cloud-backed, folder-structured inventory that follows them to any machine after login, and items spawn into any world. Items CAN leave the platform, as `.resonitepackage` archives — but only back into Resonite. Sharing is by public folder, which works as a capability handed out by link rather than a listing, and content in a shared folder counts only against the owner's quota. Free accounts start with one gigabyte.
It allows you to save and browse objects—such as tools, avatars, decorations, and more.
All accounts start with 1 gigabyte (GB) of storage space on the cloud. Your storage space can be increased by subscribing.
Anything in a public folder can be spawned and used by anyone who has the folder, but only the owner can save new items to it
When a public folder is created it is not immediately available for all Resonite users. It cannot be found on any public listings or systems unless it is shared with those systems.
persist.prefs: Some settings do follow the user rather than the machine — full-body-tracking calibration is documented as tied to the account. There is a full account data export tool published by Yellow Dog Man, so preferences and content can be pulled out. But nothing is portable to another platform: the export tool's README names cross-engine compatibility as an explicit non-goal.
This is saved automatically and is tied to your account/settings.
We do not intend to process the contents in a way that makes it compatible with other engines such as Unity, Unreal etc.
identity.root: Identity is a Resonite account: an immutable `U-` prefixed user ID, distinct from the display username, plus a per-installation Machine ID derived from an RSA keypair hashed with SHA-256. It is a single-operator identifier with no external resolution. Notably, SAML single sign-on IS available at every tier, so an enterprise can authenticate its own people INTO Resonite — but the resulting identity is still a Resonite record and nothing exports outward.
A user's User ID (also written userid) is an immutable ID linked to their user account.
Never ever assume a user ID will match a username.
On first launch the game generates a random RSA keypair and stores it in this file.
identity.credential: There is no verifiable credential format. Authentication is a bespoke bearer token — `Authorization: res <user-id>:<token>` — with a hardware-derived UID header, plus optional TOTP two-factor. Resonite's own two-factor page names FIDO keys, magic links and web3 authentication as things it does NOT support and points people at the issue tracker. No W3C verifiable credential or decentralised identifier concept appears anywhere.
If you want support for something like a Yubikey/FIDO Key, Email codes, Magic links, Web3 Authentication etc. then please check out GitHub.
identity.exchange: The only credential-exchange protocols documented are inbound authentication ones: SAML for enterprise sign-in, and an OAuth path that Yellow Dog Man's own sample repository describes as still under construction with credentials handed out manually. Neither is a mechanism for two worlds to request and present claims about a user.
Resonite's OAuth is still under construction.
These aren't easy to get right now and are given out manually to select applications or scenarios.
identity.capability: Permission grants exist as world roles — Admin, Builder, Moderator, Guest, Spectator — and are enforced by the session host. They are not readable by any party that did not issue them; they live inside one session's data model. Separately, `resdb:///` links function as unauthenticated bearer capabilities, which is a capability grant of a sort but one that cannot be scoped, audited or revoked.
Moderator: Ability to kick, silence, respawn, and change the role of users.
Resdb links are unauthenticated and anyone with a resdb link can access its content
identity.privacy: There is no selective disclosure mechanism toward receiving worlds: identity is a single account record held by one operator, and there are no claims to reveal in part.
