render.lighting: Real-time lights with shadows, deferred shading for opaque and cutout materials and forward for transparent ones, plus baked and real-time reflection probes storing cube maps. render.post: Post-processing exists and is a user-side graphics setting — motion blur intensity, bloom, ambient occlusion — but a world cannot author or change it. logic.behaviour: This is the capability Resonite scores best on in spirit and worst on in portability. ProtoFlux is a node-based visual language that is part of the object: when you export an item as a `.resonitepackage`, the ProtoFlux goes with it, alongside the hierarchy, components and bones. The fabric file has no format-version field and the dialects still disagree inside one public repository at one commit: one sample manifest uses lower-case keys with url and hash, its neighbour uses capitalised keys with sUrl and sHash, and the signed sample's own payload uses the lower-case spelling while the unsigned source beside it uses the capitalised one. The services block is described three different ways in public: a name-keyed object in the engine note, an array in every sample, and a list of name, type, endpoint and modules records in the documentation. The vendor states outright that the format is not stable before version 1.0.0 and that fabrics made before this release must be updated. The local row records an observed link mismatch from the 2026-07 to 2026-08 generation that no public source states, and the single-Call interface has since removed that failure mode.

net.transport: Three layers in parallel: a WebSocket for signalling, WebRTC by default for real-time streams with optional legacy SRT and EFP, and HTTP or HTTPS for static assets. Reliable payloads must work over either the WebSocket or the WebRTC reliable channel and receivers must accept both for the whole session. One caution for an implementer: the normative channel table says five SCTP data channels and three other places in the same documentation set say six, so the count is not settled in the text; channels are matched by label, and five labels are defined.
TeleportXR protocol.rst, The Teleport Protocol (teleportxr/Teleport, main)

Teleport is a top-level application-layer protocol. It uses three transport layers in parallel: a WebSocket connection for signaling, a media/data transport (WebRTC by default, with optional SRT/EFP support) for real-time streams, and an HTTP(S) service for static asset retrieval.
* **WebRTC** (default): five SCTP data channels for application payloads plus zero or more RTP media tracks for audio (see :doc:`audio`). Recommended for all new implementations.
When all six SCTP data channels have opened, the server transmits the binary ``Handshake`` frame
A receiver MUST accept reliable-channel payloads on both transports for the entire lifetime of the session, not only during early connection setup.
net.media: Video and audio ride WebRTC media tracks. Audio is Opus with the payload type, sample rate, channel count, frame duration, forward error correction and discontinuous transmission all published in a seventeen-byte block inside the setup command, and both sides must advertise and honour those values in the session description. Video has its own chapters for frame structure, metadata and recovery.
Audio is carried as one or more **WebRTC media tracks** (RTP / SRTP) negotiated in the same SDP exchange that creates the data channels described in :doc:`data_transfer`.
Implementations MUST advertise these in SDP (``a=fmtp:111 useinbandfec=1;usedtx=1;…``) and MUST honour the values received from the peer in the answered SDP.
net.session: A full connection state machine with four named phases, reconnection, timeouts and an enumerated state list. The client repeats a connect message until it gets a response carrying a client and server identifier as unsigned 64-bit numbers; a matching server identifier lets cached resource and node identifiers persist across a reconnect, though the client may not assume it. Authentication of the asset service is still deliberately outside the protocol: the HTTP service is shared by every connected client with no per-client authentication. Since 2026-06-16 the reference implementations have added a session-level identity handshake on the signalling channel, which the protocol document does not yet describe; see identity.root.
A Teleport session passes through four phases: Discovery, Signaling, Handshake, and Streaming.
if it matches a previous connection from the same client, cached resource and node ids may persist (but this must not be assumed);
The service is shared by every connected client; there is no per-client HTTP authentication.
net.authority: The server owns the ground truth of the simulation. It may grant a client control of particular nodes, for example the client's own head and hands, but it stays the final arbiter, and it also decides what the client's control inputs mean.
the server is the final arbiter
The server determines the meaning of the client's control inputs.
net.interest: Interest management is the design centre: worlds are never downloaded whole, the server tells each client which nodes and resources to track, and two clients on one server may hold entirely different sets.

But the server should send
only the data any client needs at a given time.
Clients generally keep only a part of the world state at any time.
net.replication: State moves as command packets from server to client and message packets from client to server, over a setup command, a handshake and then updates. Ordering tools are per message and work identically on both reliable transports: an acknowledgement identifier that increases monotonically per session, and a separately acknowledged confirmation number on node state.
commands from server to client to update states; requests from client to server to update other states.
``ack_id`` is used by ``AckedCommand`` and is monotonically increasing per session — clients may discard any command whose ``ack_id`` is less than or equal to the highest one already processed.
net.time: Time is in microseconds. The setup command carries the session start as a server wall-clock value in Unix time and every other time on the wire is an offset from it, with a ping and pong pair for latency. The limit is stated plainly: the client's own session-relative timestamps are monotonic within one session and are not comparable across clients or to any wall clock, so this is a session clock rather than a shared ordering guarantee between participants.
Time is expressed in microseconds. The setup command specifies the session start time in UTC Unix time, and all other times on the wire are offsets from this.
Monotonic within a session; not comparable across clients or to any UTC clock.
net.presence: Presence is inferred from the scene, not announced. Another client arrives as an ordinary node on the geometry channel, and a voice arrives as an audio track whose session-description identifier is the decimal uid of the node that emits it. The protocol states outright that no signalling message tells a client anything about another client's avatar, and that client identifiers are never exposed to other clients. Two earlier claims in this row have been retracted: the peer message form and the audio participant state change command are both withdrawn upstream, and the command identifiers for AudioSourceMapping and AudioParticipantStateChange are now reserved with servers forbidden to send them.
Every avatar message concerns the recipient's **own** avatar. No signaling message tells a client anything about another client's avatar.
Client uids are never exposed to other clients.

The ``NodeDataType`` value ``AudioEmitter`` and the ``AudioSourceMapping`` / ``AudioParticipantStateChange`` command ids remain **reserved** — servers MUST NOT send them, and clients MAY ignore them if received.
net.address: A client is launched with a teleport URL and the path inside it identifies the requested session on the server; the WebSocket is opened at that host, port and path, and the path may be empty. That is a launch address, not a naming or resolution system, and the port is by convention rather than assignment.
where ``<path>`` is taken from the ``teleport://`` URL the client was launched with. The path identifies the requested session on the server (it may be empty).
typically on port 8080 (any port is acceptable as long as the client knows to try it)
net.handoff: There is no crossing between servers and no arrival with state intact. A search of the whole published documentation for the portaling standard, its standards body, the word portal and any form of interoperate returns nothing, and the chapter list confirms no such chapter exists. Whether an inter-world destination address could legitimately be a teleport URL is an open composition question that nobody owns; that framing is the project's own reading and has no public source.

scene.container: The protocol states outright that Teleport has no file format, and that the Teleport network is part of the Internet but not part of the Web. A node here is a changing object inside a live stream with no URL, not addressable from outside the session, where a world-addressing API means a fetchable, editable record by the same name. Anyone building a bridge between the two meets this on the first day. One qualification since 2026-06-16: most geometry now arrives as a mesh pointer, a URL the client fetches and decodes by file extension, so ordinary asset files do cross the boundary even though the scene itself has no document form.
The Teleport network is part of the Internet, but it is not part of the Web.
A ``MeshPointer`` chunk has the same layout as :ref:`texture_pointer_payload`, with a meaningful axes-standard byte. Most geometry is delivered this way rather than inline.
scene.graph: A node is an object positioned in three dimensions that may have child nodes forming a hierarchy, delivered as its own payload type with a fixed-size header, an optional component record, an explicit remove-nodes payload and a resource lifecycle. Nodes are also how per-client state enters the scene: one node is named as a client's origin, the frame its tracking is measured from.
An object positioned in 3D Space. A node may have child nodes, forming a hierarchy.

``SetOriginNodeCommand`` names one node as a client's **origin**: the origin of
that client's local tracking space, expressed as a node in the server's global
space.
scene.transform: Handedness and vertical axis are negotiated rather than assumed. The client declares its native axes in the handshake, the server publishes the axes its scene is authored in, and every server-to-client packet carrying geometry is already converted into the client's standard. The standard is a one-byte value with four complete named combinations and discriminator bits so that no two are the same byte, and a server must support at least the engineering and OpenGL styles. Assets fetched over HTTP are the exception: they are served as authored and the pointer chunk declares which frame they are in, so the client converts. Transforms are local to the parent, and a root node is expressed directly in the server's global space.
The protocol is intended to be easily implementable on differing hardware and software platforms, so it does not specify an axis standard but rather negotiates this between client and server.
A server must be capable of supporting clients in at least ``EngineeringStyle`` and ``GlStyle``.
* All transforms are local, i.e. relative to the parent node.
scene.units: The protocol declares the unit outright: linear units are metres. That single sentence is the thing every other subject in this group is missing, and it sits in the same conventions chapter as the axis negotiation, so scale and orientation are settled together before any geometry moves.
* Quaternions are stored as ``vec4_packed`` with the layout ``(x, y, z, w)``.
scene.geometry: Meshes are a first-class payload type on the geometry channel, with a pointer form for fetching one over HTTP and reusing an already-delivered resource. One constraint a working group should note: only Draco compression is emitted, and uncompressed meshes are not supported on the wire.
A ``Mesh`` chunk carries a compressed mesh resource (geometry + skin binding). Only ``MeshCompressionType::DRACO`` is currently emitted; uncompressed meshes are not supported on the wire.
The body fetched from the URL is **not** necessarily a :ref:`mesh_payload`; the client selects a decoder from the URL's extension:
scene.texture: Textures are their own payload type with a pointer form for reuse, and large ones are normally promoted to the pointer form and fetched over HTTP rather than sent inline.
A ``Texture`` chunk carries an inline compressed texture. Large textures (over ~1 MiB) are normally promoted to a :ref:`texture_pointer_payload` instead.
scene.material-x: A material payload carries a metallic-roughness description with a list of extension records, and textures it names travel as their own chunks, so a material does cross between implementations. What does not work is the per-object variation: the MaterialInstance payload type exists in the enumeration but is reserved, is not emitted, and has an unspecified body that receivers must skip. An earlier claim in this row that a shared definition and its per-object variations travel independently was wrong and is withdrawn.
A ``Material`` chunk carries a PBR (metallic-roughness) material descriptor and a list of extension records.
Reserved. ``MaterialInstance`` (id 3) is not currently emitted; the body is unspecified and receivers must skip the chunk by advancing past ``payloadSize`` bytes.
scene.animation: Animation is a payload type on the geometry channel, carrying per-bone keyframe tracks, and clips are more usually delivered out of band as files through an animation pointer.

An ``Animation`` chunk carries a per-bone keyframe track. Clips are more commonly delivered out-of-band as files via an :ref:`animation_pointer_payload` chunk; the inline form below is what the fetched body decodes to when it is not a glTF-family file.
scene.skeleton: A skeleton payload is the ordered list of bone-node identifiers making up a skeletal hierarchy, and the bones themselves are ordinary scene nodes. A mesh names the skeleton it is skinned to and maps its own bones onto it, with an explicit marker for an unmapped bone.
A ``Skeleton`` chunk gives the ordered list of bone-node uids that make up a skeletal hierarchy. The bones themselves are normal scene nodes sent as :ref:`node_payload` chunks.
- Per-bone joint indices into the referenced skeleton. ``-1`` marks an unmapped bone.
render.text: Text in three dimensions has two payload types of its own, a font atlas holding glyph-position metadata keyed by point size and a text canvas holding the renderable contents, so legible text is a protocol concern rather than an application one.
A ``FontAtlas`` chunk carries the glyph-position metadata for a font, keyed by point size. The actual glyph bitmap is delivered as a separate ``Texture`` whose uid is given here.
A ``TextCanvas`` chunk carries the renderable contents of a text canvas referenced by a Node's :ref:`TextCanvas component <node_payload>`.
audio.stream: Audio has a full chapter: Opus with named defaults for payload type, sample rate, channels, frame duration, forward error correction and discontinuous transmission, a selective forwarding topology, a seventeen-byte configuration block inside the setup command, a per-listener cap with five named selection policies, and a lifecycle. Codec, sample rate and channel count cannot be changed mid-session.
A 17-byte block inside :ref:`setup_command` describing the audio configuration the server will use for this session. Clients MUST configure their decoder and microphone path to match.
Mid-session reconfiguration of codec, sample rate or channel count is **not** supported: changes to :ref:`audio_config` require a new ``SetupCommand`` (i.e. a fresh session).
audio.voice: Live voice between participants is carried by the same audio chapter. In a room session the server is a selective forwarding unit: each microphone arrives on one inbound track and a chosen subset is forwarded to every other listener as separate outbound tracks, with loopback suppression required and hysteresis recommended before a speaker is dropped from a listener's set.
In a multi-client (room) session the server acts as a **Selective Forwarding Unit (SFU)**
The SFU MUST NOT forward a participant's own microphone back to them (loopback suppression).
audio.source: Positioning a sound is now a single rule and it is a good one: the outbound track's session-description identifier is set to the decimal uid of the node that emits the sound, and that is the only binding between the audio transport and the scene. Identifier zero, or one naming a node the client cannot place, plays without position, so an announcer or a music bed needs no node. Because that identifier cannot change for the life of a media line, the binding is stable for the whole session. The earlier claim in this row, that an audio source mapping command binds streams to places, is withdrawn: that command is now reserved and servers must not send it.
An outbound audio track is bound to the scene entirely by its SDP ``mid``: the server sets ``mid`` to the **decimal uid of the emitting node**
Earlier drafts carried an ``AudioEmitter`` node component and a per-stream *audio stream index*; both are withdrawn in favour of ``mid = node uid``.
input.controller: Input is negotiated rather than fixed. The server declares the inputs it expects as a list of identifier, type and path, where the path is a regular expression matched against the client's own control paths, and the client decides which physical control satisfies each one. A new declaration replaces the previous set wholesale and invalidates every earlier identifier.
Teleport has a dynamic input model: the server tells the client which inputs it expects, and the client reports their values each frame.

``path`` is a regular expression matched against the client-side control path (e.g. ``"/user/hand/left/input/trigger/value"`` on OpenXR). The client decides which physical control satisfies each regex; multiple controls may match, in which case the client picks one.
input.devcaps: Two mechanisms exist and one of them is empty. The server does tell the client which control inputs it expects, and the client declares its axes standard in the handshake, so the parts that matter for drawing and for input do flow. But the general capability bag on the connect message has no defined keys at all: it is an extension point with a rule that unknown keys must be ignored, and the conventions chapter says plainly that there is no formal capability negotiation beyond the rendering features flag and the session-description exchange. This row was previously scored native; that overstated it.

``capabilities`` (optional) is a free-form object advertising optional protocol features supported by the client. Unknown keys MUST be ignored, so the set can grow without a version bump. No keys are currently defined; the member is the extension point for future signaling-level capabilities.
There is currently no formal capability-negotiation handshake beyond ``RenderingFeatures`` and the WebRTC SDP exchange.
avatar.body: Avatars are negotiated rather than defined, and the negotiation has grown teeth since 2026-06-16. The server advertises a policy; the reference structure for that policy now carries first-class limits for accepted formats, file size, triangle count, height and width in metres, texture count and total texture pixels, a named skeleton, and a list of allowed licence tags. The client offers a URL with a declared format and byte count, and the server accepts or refuses and says whether delivery is by relay or by import. A relayed URL must end in a recognised extension because clients pick a decoder by extension; the extensions named are glTF binary, VRM and glTF. The avatar file's own contents remain out of scope.

The signalling chapter still says the identity member is an opaque string supplied for application-level authentication that may be empty. Both reference servers now treat that bare string as a legacy shape and accept an object with a provider, an issuer, a subject and a display name, sorted into three trust levels: anonymous, asserted, and verified. Asserted gets its own keyspace precisely because anyone can claim anyone's subject; verified keys derive only from the token's own claims and never from anything the client typed. One of the four is implemented; the rest are left to host applications. The implemented one is careful: the identity token is bound to a long-lived client key by putting the key's thumbprint in the token's nonce, and a live challenge-response proves the presenter holds that key, so a token captured by one server cannot be replayed at another. identity.capability: Permission is expressed as consent records inside the signed envelope, each naming the operations it allows, the purpose it allows them for, and a validity window; a separate pointer type declares delegated session authority for an agent. deliver.version: Versioning is explicit and the honesty about its cost is unusual. Each version has its own document set, its own context URL and its own conformance fixtures, v0.3 is named as the stable published reference and v0.4 as the production-candidate milestone, and the specification states outright that while the line is still 0.x a minor bump may include breaking changes in a new version folder. So a reader can always tell which vocabulary it is holding. What there is not is a negotiation mechanism: an evaluator either accepts a context value or does not. A deprecation policy does exist, in the optional extension: profile identifiers move through active, deprecated and sunset states in a registry published apart from the specification, an evaluator should warn on a deprecated profile but must not reject a manifest for it until the profile is sunset at a major-version boundary, and an identifier is never reused after deprecation.

sense.semantics: Mesh classification arrived in AR Foundation 6.4 and applies semantic labels to detected meshes, read back per mesh identifier. The label set is the indoor one — ceiling, door, floor, seat, table, wall, window and other — and it works only where the platform underneath supports it.

The AR Foundation meshing feature generates a mesh based on scans of the physical world.
sense.depth: The occlusion manager acquires per-frame images from the platform holding depth or stencil data, with an environment depth mode at four quality settings, optional temporal smoothing, and separate human segmentation stencil and depth textures. sense.occlusion: AR Foundation hides content behind physical objects, and offers both a cheap hard occlusion with a jagged edge and a costlier soft occlusion with a smooth one. It ships as a shader occlusion component and sample material inside the package, not in the engine core.

render.passthrough: The engine itself draws nothing of the real room; the AR Foundation package does. input.face: Face tracking is an AR Foundation subsystem, not part of the engine: a face manager component creates a trackable for each detected face, and the platform behind it decides what arrives. scene.navmesh: Navigation left the engine core and lives in the AI Navigation package, where navigation meshes are created from the scene's own geometry and baked into it, with links and dynamic obstacles on top. logic.namespace: Unity has the shape of the row without the guarantee. A package is named with a unique multi-part identifier in reverse domain notation, and a registry refuses a package whose manifest does not carry one, so within a registry two packages cannot collide. Nothing makes the name permanent or unclaimable outside that registry: the same identifier can be published to a different registry by somebody else, and a private registry can serve anything under it.
A unique multi-part identifier that conforms to the Unity Package Manager naming convention, which uses reverse domain name notation.
If these properties aren't present, either the registry refuses the package when it's published, or the Package Manager can't fetch or load the package.
deliver.moderation: Unity is an engine and an editor. Finished content leaves it as a built application, and any review that stands between that application and its audience belongs to the store it ships through, not to Unity. Unity does publish a first-party Moderation package (com.unity.services.moderation) for its Gaming Services, but it is for live player conduct: it manages players' safety in game text and voice chat and lets players report toxic players. That is action against people after release, not review of finished content before it reaches an audience, so the cell stays out of scope.
It combines the latest technologies and tools to deliver high-quality, high-performance experiences for all supported platforms.

The starting point of the ray in world coordinates.

scene.containment: USD has seven composition arcs — sublayers, references, payloads, variants, specializes, inherits and relocates — that let one scene embed another's structure with encapsulation: the internal referencing of a composed arc cannot be altered by stronger layers. It composes data, not running logic, and defines no boundary protocol for how messages cross between host and contained experience.

render.raster: A coding standard, not a renderer. It stops at decoding and reconstruction; the immersive video half describes a reference renderer and then says nobody has to follow it.
Text of ISO/IEC FDIS 23090-5 Visual Volumetric Video-based Coding and Video-based Point Cloud Compression (MPEG output document w19579)

This document specifies a generic mechanism for visual volumetric video coding, i.e. visual volumetric video-based coding. The generic mechanism may be used by applications targeting volumetric content, such as point clouds, immersive video with depth, mesh representations of visual volumetric frames, etc.
White paper on MPEG immersive video 2nd edition, ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 29/AG 3 N 234 (MPEG output document w25996)
A non-normative hypothetical reference renderer (HRR) is also described in the specification, but renderer implementations are not required to follow the operations of the HRR.

persist.world: Persistence in Verse is per person, not per world. A module-scoped map keyed by player, holding any type marked persistable, is saved and is loaded again automatically when that player next arrives. There is no world-scoped store: nothing in the reference persists the state of a place, only what each participant carried.

Persistable data is stored using module-scoped `weak_map(player, t)` variables, where `t` is any persistable type. When a player joins a game, their previously saved data is automatically loaded into all module-scoped variables of type `weak_map(player, t)`.

logic.namespace: This is the row's definition made into a language feature. Every module has a globally unique path shaped like a web address, and once a module is published at a path that path belongs to it forever with no other module able to claim it, so a dependency always resolves to the code it named. The domain part says who maintains it, an email-shaped identifier lets an individual hold a namespace without owning a domain, and strict backward compatibility rules keep the code behind a path usable as its author improves it.
Book of Verse: Modules and Paths

Persistent and unique identification : Once a module is published at a particular path, that path belongs to it forever. No other module can ever claim the same path, ensuring that dependencies always resolve to the correct code.
Book of Verse: Modules and Paths

The module system is designed to support the vision of a persistent, shared Metaverse where code can be published once and used by anyone, anywhere, with confidence that it will continue to work even as the original author updates and improves it.

render.raster: VRChat renders through the Unity game engine, and the evidence points to Unity's older "built-in" renderer rather than either of Unity's newer pipelines: the allowlist of components a world may contain includes Halo, LensFlare and FlareLayer, which only exist in the built-in renderer, and the supported add-on list names Post Processing Stack v2, which is also built-in-only. No VRChat page states the pipeline by name, and creators cannot add or reorder render passes.
FlareLayer Grid Halo HingeJoint LODGroup LensFlare
In VRChat, you can create and visit custom worlds, powered by Unity!
render.material: Surfaces are described by Unity materials and shaders. On phones and headsets running Android, creators may only use the small set of shaders VRChat ships. A world can push global shader values from a script, but only under names beginning with `_Udon`. None of this leaves VRChat: a material is only meaningful to a Unity build of the same version.
VRChat on Android or Quest only permits the shaders provided with the latest SDK on avatars.
the property name must be prefixed with '_Udon', or be the literal string '_AudioTexture.'
render.lighting: Full Unity lighting is available in worlds — real-time lights, baked lightmaps, light probes and reflection probes are all on the component allowlist. VRChat tells creators targeting phones and standalone headsets to bake everything and treat real-time lights as unaffordable.
It is not unreasonable to write off real-time lights completely, as they are very expensive.
render.post: Worlds may use Unity's Post Processing Stack v2, and VRChat ships a worked example of saving and reloading a player's post-processing choices. Post-processing is switched off entirely for avatars on Android and standalone headsets.
render.lod: Unity's LODGroup component is allowed in worlds, so a creator can swap mesh detail by distance. There is no streaming order: a world arrives as one packaged file that must finish downloading before you enter, and VRChat publishes nothing about sending nearer geometry first.
the VRChat SDK packages it into a Unity asset bundle and compresses it
render.splat: Nothing in VRChat renders Gaussian splats or radiance fields. The list of components a world may contain is closed and contains no splat or radiance-field renderer, and a creator cannot add one because custom engine code is not permitted.
The following is the complete list of scripts usable within worlds. Components that are not in this list will not work.
render.volumetric: No point-cloud, voxel or volumetric-video rendering. Unity particle systems are allowed but they draw sprites, not captured volumes. The closed component list has no volumetric renderer.
The following is the complete list of scripts usable within worlds. Components that are not in this list will not work.
render.text: Text in three dimensions is handled by TextMeshPro, which VRChat supports and documents with its own script pages for text, input fields and dropdowns. Unity's older TextMesh is also allowed.
enableWordWrapping Bool Controls whether words that exceed the available space will be put on a new line.
render.camera: A world declares where people appear and what camera settings they inherit through its scene descriptor, and scripts can read and change camera settings at run time. Cameras are also on the component allowlist. All of this is expressed in Unity terms and does not travel.
Settings from this camera are applied to users in the room. Can be an object in the scene or prefab.
An array of transforms used as reference for spawn points of the world
scene.graph: The scene is a Unity hierarchy of game objects and transforms. VRChat's own tooling confirms this — network identifiers are attached to individual game objects and are matched between builds by their path in the hierarchy.
A network ID is simply a number assigned to a GameObject.
scene.transform: VRChat states its convention plainly in its Open Sound Control pages: left-handed, Y is up, one unit is one metre, and rotations given as three angles are applied in the order Z, X, Y. This is Unity's convention. It is the opposite handedness to glTF and to most of USD, so any exchange in or out needs an axis flip.
Euler angles are in degrees and will be applied in order of Z, X, Y when used internally to produce a quaternion.
For vectors, it's the standard Unity format of +x right, +y up, and +z forward
scene.container: This is the single largest interoperability problem. A VRChat world or avatar is not shipped as a model file at all — the upload tool converts the Unity scene into a Unity asset bundle, a compiled binary keyed to one pinned Unity editor version and to one target platform. Separate bundles must be built and uploaded for Windows, for Android and for iOS. Nothing outside a matching Unity build can open the result, and there is no way to get an asset back out. VRChat reads FBX at authoring time inside Unity; it writes nothing any other tool can read.
the VRChat SDK packages it into a Unity asset bundle and compresses it

The version you're uploading depends on the originating project's build target. If you're on a project set up for Android, it'll upload for Quest. If the build target is Windows, then you're uploading a PC version.
Upgrading your version will result in content not loading once uploaded to VRChat - make sure to stay on our recommended version.
scene.geometry: Creators author meshes in a modelling tool and bring them into Unity as FBX. VRChat then publishes triangle budgets per platform, but the encoding that actually ships is Unity's internal mesh format inside the asset bundle. No standard geometry compression (such as Draco or meshopt) is offered, and there is no export path.
We recommend that you budget approximately 250,000 triangles for your world in total.
We recommend that you aim for under 10,000 triangles for your avatar.
scene.texture: Textures are compressed by Unity into the platform-specific bundle, which is why a separate upload is needed per platform. VRChat gives resolution guidance and total size caps but does not name the compressed texture formats it targets, and the compressed images cannot be read back out.
You should aim for using 1k (1024x1024) resolution textures at maximum.
You cannot upload or access worlds that exceed 100MB in size after build-time compression for VRChat on Android.
scene.material-x: There is no way to carry a material definition into or out of VRChat so another renderer can reproduce it. VRChat does have an internal degradation mechanism — a shader can declare a tag naming a simpler stand-in for the safety system to substitute — but that only picks from VRChat's own built-in shaders and means nothing outside VRChat. MaterialX is not mentioned anywhere.
When a shader is blocked by the Safety System, it is first checked for one of the internal pre-compiled shaders in this list.
scene.animation: Animation is Unity animation clips driven by Unity animator state machines, layered by VRChat into named "playable layers" for avatars. It is thoroughly documented, but the clips ship inside the asset bundle and cannot be exported.
When you create animations for your VRChat avatar, you'll utilize VRChat's 'Playable Layers.'
scene.skeleton: Rigs must be mapped to Unity's Humanoid bone set, which is a real shared convention across Unity content and is what VRM also builds on — but it is Unity's, not an openly published specification, and VRChat adds requirements of its own about which bone must parent which. Bones are named by mapping into Unity's slots rather than by an agreed public naming scheme.
Humanoid avatar must have head, hands and feet bones mapped.
make sure that Pelvis, Spine, Chest, Neck and Shoulders are mapped.
scene.morph: Shape deformation is Unity blend shapes on skinned meshes, used for mouth shapes and eyelids. The mouth-shape set is a named, shared one (see avatar.expression), but the blend shapes themselves are baked into the bundle and cannot be read by anything else.
We use the Oculus viseme index
scene.instancing: Scripts can draw one mesh many times in a single call, and VRChat tells creators to switch on Unity's per-material instancing option for performance on standalone headsets.
enable 'Enable GPU Instancing' on your materials
Draw the same mesh multiple times using GPU instancing
scene.compose: Searched creators.vrchat.com (all 311 pages in its site map), docs.vrchat.com (all 281 guide and release pages in its index) and the VRChat help centre (84 articles) for prefab, additive scene, scene loading, reference another world, override, layering on 2026-10-19; found Unity prefabs only as authoring tools, per-platform avatar overrides (a build-time substitute for the same avatar identifier) and per-player object copies. There is no layering, referencing or overriding of a scene from several sources. Unity prefabs exist while authoring, but the upload flattens everything into one compiled package, and a world cannot reference or pull in another creator's scene at run time. The only composition VRChat does at run time is giving each visitor a private copy of a designated object. The one override mechanism that does exist works the other way — it lets a creator substitute different content per platform for the same avatar identifier, which is a build-time variant, not a composition model.
the VRChat SDK packages it into a Unity asset bundle and compresses it
PlayerObjects allow you to automatically give each player who joins your world a copy of a GameObject, such as a flashlight, a health bar, or a sword.
After setting up per-platform overrides, the SDK will build and upload the "override" version of the avatar for each platform when you do a multi-platform build.
scene.units: One unit is one metre, stated outright in VRChat's tracking documentation, and avatar height is expressed and clamped in metres. This is the cleanest agreement VRChat has with the rest of the industry.
The height above 0 (Y component in transform position) of an avatar's viewpoint while in a T-Pose.
scene.licence: Searched creators.vrchat.com (all 311 pages in its site map), docs.vrchat.com (all 281 guide and release pages in its index) and the VRChat help centre (84 articles) for licence, license, licensing, permitted use, cloning on 2026-10-19; found only a creator instruction to hold a licence for third-party models before upload and the avatar-cloning switch (a public avatar can be cloned unless its wearer turns cloning off), and no licence or permitted-use field carried in an uploaded asset or readable by a recipient. VRChat has a marketplace with its own terms, but nothing about permitted use travels with the asset.
Ensure that you have a license to use the model in VRChat.
If the avatar is Public and the user has "Allow Avatar Cloning" enabled, the "Clone Avatar" button will be available.
scene.provenance: No signed record of authorship travels with content. The only link between an asset and its maker is the blueprint identifier held in VRChat's own database, which is an account record on VRChat's servers, not a signature a third party could check.
The unique id for the avatar or world
avatar.body: An avatar is not a portable body description. It is a compiled, per-platform Unity asset bundle behind a VRChat identifier. VRChat can consume a VRM file only after a community-written third-party converter turns it into a Unity project, and VRChat's own page warns that the VRM format is not natively supported. VRChat exports nothing. An avatar cannot leave VRChat, and a VRM, glTF or USD body cannot enter it without an out-of-band conversion step.
the VRChat SDK packages it into a Unity asset bundle and compresses it
VRoid Studio outputs avatars in the .vrm format, which isn't natively supported by Unity!
If you'd like to import a VRoid Studio model directly for use in VRChat, you may want to look into the community-created VRMtoVRChat converter for .vrm avatars.
avatar.skeleton: The bone structure is Unity's Humanoid mapping with VRChat's extra rules layered on top — head, hands and feet must be mapped, the chest must parent both shoulders and the neck, and eye bones must be axis-aligned a particular way. Animation transfers between VRChat avatars because of this, but the agreement is Unity's rather than an open published standard.
Humanoid avatar must have head, hands and feet bones mapped.
The Y axis should point up. The Z axis should point forward.
avatar.expression: Mouth shapes for speech use the fifteen-entry Oculus viseme index, which VRChat names explicitly — that part is a genuinely shared convention and is the most portable piece of VRChat's avatar model. Everything else about expression is VRChat-specific: a set of named animator values and a menu system that only VRChat understands, with a fixed budget of synchronised values per avatar.
We use the Oculus viseme index
Up to 8 controls can be added to a single menu.
avatar.retarget: Because avatars are mapped onto Unity's Humanoid skeleton, an animation authored for one body plays on another. VRChat also reports back how much of the wearer's real body is being tracked, from unknown through hands-only up to full-body, so animation logic can adapt.
Humanoid avatar must have head, hands and feet bones mapped.
avatar.wearable: There is no wearable or attachment format. An avatar ships as one indivisible package, so a hat or a bag authored for one avatar cannot be transferred to another at run time. Worlds can hand out spawnable objects, but VRChat says scripts cannot even see those objects, and they are not worn on the body.
Udon programs in your world cannot reference items. If one of your scripts finds an item, it appears as a null object.
avatar.lod: This is one of VRChat's strongest areas. Every avatar is scored against published numeric budgets and given a rank; viewers can refuse anything above a chosen rank. Above that sits a generated stand-in ("impostor") and below it a plain substitute avatar. VRChat generates the impostor itself, including automatically when an avatar was only built for Windows and is being viewed on a standalone headset. None of these reduced forms can be exported.
Impostors are avatar body doubles, allowing you to see avatars in situations where you would typically see a fallback avatar or robot.
avatars built for Windows cannot be displayed on Quest/Android because of the difference in platform build processes.
Aim for Good ranking. If you can't hit that, Medium is perfectly fine.
avatar.identity: An avatar is bound to a VRChat account and nothing else. Both carry VRChat identifiers — the avatar an `avtr_` value, the person a `usr_` value — and the binding is a row in VRChat's database. There is no verifiable credential, no decentralised identifier, and no way for another operator to check the binding.
physics.rigid: Worlds get Unity's rigid-body physics. Rigidbody is on the component allowlist and there is a dedicated component that shares an object's position, rotation, scale and rigid-body state with everyone in the instance. It is switched off entirely on Android and standalone headsets for avatars.
the Transform (position, rotation scale) and Rigidbody (physics) of the object you put it on
physics.collision: The full Unity collider set is allowed in worlds — box, sphere, capsule, mesh, terrain and wheel. VRChat also fixes which numbered layers collide with which, and overwrites any change a creator makes to that table on upload, leaving only a block of ten layers free for creators.
If you change the collision matrix, rename, or remove built-in layers, your changes will be overridden when you upload your world to VRChat.
Layers 22-31 are unused 'User' Unity layers. You can edit them freely, and changes to these layers will not be discarded when you build & upload your world.
physics.joint: Unity's joint components — hinge, fixed, spring, character and configurable — are all on the world allowlist. As with rigid bodies, joints are disabled for avatars on Android and standalone headsets.
physics.soft: Unity's cloth component is allowed in worlds and on avatars for desktop computers, but is switched off for avatars on Android and standalone headsets. VRChat's own secondary-motion system (see below) is a bone chain, not a true soft body.
physics.trigger: Regions that fire when someone enters are well supported. A script receives separate events for a person's capsule entering, staying inside and leaving a trigger region, plus equivalents for physical contact and for particle hits. VRChat warns that the physical-contact events only fire when the object moves into the person, not the reverse.
OnPlayerTriggerEnter is called when a player's capsule enters a Trigger Collider.
These events WILL NOT be called when a player 'walks into' a stationary object.
physics.determinism: VRChat makes no determinism claim anywhere. Its networking model is the opposite: one client owns an object, simulates it and sends the result, and everyone else receives values. Where an owner's updates are lost, VRChat says it guesses the missing values rather than re-simulating them, which rules out matching outcomes on different machines.
intermediary value approximation to recover lost data
audio.source: Sound is placed in the world with a VRChat component wrapping Unity's audio source. It exposes a volume boost, a near radius where fall-off begins, a far radius where the sound reaches silence, and a radius that makes a sound seem to come from a region rather than a point.
The far radius, in meters, where volume falls off to silence. By default, it is set to 40m
Falloff of audio intensity is roughly inverse-square by default.

net.replication: Well documented and precisely bounded. Scripts mark variables to be shared; each script may send about eleven kilobytes a second; a continuously shared update is capped at roughly two hundred bytes, a manually triggered one at roughly two hundred and eighty thousand. Every shareable type is listed with its size in bytes. All of this is VRChat's own scheme with no published wire format.
Udon scripts can send out about 11 kilobytes per second.
The process of packing and sending the variable is called Serialization, and Deserialization is when the data is received and unpacked.
net.authority: Clear and simple: one person owns each networked object and only that person may change its shared values. The first person into an empty instance owns everything not otherwise assigned. Ownership can be requested and transferred, and a script can approve or refuse the request. There is no server-authoritative option — authority always sits on somebody's computer.
The first player to join an instance becomes the owner of all networked objects by default.

On the privacy side, VRChat requires the person to consent before it starts sending tracking data out to a discovered companion program. logic.script: World rules are written in Udon, which is VRChat's own language running on VRChat's own bytecode interpreter. Creators usually write a restricted dialect of C# which the tool compiles down to Udon assembly, and VRChat states plainly that this dialect follows no version of the C# standard. Generic classes, interfaces, method overloads and properties do not work. The compiled program only runs inside VRChat and can never be moved to another runtime. The compiler itself is open source under a permissive licence, which is a real positive, but it only ever emits VRChat bytecode.
VRChat Udon is technically a virtual machine running bytecode compiled from Udon Assembly.
UdonSharp is not conformant to any version of the C# language specification.
The Udon VM and Udon Assembly
The Udon VM is a bytecode interpreter designed to run compiled Udon Graph programs.
UdonSharp is a compiler that translates C# to Udon assembly, so you can create interactive VRChat worlds by writing C# code.
logic.behaviour: VRChat has a visual node graph for interactivity, which sounds like the portable declarative behaviour other systems are converging on — but it is not. The graph compiles in the background into the same VRChat-only assembly as everything else, so the interactivity does not travel with an asset; it is baked into a proprietary bytecode blob inside a Unity asset bundle.
VRChat Udon is technically a virtual machine running bytecode compiled from Udon Assembly.

logic.sandbox: This is VRChat's strongest capability. Guest content cannot run arbitrary code: worlds and avatars may only use components from two published closed allowlists, anything else is refused at upload, and all scripting goes through the interpreter rather than the host runtime. Reaching the network is gated by an address allowlist that a person must deliberately override. On top of that sits the trust and shield system that decides how much of a stranger's avatar to render at all.

logic.budget: VRChat publishes hard numbers for almost everything guest content may consume, which is rare and valuable. Network traffic is capped per script and per update. On top of that the performance rank system turns the whole avatar budget into a single score that viewers can filter on.

scene.skeleton: Binding and skinning are glTF's; the part VRM adds is the mapping from each named human bone to a glTF node, which is what makes the rig readable by a runtime that never saw the model. Bone transforms are constrained further: scale must be uniform and positive.

All node transforms must be in a positive uniform scale.
scene.morph: The shape deformation itself is glTF's morph targets, which VRM does not change. What VRM adds is naming: expressions bind groups of morph targets to an agreed name, and because glTF has no name for a morph target the specification recommends putting one in the mesh extras. Missing: VRM specifies no encoding of its own.
scene.animation: A VRM file carries no animation: the core says the glTF animations and cameras arrays are not used. Humanoid motion lives in a separate file defined by VRMC_vrm_animation 1.0, which reuses glTF's own keyframe machinery and adds the mapping to named bones, expressions and gaze.

scene.geometry: Mesh encoding is glTF's and VRM specifies none of it. What VRM adds is two restrictions aimed at making models load the same everywhere: stored tangents may be left out and recalculated, and morph target tangents should be neither exported nor imported.

scene.texture: Image encoding is glTF's. VRM adds one restriction and it is a narrow one: the model thumbnail must be square and must be a jpg or png supported by glTF's core, with extension formats forbidden. Missing: nothing is said about texture compression for the model's own textures.
Use of other formats using extensions is not allowed.
scene.transform: Handedness and axis order come from glTF and VRM restates none of it. VRM does add the convention glTF lacks for characters: in the rest pose the model stands facing positive Z, symmetrical about X, arms out along X, and every node scale must be uniform and positive. A binding to the newer interface exists as an editor's draft that has never been published on the technical reports track, so today a page cannot use the newer graphics interface in an immersive session.
WebXR Device API, W3C Candidate Recommendation Draft, 9 June 2026
An XRWebGLLayer is a layer which provides a WebGL framebuffer to render into, enabling hardware accelerated rendering of 3D graphics to be presented on the XR device.
WebXR Device API, W3C Candidate Recommendation Draft, 9 June 2026
While this specification only defines the XRWebGLLayer layer, future extensions to the spec are expected to add additional layer types
WebXR/WebGPU Binding Module - Level 1, Editor's Draft, 12 August 2026
This specification describes support for rendering content for a WebXR session with WebGPU.

geo.anchor-local: Through the WebXR Anchors Module, which asks the device to keep correcting a placed pose as its map of the room improves. Note the status carefully: this module is an editor's draft dated 27 April 2026 and does not appear on the Working Group's publications page, which lists only Candidate Recommendation Drafts and Working Drafts (checked 2026-10-19), so it is weaker than every Working Draft in the family.
WebXR Anchors Module, Editor's Draft, 27 April 2026 (never published on the W3C technical reports track)

WebXR Anchors module enables applications to ask the underlying XR system to track changes to a particular three-dimensional pose (position and orientation) as the system’s understanding of the world changes.
Page contents Candidate Recommendation Drafts Working Drafts
geo.anchor-shared: Half met, and the missing half is in the specification rather than in implementations. Persistence works: an anchor can be given a handle, listed, restored and deleted across sessions. It is bounded twice over, to one device and to one web site, and the identifier must be known only to that site. Sharing is entirely absent: the words share, shared, sharing, cross-device and cloud do not appear in the anchors document at all, and the module's own explainer still lists persisting and sharing as out of scope even though persistence has since been added. Sharing between devices is an open request in the module's issue tracker.
WebXR Anchors Module, Editor's Draft, 27 April 2026 (never published on the W3C technical reports track)
This map is populated and stored by the XR device and restricted to only the set of persistent anchors created and not yet destroyed by any XRSession on origin.
WebXR Anchors Module, Editor's Draft, 27 April 2026 (never published on the W3C technical reports track)

scene.graph: Clause 4 defines the scene graph, the transformation hierarchy and the rules for ancestors and descendants, including that a node may not be its own ancestor.

X3D includes the notion of local coordinate systems , defined in terms of transformations from ancestor coordinate systems. The coordinate system in which the root nodes are displayed is called the world coordinate system .
scene.transform: One fixed convention, right-handed with the vertical axis up, stated in the concepts clause. It matches the common asset format, which makes exchange between them straightforward.

ISO/IEC 19775 uses a Cartesian, right-handed, three-dimensional coordinate system. By default, the viewer is on the Z-axis looking down the -Z-axis toward the origin with +X to the right and +Y straight up.
scene.units: Metres by default, with base units for angle, force, mass and time each tied to an international units standard. Unlike the common asset format, a file may declare a different length unit, so a reader must honour the declaration rather than assume metres.

ISO/IEC 19775 defines the initial base unit of measure of the world coordinate system to be metres. However, the world coordinate units may be modified by specifying a different length unit using the UNIT statement.
scene.container: The architecture part defines the scene contents; the byte-level encodings that carry them sit in a companion part of the same standard, not in this document. Cite the encodings separately if the question is about file bytes.
This document is Edition 4 of ISO/IEC 19775-1, Extensible 3D (X3D).
scene.geometry: Three separate clauses cover rendering primitives, three-dimensional geometry and two-dimensional geometry, with a further clause for engineering geometry.
Geometry3D component provides a detailed specification of the Geometry3D component of X3D.
scene.texture: A texturing clause plus separate clauses for three-dimensional textures, cube maps and texture projection.
Texturing component provides a detailed specification of the Texturing component of X3D including advanced material characteristics.
scene.material-x: The physically based material node was deliberately aligned with the common asset format's material, and the standard says so in a note. This is the clearest worked example on the whole map of two standards bodies making an exchange lossless on purpose.

The physical material properties of X3D are also deliberately consistent with the glTF 2.0 material definition. Effectively, converting (in either direction) between X3D PhysicalMaterial and glTF 2.0 material definitions is equivalent.
scene.animation: Animation is expressed as interpolator nodes driven by a time sensor and wired to targets by routes, rather than as a clip. That makes it flexible inside the file and awkward to lift out as a portable clip.
Interpolation component provides a detailed specification of the Interpolation component of X3D.
scene.skeleton: The humanoid animation clause defines a joint, a segment and an attachment site, giving a bone hierarchy with defined semantics rather than an anonymous tree.
26.3.1 HAnimDisplacer 26.3.2 HAnimHumanoid 26.3.3 HAnimJoint 26.3.4 HAnimMotion 26.3.5 HAnimSegment 26.3.6 HAnimSite

avatar.skeleton: The humanoid clause binds a separate international standard for humanoid animation into this one, so bone names and structure are agreed rather than left to convention. This is the answer that the common asset format still lacks.
The HAnim component of X3D defines the node bindings and other specifics for implementing ISO/IEC 19774 (see [I19774] ) within X3D.
avatar.body: A humanoid node gathers the joints, segments and sites into one figure, which is the portable description of a body. It does not specify clothing, wearables or expression sets.
This component maps the functionality defined in ISO/IEC 19774 to a set of X3D nodes. The semantics for these nodes are as specified therein.

render.lighting: A dedicated clause gives the lighting equations and the shadow requirements, so the standard says how a lit surface should look rather than leaving it to each reader.
Lighting component defines lighting and shadow requirements for visually rendering X3D models.
render.volumetric: Clause 41 covers rendering volumetric data sets inside a scene, which no other subject on the asset side of this map has in a ratified form.
Volume rendering component provides a detailed specification for the rendering of volumetric data sets as part of X3D worlds.
render.gpu-api: A programmable shaders clause with three named shading language bindings in the annexes. This is the opposite choice from the common asset format, which stays deliberately neutral. Shader source in a file is by nature not portable across graphics interfaces.
geo.crs: Every node that carries geographic coordinates has a field naming its spatial reference frame, with geodetic, transverse mercator and geocentric forms, a table of ellipsoids and a geoid for mean sea level.

All the X3D nodes that allow inclusion of geographic coordinates support a field called geoSystem . This field is used to specify the particular spatial reference frame that will be used for the geospatial coordinates in that node.
geo.pose: A geographic location node places content at a point on the Earth and orients it to the local frame, with the vertical axis up and one horizontal axis pointing north. Note it defines its own way of saying this rather than referencing the separate pose standard from the geospatial consortium.

axis is the up direction for that local area (the normal to the tangent plane on the ellipsoid), −Z points towards the north pole, and +X is east.
geo.tiles: A terrain level-of-detail node holds up to four child addresses in a quadtree and manages loading and unloading, which is tiled terrain streaming written into an international standard long before the tiled formats in current use.

The GeoLOD node provides a terrain-specialized form of the LOD node. It is a grouping node that specifies two different levels of detail for an object using a tree structure, where 0 to 4 children can be specified
logic.behaviour: Interactivity travels inside the file as a graph of one-way connections between fields, changeable while running, with a defined propagation order. This is a ratified answer to the same question the common asset format is still trying to ratify.
The event model of X3D allows the declaration of unidirectional ROUTE connections between fields and a model for the propagation of events along those connections.
logic.script: Clause 29 defines a script node with an initialize and shutdown lifecycle, event handling and field access. The language bindings themselves live in a companion part of the standard.
This includes how Script nodes are used to effect changes in X3D worlds.
logic.sandbox: Some real precautions are written into the text: a model may not include itself, directly or indirectly, and readers are told not to honour such loops; automatic reloading carries an explicit warning. What is missing is everything general. There is no isolation model for scripts, no permission model and no resource budget, so a scene that runs a script is trusting it.
X3D browsers shall not honor self-referential loading of Inline model loops in order to avoid security vulnerabilities.
net.replication: Clause 28 binds a long-standing distributed simulation protocol into the scene, with entity state, transmitter, receiver and signal messages. Two cautions: it shares platform-level simulation entities, not general world state, and it lives in the fullest profile only. It is nonetheless a ratified international standard for sharing state between running instances, which the rest of this map does not have.
X3D 4.0 clause 28 Distributed interactive simulation component

The Distributed Interactive Simulation (DIS) component provides networked interoperability with the IEEE DIS protocol (see [IEEE1278] and [SISO] ) for sharing state and conducting real-time platform-level simulations across multiple host computers.
scene.compose: A scene can pull in another file, and named values can be imported and exported across that boundary; prototypes let a definition live in a separate file. What is missing is override: there is no way for one source to change a value inside another, and no layering with a strength order. That is the gap the scene description standard was built to fill.

deliver.conformance: A whole clause on conformance, separately for files, generators and readers, with a base profile that sets minimum requirements and stated aims of eliminating arbitrary subsets and promoting uniform tests. Very little else on this map has this.

persist.world: Nothing survives a restart because nothing is ever written back. The standard's own list of what an X3D application does covers the world coordinate space, the objects in it, hyperlinks, behaviours and connection to external code, and stops there; there is no store, no save, and no notion of a world that is resumed. The two places the word persistent appears both mean the state of a node's fields while the scene is running, not across a restart. Clause 28 shares live entity state between hosts and keeps none of it. Checked clauses 4 Concepts, 7 Core, 8 Time, 9 Networking, 28 Distributed interactive simulation and 29 Scripting.

Each X3D application: implicitly establishes a world coordinate space for all objects defined, as well as all objects included by the application; explicitly defines and composes a set of 2D, 3D and multimedia objects; can specify hyperlinks to other files and applications; can define object behaviours; can connect to external modules or applications via programming and scripting languages.
The field values can be read or written and are persistent across method call, and changes to a field can notify the node through its update method.
persist.prefs: There is one settings vocabulary in the standard and it does not belong to the user. Clause 9.2.4 names nine browser options, among them antialiasing, shading mode, render quality while moving and texture quality, passed in at start-up and held either as parameters on the embedding tag or, in the standard's own words, in an application-specific configuration file or registry entry. Support for them is recommended rather than required, none of them is an accessibility choice, nothing ties a setting to a person, and nothing carries one to another world or another reader. Navigation type, viewpoint and headlight settings in clause 23 belong to the scene, and the reader's own interface for them is explicitly left implementation-dependent. Checked clauses 4 Concepts, 7 Core, 9 Networking, 23 Navigation and 24 Environmental effects.

Browser options may be set as HTML PARAM values within an EMBED or OBJECT tag if the X3D browser is running as an embedded control within a World Wide Web browser, or through an application-specific mechanism such as a configuration file or system registry entry if the X3D browser is running within some other containing application. Support for X3D browser options is not required but is strongly recommended.
avatar.wearable: Half of this is answered, and answered by name. An HAnimSite is a grouping node whose stated second purpose is an attachment point for accessories such as jewelry and clothing; it takes children, so a hat or a strap hangs beneath it, and the humanoid node keeps a list of its sites. The names come from the humanoid animation standard that this clause binds in, so the same point means the same thing in two files from two authors, which is more than the common asset format offers. What is missing is the item. Nothing defines a wearable as a separate thing that can move from one avatar to another, there are no fitting or scaling rules for bodies of different shape, there is no ownership, and there is no way to put something on or take it off. A garment travels only inside the humanoid that already carries it.

An HAnimSite node serves three purposes. The first is to define an "end effecter" location that can be used by an inverse kinematics system. The second is to define an attachment point for accessories such as jewelry and clothing.
identity.exchange: Nothing in the forty-two clauses asks for or presents a credential. The words credential, authentication, certificate, password and authorization do not occur anywhere in this part; permission and privacy occur once each, in a single security sentence on the microphone node that hands the question to the host application. The only identifiers the standard itself defines are simulation numbers in clause 28, a site, an application and an entity, and those are allocation conventions inside one exercise rather than proof of who anyone is. Checked clauses 6 Conformance, 7 Core, 9 Networking including the browser options table, 16 Sound, 28 Distributed interactive simulation and 29 Scripting.

net.time: The time half is specified better here than in most of this map. Zero is midnight Greenwich time on 1 January 1970, absolute times are seconds in double precision, a whole clause defines the reader's clock and the nodes that follow it, processing an event at a given time may only produce events at that time or later, and everything in one event cascade carries the same timestamp and is treated as simultaneous. Ordering inside one reader is therefore exact and written down. The shared half is absent. The clock is that reader's own, the one networked clause stamps an arriving message with the moment it reached the local machine, and nothing in the standard agrees a clock between two hosts, estimates the offset between them or orders events across them.
All events generated during a given event cascade are assigned the same timestamp as the initial event, since all are considered to happen instantaneously.

identity.root: The only base identifiers are the simulation numbers in the networking-for-simulation clause, a site, an application and an entity, valid for the length of one exercise. persist.inventory: A scene has no concept of a user holding items, and nothing is written back from a running scene to anywhere that outlasts it. avatar.expression: The humanoid component has a displacer node holding named vertex offsets with a weight, and its own example is the vertices of the left eyebrow, so the mechanism for facial shape changes exists. avatar.retarget: The humanoid component carries motion data per named joint and channel, and the joint names come from the shared humanoid standard, so a motion can in principle be played on another figure that uses the same joints. Missing: any rule in this part for adjusting a motion to a body of different proportions; the separate humanoid standard was not read.
Raw motion data, for example, motion capture data, details the number of frames, the frame display time, and the parameter values for the motion from each channel at each frame.
avatar.lod: The humanoid and motion nodes carry a level-of-articulation field with values from minus one to four, and the skin field accepts a level-of-detail node, so reduced figures can be expressed. geo.indoor: Geographic positioning, dataset metadata and terrain are specified, but nothing describes the structure of interior spaces such as floors, rooms, openings or connections. render.material: The shape component gives three lighting models for a surface: a Phong material, a physically based material (with metallic and roughness terms) and an unlit material, with texture bindings for each and an alpha mode, plus shader nodes for anything beyond them. The physically based node was aligned with the common asset format's material.
render.raster: The standard defines the visual result of drawing, through clipping planes, lighting equations, alpha modes and an ordered list of layers rendered one over another. Missing: any render graph or pass structure; how geometry becomes pixels is left to the implementation.
The 3D graphics rendering pipeline uses an implicit step of trimming objects that are partially in the view frustum called clipping.
The LayerSet node specifies a list of layers and a rendering order.
render.post: Fog blends the colour of every object toward a fog colour by distance from the camera, which is blending of object colours and not a stage applied after the main render pass, so no part of the definition is met. Searched Part 1 of ISO/IEC 19775-1 version 4.0, 57 clause, profile and front-matter pages, for post-process, bloom, tone map, blur, depth of field, screen space and after render on 2026-10-20; the only tone-map hits are ToneMappedVolumeStyle, a volume rendering style, and the only blur hit is MotionBlur, an optional browser-option flag (Boolean, default false) with no post-pass stage defined.

render.splat: Captured data can be drawn as point sets or as volume data, but there is no splat primitive and no radiance-field representation or rendering rule. Searched Part 1 of ISO/IEC 19775-1 version 4.0, all component clauses and annexes, for splat, Gaussian, radiance field, NeRF and neural on 2026-10-20; no match.

render.color: One colour space is fixed for the whole standard: RGB with each component from zero to one. Missing: any way to declare a different colour space, a transfer curve or a wider output range on an image, texture or surface, so a receiver has nothing to convert from.

render.layer: The layering component gives an ordered set of independent layers, each with its own viewpoint and navigation and a viewport that confines it to a sub-region of the display, composed in the stated order. Missing: layers that are images with their own shape, pose and blending properties handed to a compositor; the layers here are sub-scenes.

tooltips.render.raster: This row asks whether a subject turns scene geometry into pixels itself: the loop that draws triangles onto the display, and the order its passes run in. Built in means the subject owns that loop. Thirteen do, two are partial, and seven score out of scope and are hidden, because a delivery format says what to draw, not how a frame is assembled. Most of these pipelines are engine-private, so a filled cell is not a shared pass structure.
tooltips.render.gpu-api: This row records which driver-level graphics interface a renderer speaks: Vulkan, Metal, Direct3D or WebGPU. Built in means the choice sits in the subject's own core. Eleven score that way, one reaches it only through an extension, two are partial and two are out of scope and hidden, so the answer here is settled. Read it beside the immersive session row: both read supported and still do not compose, so a filled row is never proof that two systems will work together.
tooltips.render.material: This row is the numbers a surface carries so light behaves the same on it in two renderers: base colour, metal, roughness. Built in means the subject defines that surface model itself. Twelve do, one reaches it through an extension, one is partial, three are out of scope and hidden, and one conflicts. Horizon Worlds reads a surface's shading model out of the spelling of the material's name, so a material cannot survive the trip in either direction.
tooltips.render.lighting: This row covers shadows, bounced light and probes, baked ahead of time or worked out live. Nine subjects have a light model built in, seven are partial, one is out of scope and hidden, and Horizon Worlds conflicts by baking light into mesh vertex colours. One reaches it only through an extension: the common transfer format has ratified punctual lights and no shadows, probes or baked light, while the older ratified scene standard gives the equations in its core. Check the older standard first.
tooltips.render.post: Post-processing is what happens after the main draw: bloom, tone mapping, anti-aliasing. Seven subjects have it built in, two reach it only through separate packages, one is partial, one is absent, and four are out of scope and hidden. Read supported carefully here: on this row it often means an add-on rather than engine core, and Resonite's effects are a viewer setting that no scene can carry with it.
tooltips.render.lod: This row is choosing how much detail to draw, and what to send down the wire first. Six subjects have both halves built in, one reaches it through a single-vendor extension, ten are partial, and three are out of scope and hidden. Partial here almost always means detail selection works and send order does not. It is the one rendering row settled at connection time, because once geometry streams the sender and the receiver have to agree on the order.
tooltips.render.splat: This row draws a captured place as many soft blobs instead of triangles. Four subjects have it built in, one reaches it through addons, two are partial, seven are absent, and three are out of scope and hidden. The absent ones are engines and platforms that could carry such a renderer and ship none. The extension that would move splats between tools is at release candidate stage, announced 2026-02-03 and not ratified, and it says how to store splats, not how to draw them.
tooltips.render.volumetric: This row covers point clouds, voxels and volumetric video rather than surfaces. Two subjects have it built in, one reaches it through a plug-in, ten are partial, two are absent, and three are out of scope and hidden. Partial nearly always means the same thing here: a static point cloud can be shown, while volumetric video is missing and often the voxel path too. Do not read a partial cell as support for captured moving volume.
tooltips.render.text: This row is words that stay legible inside a scene, with real fonts and layout. Nine subjects have it built in, two reach it through addons, three are partial, one is absent, and three are out of scope and hidden. It matters because a shared world that cannot draw the same label twice cannot carry a sign, a menu or a name badge across a boundary. One limit: the TeleportXR claim on this row rests on local files and has no public source yet.
tooltips.render.camera: This row is how a viewpoint is defined, attached to something, and moved between. Fourteen subjects have it built in, eight are partial, and one is out of scope and hidden, so the answer here is settled. One caution: the transfer formats and the immersive runtimes each define a camera and they are not the same object. A file's camera carries projection settings, while a runtime hands the application a viewer pose and one projection per view every frame.
tooltips.scene.graph: The scene graph is the tree that says what exists, what it hangs off, and where it sits. Seventeen subjects have one built in, one is partial, one conflicts, and four are out of scope and hidden, so the answer here is settled. Keep the qualifier: in the major engines the tree is the engine's own and no outside tool reads it, yet three ratified standards define one natively. The RP1 and TeleportXR claims here rest on local files with no public source.
tooltips.scene.transform: This row is handedness, which axis points up, and the order transforms multiply in. Twelve subjects settle it in their core, eight are partial, one is absent, and four conflict. This is where silent failure lives. The draft avatar format writes its matrices the other way round from the common transfer format, and one platform is left-handed with Y up and positive Z forward, so a converter that copies the numbers straight across loads with no error and places the thing wrongly. TeleportXR's claim has no public source.
tooltips.scene.container: This row is the single file you hand somebody: the binary transfer file, the zipped scene package, the platform bundle. Twelve subjects have one built in, two reach it through an extension, seven are partial, six are out of scope and hidden, and four conflict. Horizon Worlds, Roblox and VRChat compile an upload into a private bundle nobody else can open, and TeleportXR states it has no file format at all. The RP1 claim rests on local files with no public source.
tooltips.scene.geometry: This row is how a mesh is written down and squeezed: vertex data, index data, compression. Nine subjects have it built in, ten are partial, one is absent, three are out of scope and hidden, and one conflicts. Partial usually means meshes move while the compressed forms do not. The conflict is Resonite: every mesh that enters is converted to its own representation and the link to the source file is dropped, so it cannot give the file back. TeleportXR's claim has no public source.
tooltips.scene.texture: This row is the image formats and compressed forms a target device can actually decode. Eleven subjects have it built in, nine are partial, and two are out of scope and hidden, so the answer here is settled. The thing to notice is that this is decided by the device rather than by a standard: one asset usually has to carry two or three compressed forms to reach a phone, a desktop and a headset. TeleportXR's claim here has no public source.
tooltips.scene.material-x: Material exchange is handing a material from one renderer to another without the surface changing. Two subjects have it built in, one through an addon, seven partial, six absent, two conflicting, three out of scope and hidden. The absent ones could carry a neutral material description and none does. The best case is here: the older ratified scene standard says its material is deliberately consistent with the common transfer format's, so converting either way is equivalent, unlike the lossy partial scores. TeleportXR's claim has no public source.
tooltips.scene.animation: This row is keyframes and clips: what moves, when, and how it is worked out between keys. Thirteen subjects have it built in, one reaches it through a separate file, four are partial, one is absent, one conflicts, and three are out of scope and hidden, so the answer here is settled.
